div.head: WORKINGMEN'S DEMONSTRATION AT RUNCORN. SPEECIIES BY MR. BRUNNER AND MR. DEACON.
div.p: WORKINGMEN'S DEMONSTRATION AT RUNCORN. SPEECIIES BY MR. BRUNNER AND MR. DEACON.

A demonstration of working-men in support of Mr. J. T. Brunner, the Liberal candidate, was held at Runcorn on Saturday afternoon. Devonshire Square was the place of assembly, and at half-past three several hundred people had arrived there. Some delay was caused by the non-arrival of Mr. Brunner, who had been unavoidably detained. To the music of three bands, the Weston, the Wet ton Point, and Runcorn Roman Catholic, about 400 working-men marched from the Square, and by the time they had reached Delph Bridge the numbers had swollen to 1,500. In the ranks were displayed such sentiments as "Vote for Brunner and the G.O.M "; "Justice, Equality, Liberty"; "Be Just, and Fear not"; "The Tories say they are the friends of the workingman. Do not believe it, and vote for Brunner, the true friend of the workingmen." Hundreds had walked to the meeting place, the field opposite Run- corn Soap and Alkali Company's Works, and when the proceedings commenced about four o'clock there would ,be an audience of about 3,000 persons. A luny was I used as a platform, and Mr. A. R. Norman occupied the chair. He was supported by Mr. Brunner (who was accompanied by Mrs. and Miss Brunner), Mr. H. Wade Deacon (Liberal candidate for Widnes), Cotnacillor Flood (Warrington), Mr. P. Speakman, C.C., Messrs. T. Clegg, T. Lea,E. Gatley,F. Hartland, J.Withington, A. Fletcher, and others. The Chairtnan, in opening the proceedings, said in two previous elections Mr. Brunner had

itOUTED A LOCAL dENTLEMEN and one who although not outside the county was out- side the district, in the shape of Lord Henry Grosvenor. Now his opponent came from not only outside the dis- trict, but outside the county, and he hoped that they would rout him in a more severe form than they had the gentlemen before, and that would put an end to the opposition to Mr. Brunner. (Cheers.) Alluding to Home Mile, the Chairman said he supported it because the Irish people demanded it through a very large majority of their representatives in the House of Com- mons, and the' voice of the people in, to be obeyed. As to the statement that the Roman Catholics would crush the Protostanta-knd Nonconformists, the Duke of Norfolk, a representative Roman Catholic, opposed Home Rule because the Roman Catholic Church in Ireland would suffer. This showed" the absurdity.: of the whole charge. He quoted , facts to show that the persecution and Intolerance at the present time was all on the side of the Protestants. The cry of Catholic intolerance was baseless and was made to catch the votes of the Protes- tants and Nonconformists in this country. (Cheers,) Mr. Brunner, who was received with loud cheers, said they had • • ' •

div.head: XNOWN DIM A GOOD MANY YEARS
div.p: XNOWN DIM A GOOD MANY YEARS

and they would know that it was not his habit to put his convenience before theirs, and they would know therefore that he was not in Devonshire Square in time simply because it was impossible.,Hetvas that morning in a town in north Lancashire, in which he had taken considerable interest for the last few Months. Some of them would have been guessing what was the name of the town—it was Blackburn. (Laughter.) He had had several pressing invitations tor and speak in Blackburn, and he could not resist the temptation when he found that his tyrant, Mr. Wm. Handley, had left a night open, so he went on the previous day. His coming had appeared to have created some interest ',and he found in the Exchange A meeting of over 3,000 determined Liberals— (cheers)—cheering .as they did for the Grand Old Man, cheering as they did for the Liberal Candidate, and determined, as they were, he believed, to put the Liberal candidate at the head Of the poll. ' (Cheers.) Blackburn had been known to active politicians for a quarter of a centuty as the most corrupt town in -the North of England, and he went to Elackburr on the previous day five and a half hours before the meeting began in order to learn something of Blackburn political tricks, and he I had come back from Blackburn' with, all his cdurse mapped out for him from them until the evening of the poll. (Hear, hear.) 'He had made up his mind that, come what might, they would have none of the

DIRTY TRICKS OF BLACKBURN in Northwich Division. (Cheers.) It was old business he had to tell them, and he gloried in it that the first vote he gaye in South West Lancashire was a vote in 1868 for the Grand Old Man. (Cheers.) Mr. Gladstone was defeated by a gang of corrupt scoundrels from Blackburn, (Cheers.) These Blackburn men personated absent voters at the election to Such an extent that Mr. Glad- stone was'defeated. It was not the men of South West Lancashire who declined the offer of his services ; it was scoundrels from Blackburn who dishonestly 'personated South West Lancashire %%4;73 and voted in their name and thus turned the seale, and Cross, and Blackburn were returned in his place. He heard not long ago a -Reify from their friend Mr. Waddy. (Cheers.) That might at this time interest them. When Mr. Waddy was contesting Sheffield he heard that a number of per- sonators were coming, and he set a number of men from Blackburn to watch these personators, with the result that one was brought before two of her Majesty's judges and he was sent into retirement, for some time to lodge at her Majesty's expense. (Laughter.) But the amus- ing part of the story was this—that the leader of the gang whom Mr. Waddy employed from Blackburn, to track these personators was one evening looking over the register. At this time Sheffield was Buffeting from depression of trade, and a very large number of houses were empty. As Mr. Waddy turned over the register page by page, there was the word empty, empty, empty over and over again. This man from Blackburn said " What a l•vely register! We could personate 2,000 here." Now he (Mr. Brunner) wanted them to be good MOugh to inform the Tory canvassers and the Tory officials that at this coming election on July 18th, there would De a Blackburn man

div.head: WATCHING EVERY POLLING PLACE
div.p: WATCHING EVERY POLLING PLACE

in Northwich Division. (Cheers.) And what was more, they were fighting that election with a gentleman who at Blackpool said he was coming to defend the interests of the liquor trade and at Wincham said he had no interest in the trade direct or indirect. Now there would be a man who 'should not be known watching every Tory public-house in the Division from Winsford to Weston. (Cheers.) He hoped they had made up their minds as he had made up his that there should not be any dirty Blackburn political tricks in Northwich Division. (" We will Blackburn them, if they come." Cheers.) He thought h.,. had spent his time well in Blackburn. (Hear, hear.) There was about to be issued his fourth address to the electors of North wi ch Division, and it had occurred to him that if that book had been in the hands of the electors for the last month a great many worthy men would have been saved a con- siderable amount of trouble in asking him questions. That book showed HOW HE HAD WORKED AND VOTED

in the House of Commons, and his address was a pledge that as he had worked and voted so he would if they sent him back again to Westminster. (Cheers.) He had not a shadow of doubt that he would be returned by a very much larger majority, if only there were no Black- burn tricks introduced there. (We won't have them.) It that election was to be conducted on pure principles and to be the result of the expression of opinion of honest men upon political questions, there was no doubt the result would be better than before. (Cheers and "No free houses here.") One aspect of the coming election which struck him forcibly, as he road the newspapers and went from town to town, was that this election was not going to be settled by professional politicians. This election was going to be determined—and mark his words—by the people of England. (Cheers.) Where- ever he went men were coming out to take part in this ' election who had never taken a share in party politics before. These men said that upon this election would depend whether the workingmen and workingwomen and their children were to obtain the enormous benefits of the power being put into their hands for the

REGULATION OF THE DRINK TRAFFIC. and it was upon this question these people were coming forward. When he compared the people who lived in districts where there were no public-houses with the people who lived in districts where they were thick upon the ground, he would beg of them not merely to return him to the work he loved so well in the House of Com- mons, but for the sake of their fellows and those who were dear to them and dependent upon them—and far God's sake,to vote Liberal at the election. (Cheers.) He noticed that wherever he went the people were convinced that Mr. Gladstone would no premier for the fourth I time. (Cheers.) There was no man in the three kingdoms more satisfied of that than the Grand Old Man himself. (Renewed cheers.) He found also that my Lord Salis- bury and Mr. Goschen were just as thoroughly satisfied of this as Mr. Gladstone himself. (Laughter.) For whenever they spoke or wrote letters, they talked of what was going to be in

div.head: HOME RULE BILL
div.p: THE HOME RULE BILL

next year. (Laughter.) Did not that show, if there was going to be a Home Rule Bill, that the Liberals were going to win at the elections. (Laughter and cheers.) Three days ago in Edinbro' Mr. Gladstone promised that he would maintain the six conditions which animated him when he framed the Home Rule Bill of 1886. It would be provided that the Imperial Parliament should be supreme over the whole of the Empire, including Ire- land (cheers) ; that the pecuniary adjustments—the incidence of taxation—should be fair between Ireland and Great Britain • that the rights of minorities should be protected and there would be provision for the repre- sentation of Ireland in the Imperial Parliament. The Liberals were not Separatists, and he did not think that his hearers had any cowardly fears of what Ireland would do when they gave Ireland this subordinate Par- liament. The Irish were 5 millions, we were 32, were we going to be afraid of these 5 millions? "No " and laughter.) Supposing that instead of 5 millions the Irish were 30 milions and we were 30 millions, if we made up our mind to be kind to them, and they made up their minds to be kind to us there would be no need to fear. We had made up our minds to deal with the Irish people as with brethren, and we might dismiss from our minds fears of quarrels in the future. (Cheers.)

div.head: EXAMINEIL SAIRDAY: JULY 9:' 189 i.
div.p: THE EXAMINEIL SAIRDAY: JULY 9:' 189 i.

Mr. H. Wade Deacon, who had a most enthusiastic re- ception, said he was delighted to come to help Mr. Brunner if he could, because Mr. Brunner had assisted him, but it was perfectly obvious that that Division -Meant to return him without any outside assistance. He was sure he was pleased to see it. He was pleased to have the Opportunity of speaking to the men of Run- corn. Widnes and Runcorn were close together, intim- ately connected in many ways, and if the County Coun cils would make up their minds to make a bridge across- the Mersey, then they would be more connected still. (cheers.) If ever there was a time when Liberals should sink any little personal animosities, and sink any re- ligious differences that might exist, this was the time. 'ihey had before them at this election THE MOST IMPORTANT

that had ever been placed before them within the meal- oFy of living man. On this election depended the happi- ness of the two countries of Great Britain and Ireland, and he looked forward to the settlement of the Irish question in such a way that it would never have to be raised again at any other election. (Cheers.) The question was., would they have a continuation of the present policy of coercion or would they give Ireland a measure of self-government? There was no other poli4. 'She Tories Said there was the Local Government Bill. Well they knew what the Local Government Bill of the 'Thaw; was, and that when Mr. Balfour introduced it, he said it was a small affair and not halt as good as a coercion bill. That was the Tory idea of a Local Gov- rirnment Bill for Ireland and they might call it a policy if they liked, but there were no policies but two Other

HOME ante, OR PERPETUAL COERC/Obt and the voters must settle at this election which it would be in the future. the Tories now dropped 4toercien beeause a general election was at• band. (laughter.) A general election and coercion could never be seen together. (Laughter and cheers.) Alluding to the religious persecution cry, he said it did not exist where the Protestants were few but where they were many, and when he was in Ireland the Irishmen of the (icrth of Ireland showed signs of bigotry be saw no- where else in the whole' of Ireland. Ile,had great hope that when this question of Home Rule was settled there would be an end to this, and he instanced a, similar transformation in Newfoundland: There wculd be a some Rule Parliament next year, and many of them living that day would see the beneficial results that would follow the Home Rule Bill. (Cheers.) Besides their HOMO Rule policy ,the Liberal party had a genuine programme* to lay before them. What had the Tories to lay before them? 'They had absolutely nothing-410- thing but " I am opposed to this," "I am opposed to that," and "I am opposed to the other." The Tory party was a party of opposition and they would be in their right place. (Laughter and cheers.) Mr. John Withington moved "That this meeting of workingmen, believing that the Liberal party both from its past history and present policy is ' the only party to which the industrial classes can look with any confidence for the realisation of those much needed reforms, so essential to their social and material well being, cordially declares its confidence in Mr. J. T. Brunner, as a tried and trusted exponent 0 their political aspirations, and resolves to vote and work to secure his triumphant return to the House of Commons in the forthcoming election" (Cheers.) Mr. Ellis Gatley seconded the motion and he said he ;supported Mr. Brunner, because he believed in," Home Rule "secondly because he believed in Liberal policy,and thirdly because he believed in Mr. Gladstone, having the right to give to Ireland, that which every man if he were au Irishman would want at the hands of somebody. (Cheers.) 'He believed that Mr. and Mrs. Brunner, thought it a right thing to unfurl , • THIi WATERMAN'S BANNER. . He (Mr.. Gatley), had - received a letter, offerieg £.5 reward for information about a man that had said some- thing. In the letter there was nothing at all with res- pect to what was really said at the meeting he (the speaker) was at. It was something different altogether. ,Perhaps it was another Tory dodge. (Laughter.) Not only so but he had seen it reported that Mr. Whiteley, had sent a round about request to be invited to the unfurl- ing of the banner. They could tell a man had a great deal a bout him when he had the audacity to ask them ,to lethim come where they didtiot want him. (Laughter.) If they had wanted him they would have sent for him. He wished to know where that request had got to; It had never reached them nor any of the officials of the Union. Mr Gatley then described how trades Unions owed every privilege they 'possessed .to the Liberal party and strongly advised his hearers to vote for Mr. Brunner. , Addresses were also delivered by Councillor. Flood (Warrington) Mr. Blege, (Winsford,) Mr. G. E. King, (Northwich) and Mr.-F. Hartland (Widnes) the resolu- tion was berried with enthusiasticaly unanimously.

MR. WHITELEY AT HALTON. On Saturday evening, a public meeting was held in Halton Girl's School, in support of the candidature of Mr. George Whiteley, the Conservative candidate for the Northwich Division. Mr. Charles Reynolds, 3.1'., pre- sided and there was a good attendance. Mr. Whiteley, ,who was received with loud applause, said at a recent meeting in that room Mr. Brunner took credit for the Liberal party that they had passed the Free Education Bill—or at any rate that more Liberals voted for the measure than Conservatives. It was not the first time that Mr. Brunner had made that statement and he had refuted it time after time and wherever he went he would track him out and refute it in the same place. (Applause.) He said distinctly it was

_ _ AS FALSE A STATEMENT as could be made. Before 1885 the Liberals were in office 12 out of 17 years and not the slightest murmur or whisper of Free Education was heard in the Radical camp, and when Mr. Chamberlain brought it forward in 1885, Mr. Gladstone declared that the iiiibject was pre- mature. Then the Unionist Government came into power, brought in the Bill and the second reading was carried by 318 against 10. Only ten members out of the whole 670 voted against Free Education, and yet Mr. Brunner had the audacity to tell them that it was passed more by Liberal votes than by Tories. The Lioeral Gladstonian party had nothing more to do with passing Free Education than they had to do with

Halton. (Laughter.) That marvellous mass meeting at Runcorn, advertised on six feet bills with a very great number of names upon it, and summoned by four brass bands had ended in a fiasco and a fizzle. (Laugh- ter.) ' And that when they escorted their opponent up to that field where this wonderful meeting was to be held, the number of bandsmen and musicians they had outnumbered the rest of the audience. (Laughter and applause.) And that if the Conservatives present bad seen fit to go away in a body, the residue would only have been made up of women and children. (Laugh- ter.). So much for the demonstration that was goinf to convert Runcorn. (Applause.) He concluded by moving a vote of thanks to the Chairman. Mr. Thomas Wright seconded, and it was carried by acclamation.

PORTRAITS AND CARICATURES IN CHURCH.

One of the most curious of Jacobite anecdotes is that concerning the revenge which art took on White Kennett, Dean of Peterborough, for his famous sarmon on wichcralt. Walton, the Jacobite rector of St. Mary's, Whitechapel, ordered an altar piece for his church, the subject to be the Last upper. When finished the piece attracted no par- ticular attention till somebody remarked that Judas Iscariot was unusually prominent, and that the fate was wonderfully like Dr. White Kennett's. It was, in fact, the dean's portrait. When this fact became known, all London flocked to Whitechapel to see the pillorying of Kennett. Eventually the bishop had to interfere and order the altar piece to be removed.

The astonishment of the person who first identi- fied Kennett with Judas Iscariot has been paralleled quite recently. A German who was being shown through a Derbyshire church shocked his guide by ejaculating" Bismarck !" Sure enough, when the other looked closely, there was on one of the walls a recognisable portrait, carved in stone, of the great statesman. The sculptor must have been seized by a fit of whimsicality similar to that which possessed the designers of some new gargoyles, or waterspouts, at the south transept ot Chester Cathedral. On these the heads of Gladstone Ilea- consfield, Manning, and others are represented. southern vicar ~ too, not long ago, made the dis- covery that the figure of a man holding a key in one hand and the model of a building in the other was not St. Peter, btu the founder of the particular church in which it is.

Bccentricities of this sort, however, pale before the caricatures to be seen on some of the carved oak of old churches. W imborne Minster, for example, contains a few curiosities in this way,and the stalls of almost any cathedral will supply speci- mens of ancient satire on the priesthood. The marvel is, not only that such things are there, but that some ruthless hand has not destroyed them.

CHAPTER LTV. MUSSEL GATHERING.

Since the loss of the smuggling sloop, and with It of the principal part of his fortune, old Carr had been obliged to return to his former calling of fisherman; and to pursue it with much • greater diligence than he had required to do during the prosperous days of the Beonny Bess. It came very hard on the old man ; who was in reality much crippled with rheumatism, and who found it difficult to compete with younger and more active members of the craft ; while he was also not able to afford the assistance which might have helped him over the drudgery. More than all it went to his heart to have to force Ailsie to apply herself to the same sort of work that the Other fisher lasses simply accepted as part of their duties.

Of course, as a fisherman's daughter, she knew all about preparing the bait and setting the lines; but she had always objected to doing this, and her doting parent had felt rather proud than other- wise of her fastidiousness ; while as for the heavier tasks of seeking the bait, and carrying a heavy creel back from the mussel scarp, that was not to be thought of for a moment. There was a certain obstinate and dogged manliness about the old fisherman, which kept him from grumbling over his misfortunes—at least audibly. . ' As he had declared to Dick Daglish, there wasno Sense in whining about things ilk...G.:spoilt child. Ailsie could do sufficient repining for both.; poor lassie, it was eitcusable in her! Wherever he could, he spared her anything un- pleasant, and it was upon his ricketty old shoulders that the heaviest burdens felL'

The wreck of the Bonny Bess had proved a heavy blow to freetrading in that district. No. one appeared to have either cart or courage to set about the task of raising money for the purpose of purchasing another vessel. • It was not only the• value of sloop and cargo gone for ever, but the• thought of the precious lives losralong with them, that paralysed the nerves, and fettered the energies of those few who were left still interested in, smuggling. The small capital he had saved from the wreck, therefore, the old fisherman .kept carefully put away in a cracked teapot, hidden in a hole in. the• wall, and decided that itmust there wait until such times as a leading and adventurous spirit should arise and fill the place of Dick Daglish ; when he,. Tom Carr, would again be ready to risk his all in a new- enterprise. - In the meantime they must live, he and his spoilt darling, and so he applied himself, with all the energy of which he was capable, to the fishing. ' Within a crescent of cliff, at a short distance from Frenchman's Bay, there was a mussel scarp, whither many of the fisher people resorted, to gather their bait. To this scarp a slippery and narrow but safe path had been worn across the yocks, and round the point front the bay. It was a perfectly Safe road, and most of the folks went that way with their burdens of shells. At high tide, when the rocks were covered, or when time pressed, they sometimes chose a quicker but much more dangerous one ; a narrow, uncertain sort of path leading clown the face of the crumbling sand- stone cliff. It was cven more perilous than the one leading down into Frenchman's Bay. Landslips were constantly taking place after frost or heavy rains. .

Old Carr was ascending this same path with a creel full of mussels one day when an accident happened which placed him in an exceedingly dangerous predicament. About half way up he slipped his foot, and to save himself from going further, and likewise to help and husband his feeble strength, he laid hold upon a clump of overhead bent'grass, growing just within reach.

The long continuance of wet weather had, how- ever, sapped the roots of this grass, and the clump came away in his grasp. Not only this but along with it came a fall of earth and rock this, but for the sideway course it fortunately took, would inevitably have carried him to the bottom of the cliff.

As it was he found himself perched upon a pro- jection, while for a considerable distance below and above the path had completely vanished, leav- ing a hideous gaping chasm impossible to pass, oven for limbs younge.r and more active than his. The shock this discovery gave him was com- pletely unnerving. Thereat of the fisher folk who catne to the mum' scarp for their bait had returned by the rocks long ago,, and it was only the lateness of the hour and his anxiety to get back quickly to Ailsie which had induced the old man to venture his life and limbs upon this little-used path. There would therefore be small chance of help or rescue from any of his comrades. By the time that Ailsie grew sufficiently anxious to induce some one to search for him, it would possibly be too late. The rocky projection upon which he had found momentary safety might give way under him at any instant, and precipitate him upon the sharp jagged stones he. could see far-below him. Hecould tell by the quivering vibration following upon his slightest movement that there was no security against such an event happening. And then—terrible thought—what would become of his little Ailsie Another blow to crush her young life, and to leave her defenceless at the mercy of an indifferent world. As for himself, it did not signify greatly, except that he would rather have chosen to die battling with wind and waves in his coble against a nor'- easter, when, there would at least have been some fighting of the elements before the defeat came, and when his blood would have warmed to the fray. There was something almost ignominious in an old fisherman dying such a death as this without the chance of a struggle. Then a strange thought entered his mind. Perhaps the. prayers, the blood-thirsty, venge-- ance-craving, threatening prayers of his enemy, Cuddy Widdrington, had been answered,, and in: what manner! - .

Was this present predicament a judgment for that past sin? Maybe it would have been better, after all, had: he done as Cuddy urged him, and made a public. confession of it. And yet, was not death preferable to shame and: distrust and reproach? No, he did not repent; at least not in that way,, so there was no use in telling a lie about it !. He was sorry, deep down in his heart, for the. 'wicked deed; but more because of the misery following upon it, and because of the honest nature of the victim, than from any real comprehension of its enormity. His.repentance—such. as it was—was between him and his Maker. The world had noth- ing whatever to do with it. And what right had Cuddy Widdrington to place himself upon the seat of judgment? That was what stuck in the old fisherman's throat, and roused all the dogged obstinacy of his nature. That a man young enough to be hi 3 son, and a man who was a poor hand at managing a cobla in a squall besides, should first of all disapprove of free-trading, a state of things no fisherman Breamish bred and born could understand, and secondly should hold him—Tom Carr—to blame for all the guilt and trouble, which had befallen, was intolerable.! S.

H 6 y( did Cuddy know who was the one really most tro blame in the stupid business? Why it had been half over when he, the one principally concerned in keeping secret the plans discovered by limes, came upon the scene. Even had he been so minded he could not then have .saved the man from that reckless, dare-devil, smuggling fraternity. But how was Cuddy to know this? Was he Providence, to settle a fellow mortal'e fate without let urn ? Some such thoughts as these passed rapidly through the mind of the old fisherman, and even In face of the danger a stubborn resistance to Widdrington, in his Arrogant, self-imposed office of judge, rose within the one judged. Well, if Cuddy those to act Providence, the chance was his at that moment; for in answer to the despairing shouts for assistance the fisher- man sent forth upon the air, the figure of his enemy appeared inunctliately above him; peering down the chasm the landslip had caused. Why Min alive, hoo've ye getten' there ?" shouted Cuddy, amazed at the predicament in which he found the old man. "The ground's glen' way," answered Carr at once, "an the rock aw'm stannin' on will do the same directly, aw'm feared. Unless ye can lend Ina %II an d ir) escape, it's an_ Imayith me.

div.head: DESPICABLE TORY TACTICS.
div.p: DESPICABLE TORY TACTICS.

Mr. J. T. Brnnner, the Liberal candidate for the Northwich Division, addressed large public meetings at Little Leigh and Barnton on Wednesday night. At the latter place, in responding to a vote of confidence, Mr. Brunner, spoke of the necessity of placing national schools under public control. Ile mentioned that at one school children were brought out in front of the building to cheer the Duke of Westmiaister. Re did not object to that procedure On the occasion of a friendly visit, but when his grace was in the district for political purposes he certainly did protest. At another school it was. the practice, when: presents of hampers of apples and buns were received, to distribute these among children connected with the Church of Eng- land, and not among the children of Dissenters. In another case the schoelmaSter had been dictating to the children of Liberals and Conservatives alike to write down such sentences as" Success to Mr. Whiteley." That, he contended, was absolutely wrong. Just as Mr. Brunner was about to deal with the subject of the death duties, 'a peculiar odour suddenly pervaded the room, and it became so powerful and unbearable that the people, many of wheat declared that it was a Tory ttick, rose ea masse, and expressed their intention to leave the building. The meeting shortly afterwards broke up in confusion. The smell was very similar to that of assafcetida. Mrs. Brunner, who was present, became exceksdingly faint, and was very unwell during the rest of the evening.

of the man in the moon. (Laughter and cheers.) The whole of Mr. Brunner's speech was a tissue—he would not call them falsehoods but at any rate of wrongful statements. Mr. Brunner played the same old barrel organ tune upon that occasion, but he never mentioned the question of Home Rule. He glossed it over and passed it by like the Levite did in days of old. As a matter of fact throughout the whole of Mr. Brunner's speeches the words Home Rule had not been mentioned more than twice or three times. But he drew lurid pictures of Mr. Whiteley's connection with the licensed victualler's trade in face of the statement that he (Mr. Whiteley) had often made, that, though be recognised the brewing and licensed victuallers business as quite as honest and respectable when properly conducted as that in which he made his money, he had absolutely nothing to do with it directly or indirectly. He had told Mr. Brunner personally himself and yet he kept on repeatimy, the statement in order to delude the audience he ad- dressed, and in order to draw a red herring across the path and DRAW THEM AWAY FROM HOME RULE.

(Cheers.) Mr. Whiteley described as an example of the reckless statements by whi-;11 Mr. Brunner was con- tinuously trying to delude voters with the statement that that school was under the thumb of the parson and

the squire, whereas it was managed by a committee which contained two Nonconformists and a working- man. (Applause.) Mr. Whiteley then proceeded to criticise Mr. Gladstone's speech at Edinburgh, describ- tion it as a tissue of false assertions from beginning to end, and said if they granted Ireland a similar Govern- ment to Australia, it would be separation, and he read a number of quotations from speeches of Irish members to show that they would never be satisfied until they had complete independence and total separation. And he asked, viewing the position of Irish parties to-day whether a Parliament sitting upon College Green would carry out the union of hearts, and would be anything but

div.p: A WEAKNESS AND A SORE

„ to England as long as it existed. When the Irish Par- liament was sitting in 1782 to 1800 things went back- ward all over Ireland. They knew that the Irish forced their Parliament from England when in difficulties in all parts of the world, and they could not withstand their demands. They were in intrigue with foreign nations, the french in particular, and there were abso- solute negotiations with regard to landing French troops upon Irish soil in 1791. The bloodiest revolution that I ever broke out in Ireland broke out in that year. In 1800 the union was carried. Since then Ireland had certainly not made the progress they could have wished it to do, taut at the present time Ireland was making rapid progress towards

PEACE, HAPPINESS, AND TRANQUILITY. (Applause.) Was this then the time to throw back Ire- land 50 years in its history and cause widespread trouble, probably civil-war, simply to please the senile vamity of the Grand Old Man. It would be a retrogressive step ; it would be ruin to Ireland and seriously injure and damage us in this country. (Cheers.) He asked them as Englishman, in this grave crisis, to do their best on behalf the Empire they were so proud to belong, and to abolish Mr. Brunner from public life and return him (Mr. Whiteley) who would go to Parliament a supporter of the Union and of the very best ministry they had , ever had. According to, news from Southern Russia cholera has spread along the Volga.. and is established in all the great towns as far as Tambow. A panic, attended by disturnances and bloodshed, is reported from Astrakhan.
THREE CHILDREN BURNT TO DEATH.

On Mondoy afternoon, the danger of childremplaying with fire was terribly illustrated at Birkdale, Southport, by the death of three children by burning under most painful circumstances. Joseph Gregson, aged four, and his brother Robert, aged two, sons of John Gregson,tish hawker,l9, Vaughan-road; off Everton-road, went out to play in company with a cousin, Thomas Rawcliffe, aged four, son of Robert Rawcliffe, bricklayer, of No.l in the same street. Ann Rawcliffe, a widow, and grand- mother of thr children, had been left in charge of them and the house, the parents of the , Gregsons being from home. The mother or the lad Rawcliffe had prepared for a walk, but changed her mind and sent him to play with his cousins. Soon after they went out, she saw a wooden shed behind the house in flames. Two men. John Aldis and James Snape, who live in the vicinity, at once ran out, and they, together with Mr.s. Alice Magee, another neighbour, carried water and succeeded in putt- ing the fire out near the door, behind which one of the children was found dead. In one coroner were- the charred remains of the other two children: all these being burnt beyond recognition. It is supposed that the children got a light from a boiler close by. The shed, alltraces of which are destroyed, was only 3 feet by 2 feet.

div.p: -- /veep rnyser quiet, an aw'd fetch a roper Cuddy Widdrington was off like lightning, ind the man on the ledge of rock awaited his return, with what patience he could command. Not far off on the top of the cliff was a stout post driven well into the ground: • It was used for fastening boats .to when. they were hauled up there to, be painted and cadked the spring time. In a boat belonging to' Cuddy was a coil of neW and strong rope. Fastening this round the past, he made a slip noose, intended to go round the old man's shoulder§ ; and fancied that so he, CuddY, would be enabled to haul the smuggler up like as one of the bales or barrels of contraband articles were hauled from their resting places in the cliffs; The young man advanced to the edge, all" cautiously peered over again. Old Carr had subsided into a sitting posture, partly through weakness and the trembling of be induced by having to remain so long in ene cramped position. Raving so subsided, however, his phlegmatic dis- position disposed him to make the best of the situ- ation ; and with his back against the wall of rock, he appeared perfectly composed and comfortable ; the more so that he had filled his pipe, and was smoking it with as peaceful an air as though he were sitting in his chimney corner at home. Something in the sight of this complete calmness arid indifference had a strangely irritating effect upon Cuddy Widdrington's temper. What right had the sinner to show so brave front, when. 'he had not put on that armour ei righteousness which ought alone to render him im- pervious to danger ? The devil, who should, by this time, hare beeB far from Brother Widdrington, was ready instead to seize the opportunity presented by the above- mentioned feeling of irritation. Without doubt spiritual pride lays a man OPen to Much temptation! "He is in your power now " whispered the subtle fend, "and he would not acknowledge the truth repentance you and justice of your accusation! Make him do so now. Remember it is the Lord's work, and that by bringing a sinner to are serving Old Carr, looking cautiously upward to ascertain the reason of the delay, met once more the vengeful eyes which had troubled him at the prayer meet- ing. They struck a chill into him even novt, though he affected not to notice. ye ready yet ?" he asked in an ankiaus, tone., "look sharp, ma lad, avem sick o' settm here!" "It's glen ye time to think o" yer sins !" a stern voice from aloft, "hat ye made yer peace wi' God? Are ye gaun te confess aw Wes the right, when aw bade ye come cot fro' the Fleet.; the an to pollute us not wi' yer guilt, ex' Nil' blood yc.'ve shed; the innocent blood that cries w Heaven for vengeance ?" The trembling of the old made limbs seemed to communicate itself to the stone below him, but his spirit was perfectly undaunted. He shalt his eyes while he realised the worst The fall, the thud that sickening thud he had been unfortunate enough to hear once or twice during his life, and the vivid memory of which rose before him. Ah, it was easily realised. But none of this moved him. - '

After all, a man has only to die once. he Perhaps he might choke before lie r t re bottom, and those sharp edged stones? , "If thou's gaun to pester me wi' the same sex! o' nonsense as thou did the other neet, thou eau gan aboot thy business as sune as thou chotrust oses, and leave me te ma fate! Aw wad rather , mysel' i' the hands o' Him ye're so feed:, mentionie at all times an' seasons, than 1' t hands of a daft, conceited, fyule like thou, la canna even sail a cable properly in a nor'-easter . This was the last straw. Cuddy's face hardeeeu and his eyes flashed fire. „f f. "For the last time, aw ask ye—will Ye c°—ess he shouted savagely, down the chasm. As savagely came the answer back. " Avell gee ye further forst !” Cliddy Widdrington threw the rope back 11P..°,111 the ground, and walked rapidly away. The rile; of his retreating footsteps fell upon old Carr like thie knell of doom, and with a deePt-the groan he collapsed and fell into a,ateap uP°- danoroaaledge.
(To be continued.)

div.head: WARRINGTON ELECTION.
div.p: WARRINGTON ELECTION.

One of the most spirited and strenuously conducted Parliamentary contests the borough of Warrington has witnessed was brought to an issue at the polls on Tuee- day. It is hardly necessary to say that the candidates Were—for the Liberals,Dr. Houston, Q.C., of Dublin, and for the Conservatives, Mr. R. Pierpoint,a resident of War- rington. Dr. Houston was adopted as the Liberal can- didates about six months ago after he had first addressed a large meeting of representative Literals. His able Speech on that occasion and the grasp of and thorough accord with the broadest Liberal principles which it evidenced at once won the approval of the Liberals of the town, and his acceptance as a candidate was, as a tonsequeuce, unanimous and enthusiastic. Since then the Liberal campaign has been vigorously conducted, for not only did Dr. Houston throw himself into the work of electionecriag with an ability and energy which deserved success, but he found in Mrs. Houston., a Worthy ally and one who soon became highly popular araongst the Liberals of the town. A series of " Recep- tions "was inaugurated and carried through in the most successful manner, and by means of these Dr. and Mrs. Houston became acquainted with a large proportion of the Liberals of the town. Largely attended and en- thusastic meetings have been held, and, besides Dr. Houston and local speakers, these have been addressed by, ammg others,the Right Hon. James Stanfeld, M.P., Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., Mr. Burt, M.P., Mr. Theodore Fry, M.P., Mr. W. Mather, M.P., Mr. Dixon, M.P., and Mr. C Furnesa, M.P. Dr. Hoastcra has been worthily backed up in his canvass by a large number V voluntary workers.. The Conservatives, on their side,bave also ifought 'their hardest, both in canvas- sing rand in the holding of public meetings. THE NOMINATIONS. The nominations -of the candidates'took place at , The Town Hall OR Saturday morning. It was aa purely formal affair,as it bad been mutually agreed between the two election agents (ali'. A. Browne,l Liberal ; and Mr. H. Greenall, Conservative), that I tiO objections should be made to nomination papers. she Mayor, who acted as Tcturning officer 'during the election, was present, and also the Town Clerk. Roth of the candidates were also at the Town Hall during the morning. Dr. Houston was accompanied by 'Messrs. John Croefleld, Julian Winser, Wm. Pierpoint, 'Mr. H. Roberts, -and Mr. A. Browne. Mr, Pierpoint was accompanied by Mr. Jos. Davies, Mr. John White, Mr. John Peers, sea., Ald. Francomb, and Mr. H. Greenall. Several nomination papers were banded in on behalf of each candidates. In one paper Dr. Houston was proposed by Mr.-John Rylands,secended by Mr. William Pierpoint, and assented to by Messrs. John BurgessaJulian Winser, Charles Jackson Holmes, Arthur Henry Lee, George Elackhurst, John Rymer Young, John-Henderson Fleming, and Thomas Birchall. In a secondraper he was proposed by Mr. Tomas Morris, Seconded by 'Mr. Samuel Johnson Beaman, and sup- Ported by Messrs. John Griffiths, John Allen, Thomas Malkin, George Legge, Joseph Owen, John Wesley Hay- Ward. Joseph Salt, and William Dunbobbin. He was further proposed by Mr. Robert Garnett, seconded by Mr. Thomas Jones, and supported by Messrs. Joseph Shaw Green Reginald Heber Silcock, Samuel Bennett Stringer., aiolin Toft, William Gleave, William Yates Lawton., ...John Gandy, and Walter Brough. In a fourth Paper he .was proposed by Mr. Felix Loughlimseconded by Mr. John Mullins, and assented to by Messrs. Patrick Lane, Anthony Connor, Peter Barry, John Kean, Martin Lyons, John Patrick Byrne, Michael Chambers, and James McGarty. In the -fifth paper Dr. Houston was Proposed by Mr. John Cresfield, seconded by Mr. Richard Miller, and supported by Messrs. Wm. Roberts,Chas. Sud- low, Matthew Knowles, Wm. Gilbert, Thos. Pember- ton, Edwin J. Mitchell, .Ts.s. Locker,and Joe. R. Calvert. Mr. Pierpoint was nominated in one paper by Mr. John White, -seconded by Alderman Franconala, and sup- Portedty Mr. Messrs. John Fairclough, Robert Heaton, John Roberts, James Smethurst, Thomas Hindmarsla Sutton, James Muir, Lewis Voisey, and John Edward Wright. In another paper he was proposed by Mr. Fred Monks, seconded by Mr. George Jolley, andsupported by Messrs. Arthur Bennett, William Gill, Ralph Johnsen, William Dooley, James'lllll, Percy Davies, and William Turner. In a third paper Mr. Pierpoint was proposed by Mr. Robert Davies, seconded by Mr. John Peers, son., and supported by Messrs. William Balton, William Tinsley, Linnreus Greening, James Hepherd, W. W. Westwell, Robert Anderton Naylor, Daniel Jones, and James. Tinsley. In a lcurth paper he was nominated by Mr. Joseph Davies, seconded by Mr. Joseph Harrison, and supported by Meesrs. Robert Isherwood, William Fairhurst, S. Reynolds, George Pilling,./arnes Fairclough, Chatiez Skinner, Thomas Halton, and the Rev. E. 'C. E. Carleton. The Mayor, in the course of the proceedings congratulated the candidates upon the friendly spirit in which the contest had been carried on, and expressed a hope-that the election day would pass off in thesame satisfactory fashion. The candidates both expreseed a similar wish. TIIE POLLING STAT/ONS. The following is a list of the polling distriete and polling booths : SPOLLING DISTRICT.. 1. Town Bala Ward Whitecross . or), • 4. Williams R Denham 2 R Dobson G Norman 14 -Fairhurst Vernon 2 J W Whittle J M Bate 1 C H Unsworth T Westbrook 2 W S Howard J W Howarth 1 T Cooper G Riley 2 G T Moore C H Wood 3 FaW Walker F Timperley Fairfield 1 I' 'reinstall F II Wilson 2 E Gibbon E Whittle Howley 1 S Sutton R Henry 2 E A White P L Speakmax St. Austin's 1 W J.Forshaw E Place 2 (.1 F F White E J Smith Latchford 1 T Lythgoe H Barker 2 W E Fowler E Reddish Latchford (extra municipal) P Davies A Boyle Warrington (Liverpool-road) FR Rcberts G Groulads Warrington (Orford) H Hatton T H Grainger PERSONATION AGENTS. Hackney, John Bond, Herbert Barlow, William Arthur Stone, James Maguire, John Joseph Ashworth Ernest Booth, Sydney Walter Jeffrey, George Maybury, Walter Dennett, Robert Eyes, Thomas Ellison, David Samuel Stone, Richard Dowd, Frank Arthur Jenkins, F. H. Jenkins, Charles Henry Knowles, and Alexander -Chalmers.—Conservatives, Messrs. J. A. Wood, J. C. Shaw. F. W. Radford, Wm. Taylor, Geo. Smith, Samuel Ratoliff, P. G. Wood, J. W. Isherwood, James Brierley, Alfred Taylor, J. Brown, J. A. Forshaw, Joseph Cooper, J. W. Muskett, Thomas Litton, A. Pickton, Arthur Percival, E. Horrocks, and James Grimshaw.

POLLING PLACE. Drill Shed, Bath-st. St. I3arnabas School 62a and 64 Tanners-4one, Silver-st., School Clubroom in John-st, Brick-st. School National School. Chursh-at. Cairo-st. School St. James's School
