THE POLLING_ Speaking generally the polling at the various stations passed off quietly and uneventfully. At every booth, there was of course, during the day, a gathering of spectators who, for the most part watched the proceed- ings with a quiet, undemonstrative interest. When however, one or other of the candidates drove round, matters became& little more lively, and there was cheer- ing and hooting, It was noticeable that in some of the 'districts, Dr. Houston was much the more popular candi- date, while at others the supporters of Mr. Pierpoint ,seemed to be in fairly strong force. For Town Hall Ward the polling place was the Drill Shed, and polling Proceeded very decorously during the day. TheLibemls had as a committee room, a house in Legh-st., . but the Conservatives, as usual, were favoured by being located Ph the premises, though not, of course, in the Drill Shed iteeff. Caira-st., schoolroom was the centre to which the electors of St. Austin's ward had to proceed to record their votes, and, it is said, that the voters of this • Ward to a large extent observed the injunction of Practised electioneerers to" pollearly," though we did hear of one belated Tory rushing up just as the booth was being closed. Cairo-st. seemed during the later part ot the day at all events to be a favourite cen- tre for spectators as there was generally a pretty consi- derable though undemonstrative crowd. In St. John's Ward thepolling place was the Club-room, John-st. Both parties had their committee rooms almost opposite .a.nd near together. Good feeling seemed to prevail .Powever, and the candidates who drove up in the scour& of the day seemed to meet with an impartial recep- tion. Not far away, in Tanners-lane the electors o Bewsey recorded their votes. Here the sympa- thies of the crowd were decidedly Liberal, and the blue favours of the Conservatives were not I:tsuch in request. All the displays of feelings 'were, Pewever, of the good-natured sort, and nobody had to complain of anything in the shape of ill-usage or even of p?olestation. For Orlord Ward, Silver-street schools was the voting centre and I:ere too there was little to record, .4 (4)1: had it not been for a slighPy larger gathering of hangers round "than usual arid a Motleihte display of :titection literature there would have been little else to ldicate that an election was proceeding. The quietest of all quiet election centres was, however, Orford schools where the ejectors of the man municipal part of the
town voted. Here there was absoltitely no excitement though during the day the voters of the district were steadily polled. _ . . _ . .

- The polling in Howley Ward was in the National School, Church-st., both the Liberal and the Conserva- tive Committee rooms adjoining it. At the hour for commencing the poll the school was besieged by voters, and the polling continued pretty steadily until ten o'clock. One incident occurred here which created no small ex- citement. It was discovered at about half-past nine that early in the merning a man had presented himself and personated no other than so well-known a man as Mr. William Johnson of the Public Hall Co. The dis- covery was made through Mr. Johnson himself coming to vote. On his emphatic assurance that he had never polled he was allowed to do s?, on what is called a " tendered " or pink, paper. Some consider that there was no intentional impersona- tion but merely a mistake. We have been assured, however, by the 'gown Clerk that the latter was aot the case. We understand that there are those who say they know the personator, but we do not learn that any steps are likely to be taken to bring him to account. Throughout the dinner hour the voting in Howley Ward was exceedingly brisk. In Fairfield Ward the poring booth was in Brick-st., school, the Liberal. committee room adjoining it and that of the Conserva- tives being nearly opposite. We observed the Rev. F. W. Willis, the worthy rector, enter the booth to record his vote about ten minutes to eleven o'clock. There was a considerable amount -el excitement in this thickly populated neighbourhood, women thereabouts appearing to enter heartily into the zest of the occasion, and clemourin,g with their tongues in most animated con- troversy and criticism of the two candidates. A picture exhibited in front of the'Liberal Committee room, of " Tory rule in Ireland" representing the horrors of an oviction scene, was a centre of attraction. The polling , for Whitecross Ward was in St. Barnabas's school, Bostock-st-, the Conservative committee room atoining it, and that of the Liberals being a little lower down the street. There was a great rush for the poll at eight o'clock. The number of votes recorded in this ward was much larger than in former years. Councillors Henry Roberts and Plimpton were actively engaged during the day in this Liberal ward, Mr. William Crisfield visited it during the day, as also Dr. and Mrs. Houston, who drove up in the morning accompanied by Miss Daley. Both candidates, in fact, visited the ward during the day and each met with a favourable reception, though that V.' the Liberal candidate was much more enthusiastic than that of his oppo- nent. Dr. Houston was driven through the streets in the morning accompanied by Mr.A. Browne (his election agent) and the Rev. John ‘Yonge, and Mr. Pierpoint made his appearance in the company of Mr. John White and Mr. G. Greenall. The Conservatives had been pro- vided by Lord Egerton -with a brake for use in this ward, and it was plying industriously throughout the day. In the Liverpool-road district the poll was in the Wes- leyan School, Sankey Bridges, the committee room being close by. A large number of work- men voted during the morning, and in the after- noon the balloting began to slacken consider- ably. There was no excitement in this district till evening., when the inhabitants beeame full of anxious expectancy. Dr. and Mrs. Houston were seen in the neighbourhood during the day, and were entkusiastically received. .In Latchford ward, the polling quarters were St. .games's school, the committee rooms being in the adjacent Prince's-st., facing each other. There were a large number of votes recorded during the former part of the morning, these early voters including about all the.principal men of the district. Electoral feeling ran high in the locality, men and women seeming alike ardent politicians antagonism culminating in at least one instance in a bout of fisticuffs betweeu the male partivans of the respective candidates. Quietness was the order of the day in the Latchford extra municipal district, where the remotely situated Baptist Schools in Wash-lane constituted the polling headquarters. Mr. Henry Roberts and Mr. W. Pierpoint were the first to record their votes here, and by 12 o'clock half of the voters, who numbered from 60 to 70 in all, had exercised their electoral privilege, at the rate of about one in every'twenty minutes. The presiding officer and his clerk must have had hard work—if not to keep awake as it was facetiously remarked, at any rate to keep them -selves from ennui. Mr. Arthur Browne, as election agent, and Mr. W. Pierpoint as chairman of the execu- tive, were actively employed during Tuesday, in super- intending the day's work on behalf of the Liberals.

div.head: MR. WILLIAM CROSFIELD AT WARVITiGTOINI.
div.p: MR. WILLIAM CROSFIELD AT WARVITiGTOINI.

Mr. William Crosfield, the victorious Liberal candidate for Lincoln, passed through the Central Station .War- ringtou, about half-past eleven o'clock on Tuesday morning and was met there by Dr. Houston, Mr. John Hylands, Mr. W. Pierpoint, Rev. J. 'lunge, Rev. J. .Davies, Mr. A. Browne, and others. Mr. Croe.eld expressed a hope for the success of Dr. Houston. Mr. Crodield was strongly urged to break his journey at Warringtern. He,however, had to go on to Liverpool, hut promised to return to Warrington by the'2ls train in the afternoon. This he accordingly did, and was metby Dr. Houston and Mr. A. Browne. On descending to the carriage which was in waiting in the street he .was cheered by a large crowd which had gathered. He afterwards drove to the Liberal Club and thence round to the polling booths' at which he was well received. however, did not make any speech during the day.

div.head: COUNTING THE VOTES.
div.p: COUNTING THE VOTES.

All the polling places were closed promptly at eight o'clock and the ballot boxes at once conveyed to the Town Hall where the votes were to be counted. The counting was carried out by an efficient staff under the supervision of the Mayor and Town Clerk. The total number of votes polled was Erst ascertained, and this was found to be 7,128. The counters than proceeded to find the numbers given for each candidate. It was eventually ascertained that 3,843 votes were in favour of ?dr. Fier- point and 3,258 in favour of Dr. Houston, thus giving Mr. Pierpoint a majority of 585. Thirty votes were re- jected,22 doubtful ones were allowed to Dr. Houston' and 16 to Mr. Pierpoint, after an examination by the Mayor, Town Clerk, Mr. Browne and Mr. Henry Greenall. Mr. A. Browne then proposed a vote of thanks to the Mayor and to the officials for the manner in which they had carried out the election. Mr. Henry Greenall seconded this proposal which was carried.—The Mayor briefly acknowledged ' the vote, and spoke of the valuable services rendered him by the Town Clerk. It may be mentioned that, as compared with the 7,126 votes polled on this occasion, there weve,7,244 in 1885 and 6,933 in 1886. The poll of 1885 was the largest on record. After the poll had been declared, all the ballot papers and other documents used in connection with the election were despatched by the night mail to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery.

div.head: ANNOUNCEMENT.
div.p: THE ANNOUNCEMENT.

The wide-spread interest that had been excited by the election was evidenced by the great crowd which assembled in front of the rown Hall to await the public announcement of the result. From about eight o'clock onwards there was a continual stream of people pouring into the grounds in front of the Hall, end consequently by half-past nine o'clock there was a dense semi-circle of spectators awaiting the result. There was a strong contingent of borough and county police present to keep order, and for a time they held a wide space in front of the Town Hall steps clear from the crowd. But as the time approached for the appearance of the returning officer the impatience and eagerness of the crowd grew to such an extent that the pressure upon the front ranks became too great for the officers to resist and in the end by one resistless rush they pushed the policemen back and spread over the whole of the area in front of the Town Hall. There was then owing, to the swaying of thecrowd, a considerable danger of the foremost ones being seriously crushed against the steps, but, fortunately, so far as we have heard nothing of this nature has occurred. Amongst those forming the small gathering on the steps in front of the Hall was Dr. Houston, and he at times found himself the object of the mingled cheering and booting of the crowd, though the cheering very much preclonunated. It was nearly a quarter to ten o'clock when the Mayor issued, wearing his chain of office, from the inner chamber where the counting had been carried out, bearing in his hand the paper upon which were the fateful numbers. As soon as he was observed there was a loud shout of- excite- ment from the assembled multitude, and it was not till after some minutes had elapsed that even a partial silence could be obtained. The Mayor then announced the results as follows :

PIERPOINT (C) HOUSTON (L) .. . . . Majority for Pierpoint 685 So great was the noise that not even all those on the steps could hear the announcement, but the much desired information was, almost simultaneously with the Mayor's statement, conveyed to the assembled gathering by means of a transparency displayed in one of the windows of the Town Hall. There was then, of course, a great deal of cheering on the part of the supporters of the. successful candidate. The result seemed to have been signalled across from the Town Hall to the Conservative Club almost as soon as it was known, for rockets at once begun to ascend from that building in rapid succession. It was said that this was the method of signalling the result to Walton Hall, and that an answering signal was soon sent up from the residence of Sir Gilbert Cireenall

div.head: TWO PREVIOUS CONTESTS.
div.p: THE TWO PREVIOUS CONTESTS.

_ In 1885, the election in Warrington resulted as follows :—Sir G. Greenall (C) 4,010 ; Mr. Wm. Crosfield (L). 3,234; Conservative majority, 776. In 1886, Sir Gilbert Greenall polled 3.717. and Mr. John Crosfield, the Liberal candidate, 3,216, giving a Conservative majority of 501. AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.

_ After the declaration of the poll there was a great gathering at the Liberal Club. Dr. Houston on returning there was loudly cheered, and many expressions of regret at his defeat were to be heard There was soon a large crowd on the bowling green, and
_ Mr. W. PizarolNT, who presided, Esaid that how- ever sorry• they -might be at the-real:tit ol that day's
INS

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 9, 1892
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 9, 1892

election, their sorrow Was minute as compared with his. He wished to assert in the strongest and most emphatic words he could use his opinion that the Irish vote had gone solid for Dr. Houston. (Hear, hear and Mr. Kiernan:" We will stake our lives on that: we are not the traitors" and applause.) How was it that Dr. Houston had been defeated that day? Ile would tell them. He had been defeated by gentlemen who professed to be of the Liberal shade of politics, but who went into the polling booths and had become double-dyed Tories. (Hear. hear.) He only said of those Liberal electors of Warrington, who had been traitors to the good cause, that he hoped they would be able to sleep as comfortably that night as he was assured Dr. Houston would. (Hear, hear.) Poor un- fortunate fellows that they were, they had been acted upon by the forces of demoralisation which the Tory party of Warrington were so capable of using and which they had always used. (Shame.) He had been told the day before that there were HO electors in Warrington that could he bought for 500 pints of beer. (Hear, hear.) The petition in Warring- ton was this. They had rejected one of the most able ,candidates that had ever been brought before them,one who was blameless in character, who was superlative in lability, and a man who had made his way to the very high position he occupied to-day at the Irish bar, and they were to be represented by one who was,at all events, tied hand and foot to the beer barrel. (Hear, hear, and • applause.) If the working-men of Warrington were contented to be ruled by Wilderspool brewery, well God help them. (Hear, hear.) He was afraid they would never get much good from their friend, Mr. Robert Pierpoint. He would ask them to carefully scan his votes in the House of Commons. He would venture to predict that in all cases where the interests of the masses were opposed to those of the classes the interests of the masses would have to stand aside. (Hear, hear.) The interests of men like Sir Gilbert Greenall—of millionaires —would be thought a good deal more of than those of the poor unfortunate individual who only made 30s. a week. (Hear, hear.) He believed the Liberal workers in every waid in the town had done their best (applause)—and he believed every official of the party had endeavoured to work to the best of his ability, and they might all take the comfort, that they had done their best in fighting for a good man and a good cause (Loud applause.) Dr. Housrois, who was very loudly cheered, having quoted the figures of the poll, said that 585 was for the present election the measure of their defeat. Their Chairman had accounted for the defeat by a fact which he, at all events, considered to be sufficiently established, namely, that there were in this constituency a number ef weak-kneed Liberals—(A voice: Too many)—whe had gone over, and for some reason or other sold them- selves into Tory slavery. (Hear, hear.) Their chairman mentioned another fact which had come to his knowledge, namely, that there were in the constituency 500 electors who could be bought at the moderate price of a pint of beer a head. If that be true, he should advise Mr. Robt. Pierpoint to change his name—to change it from Pier- point to Beer-pint. (Laughter and applause.) They had been defeated, but he was happy to say that they were net only not dismayed but not discouraged. (Hear, hear, and a voice : (" You will meet him in Parliament yet" and applause.) They had fought a good fight and an honourable tight. (Applause.) They had stooped to nothing that honourable men would shrink from stooping to, and they had fought that contest on lines I, of unimpeachable honour. Everyone of them could go home that night with the feeling of satisfaction that that election would leave upon his mind and upon his conscience nothing to be regretted. (Applause.) He would take that opportunity of thanking the 3,258 men of courage and of honesty and of intelligence who had recorded their votes for him that day. He could not believe that that verdict was to be the final verdict of Warrington as between Liberalism and Toryism and UcioniSM. (Hear, hear.) He was satisfied that they would not be contented with that position and that they would not lose heart and confidence, or lose faith in the great principles of Liberalism. .(Applause.) They had been defeated that day as many good men had been defeated before, but the lesson to be drawn was not without beneficial results. They would close their ranks together and would carry on the fight from that day forward perhaps with more resolution than if victory had crowned their efforts. Things moved rapidly in these days in which we lived, and an opportunity might very soon arise for impeaching this verdict, which had been obtained by means which he should not at that time stop to characterise. (Hear, hear.) When that day came he knew they would all be ready for the fight. (Hear, hear.) Let 'him thank all those who had supported and sustained him through the great con- test. He thanked, in the first place, the Chair- man and the members of the Executive. He had witnessed the splendid efforts that they had made to assure and secure success. They had left nothing undone that could be done to secure victory.; they had worked night and day and had never epared themselves. It was not for want of courage and determination to work like men and fight like men that they had not succeeded better. And they were not the only ones to whom credit was due in that struggle. They had been supported by a band of faithful men who had co-operated with them in the efforts which they were making. He should also not omit to mention the great help that they , had received from the women of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) These men and wonien had gone through the constituency canvassing and .doing better than canvass- ing, arguing and discussing the subjects which were at , issue in that controversy, and he was sure that the work they had done, if it had not resulted in a Liberal victory on that occasion, had laid the .foundatiens of a Literal victory In the future. (Applause.) He should now for the time bid them farewell. Lie was happy to th:nk that he left in Warrington no unpleasant memories behind. (Hear, hear.) Ile was glad to think that the left behind him many sterling, true and affectionate . friends. (Hear, hear.) He knew that the great heat t of the intelligent working men of that ,constituency had gone out to him as his had gone out to them. (Applause.) He was about to leave that Maya not, as had been said, to hurry home to his own country but for the purpose, he hoped, of addressing many meet- lags in many parts of England, and possibly of Wales. (Hear, hear.) He should tell them that the heart of the intelligent working-men was sound and beating in unison with the great doctrines of Liberalism. ( applause.) He urged upon them, if it were necessary for them to do se, to keep up their hearts and spirits. The enemy had -snatched a temporary and transient victory on that occaeion, but their triumph would be short-lived since the time would come when the matter would be put to the test again, and if he was not among them as
their candidate, he would at all events be amongst them as a fellow-worker. (Loud applause.) fPw wordA were also addressed to the gathering by Mr. JoaN

A large crowd had also assembled in the street, in front of the Liberal Club, and these were al,o briefly addressed by Dr. HOUSTON, —who was accompanied by Mrs. HOUSTON,—from an upper window. Dr. Housrozr, said that in dealing with reform the Tory party kept the word of promise to the ear, and broke it to the hope. Their measures of reform and remedial legislation were all hollow shams. They were the smallest and the minutest measures that could be possibly passed under the circumstances ; they were given, to the people in" dribs and drabs," and without the liberality and the generosity that characterised the measures passed by the Liberal party. (Hear hear.) Dr. HOUSTON, also thanked those who had voted for him, and expressed •his high appreciation, of the services of the workers of the Liberal party in Warrington. Cheers having been given for Mrs. HOUSTOIg, Dr. Housymz, thanked them for their mention of the name of his wife, and he thanked the people of Warrington, for the reception they had given her. They had enjoyed the friendship of very many in the town, and they had both been received in a way which was zemark- able, and which did the greatest possible credit to the the people of Warrington. They came as strangers, but they should leave behind them many who,he was certain, would wish them well, no matter where they might dwell, and for their own part they would perserve the most affectionate remembrance of the people of War- rington. (Loud applause.) Mr. Jorric WALKER said that Dr. Houston had been good enough to say that there was no fault on the side of the officials or the workers of the Liberal party. He, as a humble worker, wished to say that the fault was cer- tainly not on the side of Dr. Houston. (Loud applause.) They had seen and felt it stronger every day that War- rington could not possibly have had a better candidate than Dr. Houston. (Hear, hear.) Personally he felt prouder than ever of Dr. Houston that night, from the way in which he had taken that defeat, and the way he had given them a lesson in that matter, than if he had been returned by a large majority. From the very beginning to the very:end he had sizown that although coining from Ireland he was from head to foot an English gentleman. (Applause.) He had shown a courtesy that was thoroughly characteristic of all that was best in English and Irish life. (Applause.) He had done more than that. Although defeated, his speeches and his manners and his address had been an education to the people of Warrington, and they would profit from it hereafter. (Hear, hear.) That con- test had practically been one of beer against brains. Beer had for the moment won, and as a matter of fact, he had been told that in one ward alone, before nine o'clock in the morning, 83 persons had been counted going into the polling booths intoxicated. He did not know what would be the end of that, but it might pos- sibly end in somebody having to come back. (Loud applause.) They were indebted not only to Dr. Hous- ton, but they had also had his charming and graceful consort. (Loud applause.) If it should so happen that they would have to fight with another man, if Dr. Houston would come and help them to win, they would be doubly indebted to him for the splendid services he had rendered. (Loud applause.) The speaking then terminated, and the crowd gradu- ally dispersed.

he felt that the present triumph was a crowning of the exertions and efforts of their good old friend Sir Gilbert Greenall. (Cheers.) Before they parted he desired to say this, that his opponent had fought that election so far as he was concerned like a gentleman. (Cheers.) He was very happy in thinking that Dr. Houston and he had met together in that town, and had fought their 1 battle honourably like gentlemen. Of course in that I election there must have been some bitter things said on one side or the other, hut let them pass : they were done with now. (Cheers.) He concluded amidst another outburst of cheering. Mr. H. GREENALL congratulated Mr. Pierpeint on his acquisition of the title of M.P., and said he now had the pleasure of handing him the first letter addressed to him as such. The audience here clamorously cheered again and then struck up " He's a jolly good fellow" in Mr. Pier. point's honour, and afterwards " Three cheers for the red, white and blue." When silence was with difficulty obtained, Mr. John White read a telegram announcing the Conservative victory in Westminster. (There was again uproarious cheering, and a loud blast of triumph was sounded on a bugle in the room). Mr. White then observed that he had no doubt Mr. Pierpoint had been made very happy by his being placed in such a high position that evening, and he was sure that everyone in that room, and no one more than himself, was quite as happy as he was. (Cheers.) He (Mr. White) would much rather join in shouting than make a speech now. He felt that the time for speaking had gone by, and he would rather shout than do anything else. He must congratulate them on the victory they had won. They had all worked splendidly, better than they had ever worked in their lives. They had worked hard, and to such purpose, that they would not have to work so hard again for many years to coins. The victory would cheer and gladden the heart of their old member, who would join them in congratulation and thankfulness that Mr. Pierpoint had been nomi- nated as his successor. . . _

There was subsequently a most exciting and clamorous competition to get access to Mr. Pierpoint to shake hands with him before he descended from the table, he being pulled by the coat tails from one side of the board to the other, in order that he might dispense the favour equally all round. Finally he managed to get down, and left the room with a parting salute of stento- rian cheers.

div.head: MASS MEETING OF LIBERALS.
div.p: MASS MEETING OF LIBERALS.

An exceedingly enthusiastic meeting of Liberals was held in the VVinwick-st. Co-operative Hall, on Saturday evening, in support of Dr. Houston. Al- though a considerable proportion of the working- class population of Warrington had left the town by the various works trips held on that day, the large hall was densely crowded, and the utmost enthusi- asm was displayed by those present. Mr. W. Pier- point presided, and amongst others on the platform were the Right Hon. James Stansfeld, M.P., Dr. llouston, Q.C., and Mrs. Houston, Mr. J. F. Taylor (barrister, Dublin), Dr. Gornall, Rev. J. Yonge, Lieut. McCarthy, Miss Daley, Mrs. W. Pierpoint, Councillor Fleming, Councillor F. A. Roberts, Mr. J. Walker, Jfr. W. Roberts, Mr. A. 11. Lee, &c. . .

The CIiMRMAN, who was received with applause, ex- pressed his gratification upon having so large a meeting, considering how many of their friends had gone away on trips. He also read a letter from Mr. Ziba Armitage who earnestly desired and hoped that Dr. Houston would be returned to Parliament by a hancliome majority. It was only physical incapacity which, ff this election, pre- vented him from throwing all his energies into the scale on the side of the great Liberal party. He was anxious to make that emphatic declaration, because of a rumour which had been spread to the effect that his opinions had undergone a change. That was not the case, for, though he had a hundred votes, they would all be cast on the side of Mr. Gladstone. (Loud applause.) Dr. Flousrme, who was received with rounds of cheer- ing, said they were like soldiers on the eve of a battle. They were calm and courageous, because they were satisfied that every preparation had been made and every precaution taken to secure victory. (Applause.) On that the last occasion on which he should have the opportunity of addressing them before they recorded their votes, he begged to thank them and that constitu- ency for having so often and in such numbers and with such patience and attention heard himself and the other speakers that had addressed them, and he did not wish to confine his thanks to his political supporters. He wished to extent them to their opponents, because he was aware that many of their oppenents were present at those meetings, and yet at those meetings the most per- fect good order and good humour prevailed. (Hear, hear.) There was no disturbance and there was no interruption, and the arguments and the facts were fully and fairly heard. (Hear, hear.) He was sure that the same propriety of demeanour which had characterised the conduct of the electors of that con- stituency up to then would characterise their conduct till the last vote had been recorded on Tuesday. (Hear, hear.) He was sure that the voters of Warrington were conscious that in coming forward to record their votes they were discharging a great and impertant public duty and that the discharge of that duty was one that ought to be marked by all the propriety and seriousness which the importance of the event deserved. (Hear, hear.) He believed that Warrington occupied an honourable position in regard to the manner in which elections had been conducted, and he was quite sure that the present election would, in no respect,differ from its predecessors. (Hear, hear and applause.) He would now mention a little incident to them. As he told them the ether even- ing, the sth of July happened to be the birthday of a lady not a hundred miles off. (Loud applause.) The Tories immediately invented a birthday of their own. One of the speakers at a meeting of theirs said that the Tory candidate's birthday happened to be on the sth of July too. (Laughter.) He (Dr. Houston) thought he would satisfy himself on that point, and the best person to tell you what the date of his birthday was was the man himself. (Hear, hear.) Even though one didn't know at the time, one generally got to know upon pretty good authority on what day of the month one was born. (Hear, hear.) Well, Mr. Robert Pierpoint himself frankly admitted that he was not born on the sth July. (Laughter and a voice: He was born on the let April," a remark which was followed by much laughter.) Dr. Houston then remarked that before he was a lawyer he was a schoolmaster, and added that he was going to give them a lesson in geography. He then pointed to a map of Ireland on the wall, part of which was marked green, and a small part orange, and said that the Ulster they heard so much of was repre- sented by the littleerange corner of the map. (Laughter) He thought that he might say that if Ulster did not behave itself the yest of Ireland would be able to take

very good care of it. (Hear, hear.) That was a lesson in geography which was very simple and was easily remembered and was not likely to be forgotten. (Hear hear.) Dr. Houston then dealt in an effective and humorous style, with a sheet sent out by the Tories con- taining" reasons "why the electors should vote for Mr. Pierpoint. (Cheers.) The Right Hon. Jamas STANSFELD met with a very enthusiastic reception. He said that they knew the opponents of their candidate called themselves Unionists* He was there to say that the claim to the title of Unionist was an absolute fraud (Applause.) Union meant assent, Union without assent was conquest and subjugation. (Hear hear.) Union without assent was not Union and was not strength, it was disunion and weakness. (Rear hear.) He said that if Lord Salisbury, and his friends imagined that they could cow the spirit of the Irish people by coercion, perpetual though they might hope it to be, and crush out the instinct of nationality they were mistaken. The national instinct fed upon oppression. (Hear hear.) He con- tended that the Llberals were the only and the true Unionists,. and what statesmen and politicians had to do in order Co bring about a true Union between Great Britain, and Ireland was to find a method acceptable to England and Ireland and they maintained that they had found the method. (Applause.) Speaking with regard to the Irish Local Government Bill, he said the Govern- ment would not touch it till the fag end of the last session of a moribund and discredited Parliment. Then they brought the bill in tG keep the word of promise to tne ear, and in order that their camp followers, the Tory party and the Liberal Unionist deserters, might say , that they had kept their promise. It was enough to say I of that Bill, as Sir James Fergusson the Post-Master General, had practically said of it in Manchester the other day, that there was no party in the House of Com- mons which would have anything to do with the measure. Their own party did not like it, and their own caucus at Birmingham some months before entreated them to drop the Bill because, forsooth, the Irish were not fit for local government of any kind or description. The Liberal party were entirely opposed to it, and the Liberal Union- ist party could only pretend satisfaction. (Hear, hear.) The Irish party treated the measure with indignation. What had been the fate of the Bill they would all have seen. The second reading had been carried by a triumph- ant majority, but the Government had previously told their friends that if they voted for it this time they would hear of it no more. (Laughter and applause.) The Bill has accordingly been heard of no more. It was almost immediately withdrawn, and he had not heard of a single public man who had ventured to say that it would ever bere-introduced,except Mr. Joseph Chamber- lain. (Laughter.) He said it would be introduced in the first session of the new Parliament by the present Government. (Laughter.) That statement was a proof to him (Mr. Stansfeld) that Mr. Chamberlain was wise and foreseeing enough to know that the present Govern- ment would not be in office in the new Parliament. (Hear hear, and applause.) Speaking with regard to the Ulster question, he said that Belfast must learn that it is not Ireland. (Loud applanse.) The fears of so-called Ulster were simulated fears. Those men were too inde- pendent and of too much vigour, were too conscious of individual power and had had too much success in life to entertain the fears to which they pretended. They had been accustomed to sit in the pride of place and to put their feet upon the great majority of their countrymen, the Catho- lic people of Ireland. The basis ef their protest was not fear, that was an imposture ; it was the pride of ascendancy and bigotry. (Hear' hear.) They were told by the Unionist party that Home Rule being a "dark horse" and no one knowing what it meant, should it be passed by the New House of Commons it would be rejected by the House of Lords and another appeal to the country forced. His first argument in reply to that was, that no subject within his knowledge had ever been so thoroughly thrashed out and made understandable to the constituencies of the country as Home Rule during the last six years. (Hear, hear.) Neither Lord Salisbury nor the Duke of Devonshire would be able honestly or efficiently to argue that the constituencies had not had information on the question. Lord Salisbury had htnaself said that the vital question at this election was Home Rule, and the policy of Home Rule had been authoritatively explained to them by the head of the Liberal party. (Applause.) The House of Lords might be so ill-advised as to reject the Bill, but if they did they would not be able to force a Liberal Government, backed up by a Liberal majority in the House of Commons, to go to the country at their command. (Applause.) The question that would then arise would be the existence with its present powers of their own hereditary chamber. (Applause.) Mr. Stansfeld then proceeded to deal with other items of the Liberal programme. One of the first things the Liberals would do, he said, would be to see that schools which were entirely or almost entirely supported by public money were under some kind of popular control. (Hear, hear.) They would also complete the local government of London. If London became political she would, he said, again occupy the place she occupied centuries ago and lead the van et political progress. (Hear, hear.) They would deal with dises- tablishment in Wales—(applause)—and with the control ef the liquor traffic. They also wanted a radical reform of the land laws,and through the medium of local govern- ment they would seek to provide for the healthy, decent moral habitation of the people. (Loud applause.) He next spoke strongly in favour of registration reform, and of the repeal of the Septennial Act. He held that it ought to be as easy for a man to get on to the register as it was to get on to the rate book, and as difficult to get off—(laughter and applause)—aud that a man ought not to be disqualified for voting, simply because he had not paid his rates. It was for the collector to look after his rates. (Hear, hear.) Another reform that was needed was that of the election of the Board of Guardians— (applause)—and he contended that in the future nothing in the way of representative bodies should exist in the country that were not elected on a suffrage of one man one vote._ (Loud'applause.) . . .

, Mr. J. F. TAYLOR next gave an eloquent and powerful address on the Irish question, in the course of which he was much applauded. The Rev. Jams Yosas proposed a vote of thanks to Messrs. Stansfeld and Taylor for their addresses. He remarked that among the many floe speeches it had been his privilege to listen to he did not remember one that surpassed that of Mr. Stansfeld. Mr. Taylor, by his fine oratory, speaking as he did from the standpoint of an Irishman and a Roman Catholic, had captivated their intellects and their hearts, and they would be in- spired for the conflict next week by the words spoken that night. Ile no exceedingly anxious to clear away from some minds a little Mount of uncertainty con- cerning himself which appeared tO have take/ posses- sion of some of their friends, persons d 7 dtrong and active imaginations. There appeared to be 1,41 Sion on their part that in consequence of his not •-.'3lt 1 particularly conspicuous on the platform of the Liberal party during that campaign his opinions upon Liberal- ism and Home Rule had undergone some change. He was bound to say that it was the dream of a fevered imagination which bad no foundation in truth. (Loud applause.) It might be that his views had undergone a slight modification as to the desirableness of ministers and clergymen being particularly prominent in party politics, but be begged to assure that audience that he was as ardent a Radical as ever he was—(much applause) —and as firmly convinced of the righteousness and Christianity of Home Rule policy—and he should like also to take the opportunity of saying with what pro- found satisfaction he had been a witness of Dr. Hous- ton's candidature in Warrington. (Applause.) He bad made himself a most familiar friend—(applause)—and whatever might be the issue on Tuesday Dr. and Mrs. Houston had made in IVarrington hundreds and thou- sands of personal friends. (Loud applause and a voice : "He will walk in easy.") He would walk in easily if they all voted for him—(renewed applause)—mightily easily. (A. voice: He will.) The rev, gentlemen, after some further exhortatory observations, resumed his seat amidst much cheering. The CHAIRMAN put'the motion, which was carried unanimously and with great cheering. Mr. STANSFRLD acknowledged the compliment. The CHAIRMAN said a number of working-men had sent him a note expressing their desire to escort Dr. Houston to his hotel that night. (Loud applause.) He (the Chairman) had sent a reply that he thought the hour was too late, and that a great many of them were labouring under some political excitement, and perhaps it would be better in the interests of peace and order if they refrained from such a proceeding. Tt4 that he had had the following reply :—" The people will not be content without it." (Loud cheers.) " A Voice : "I will take him home myself " and laughter.) If the Liberal working-men electors of Warrington had got into tech a state of political excitement, if they were so determined to carry Dr. Houston at the head of the poll that they had taken the hit between their teeth and they took no notice of their Chairman, and would have this procession—("We will have it ")—for God's sake let them conduct it peaceably—(Cries of " Hear, hear ")—so that no person in Warrington could say but that they were earnest and enthusiastic politicians, who could carry on a procession at that hour of the sight quite peaceably as they ought to do. (Ap- plause.) At the close of the meeting, almost the whole of the audience met Dr. Houston at the door and escorted him to his hotel, the Patten Arms. He there addressed them from the step, thanking them for the great enthusiasni , for him shown by the compliment they had paid him, and urging them to go home peaceably and to do their duty on Tuesday.

div.head: AT THE CONSERVATIVE CLUB.
div.p: AT THE CONSERVATIVE CLUB.

The scene at the Conservative Club was one of such wild and tumultuous excitement as knew no bounds, and probably has never been paralleled in the political history of Warrington. Immediately after the declaration of the poll, there was a tre- mendous rush towards the club, and hundreds were soon struggling frantically to hustle and push their way into the premises, wile thousands were cla- mouring without for " Pierpoint" and demanding from him a speech. Mr.Pierpoint presently made his appear- ance at an upper window, and thence briefly addressed the crowd, but such was the din of acclamation on the one hand, and of counter-shouting on the other, that not a word ' could be caught by the reporter from below. Meantime, those who had en- tered the club were surging principally towards the first-class billiard room, where it was anticipated that Mr. Pierpoint would probably address his sup- porters, so soon as order could be restored. The room was presently thronged by excited members of the club, and other Conservatives, many Liberals, indeed, obtain- ing., admission there for nearly an hour. A most extra- ordinary example of what human excitability is in election times was furnished. Two or three fervent orators ascended the billiard table and endeavoured to engage the attention of those present by congratula- tory observations on the Conservative triumph, but they were saluted with such tremendous shouting and cheering as to be only audible by snatches, and it was manifest, that oratory until the fever-heat of those present had somewhat subsided was imprac- ticable. They shouted, they cheered, they sang "God save the Queen," and "Rule Britannia," comic songs, not omitting the too familiar " Tara-ra boons-de-ay," with a. clamorous effect that was indes- cribable. Women were seen among the crowd who seemed to enter into the fervour of the excitement with all the animation of the men. When Mr. Pierpoint did ultimately enter the room the cheers were almost deafen- lug. file mounted the billiard table, followed by Mr. John White and Mr. H. Greenall, and commenced to speak, but his audience were determined that they would first give him one last transcendent proof of their vocal powers; and it was about a quarter of an hour before the din sufficiently moderated to allow him to proceed. He then, amidst renewed cheering, read telegrams just received announcing the Conservative victories in Liver- pool. He then amidst continued noise addressed those present. He thanked his supporters for the splendid vic- tory that day, very largely owing, he remarked, to the chairmanship and the great exertions of his and their friend, Mr. White. (Loud cheers.) No one in that room ' knew more than he (Mr. Pierpoint) and Mr. Henry Greenall did of the indefatigable exertions of Mr. ' White during the contest and in past years, and he must be delighted that he had been enabled to lead !hem to victory. (Cheers.) Then the admirable order- ing of things, also by his friend Mr. H. Greenall had conduced splendidly to what had been accomplished ' that day. (Renewed cheering.) And through years Past they had had their good friend Mr. John Hamp- sou in his OffiCA and going about and doing work, and. being an exceedingly good agent for their associa- tion. (Cheers.) They had returned their candidate by a bigger majority than at last election which he ventured to call a true Lancashire majority. (Cheers.) div.head: MASS MEETINGS AT. BRIDGE FOOT
div.p: MASS MEETINGS AT. BRIDGE FOOT

- An out-door mass meeting of working-men was held at Bridge Foot, on Sunday morning "to discuss the ques- tions that most nearly concern the working-men of this country. Councillor Thos. Flood presided, and there were also seated en the lurry, which was utilised as a platform, Mr. T. B. Malkin, secretary of the Iron- workers' Association, Mr. A. E. Benjamin, Mr. W. Knowles, Mr. John Price, secretary of the Navvies' and General Labourers' Union, Mr. J. H. Fairfax, of Barford, Warwickshire, secretary of the Allotments and Small Holdings Association, and Mr. John Houlding. There was an immense attendance, there being from 1,500 to 2,000 persons present. The CHAIRMAN in opening the proceedings de9ed that all the promoters of that meeting were Raclitals. He

SAW Tories, as well as Liberals intim audience, socialists, as well as faddists. Yestei day week, they had a meet- ing, and they were told by the party that was always ready to strike a blow at the interests of the working. classes it was a frost, and would have no effect, and that it was called by himself. He gave an emphatic .denial to that. He had never allowrd himself to take any in- dividual action without consulting his fellow-towasrnen, land at all times had been most reluctant to occupy a position like his present one without their express and 'earnest wish. The question of payment forthat meeting was a question with which the " Obserwir " lila not the slightest business. He would ask the editor, who was an apostate in his political principles, Mr. Gill, whether his office was paid by himself for cDnducting 'the Tory business. He had no right to question who should pay for the hire of a room for a meeting of the working- classes of this town. (Hear, bear.) Referring to .the question of mining royalties the speaker said that was one of the planks in the platform of the chartists includ- ing the late Earnest Jones, with whom he as a youth had been acquainted. The question of the transfer of the land back to the people was another question of prominent importance which had also been contained in their charter. No fewer than 700 people each week came into Manchester from the agricultural districts, driven by the present land monopoly, to com- pete with the artisans there and keep down wares. There was a desire in certain quarters to keep the people discontented in the particular direction he had indicated, so that their attention might be distracted from other reforms. He had no desire to create a third or fourth party in the interest of the working classes but would recommend their support of such men as Dr. Houston. (Applause.)

Mstim then spoke. After making some observa- tions upon the subject of mining royalties, he referred to what he described as the bogey about lower wages being paid on the Continent, brought forward as an argument for reducing the wages in England. He quoted a report which showed the wages for producing a ton of steel to be in America 11•59,i015., in England 7.81d015., and on the Continent 8 I.odols. The land- lords and mining royalty owners drew from this country 500 millions per year. These were burdens that the working-men would have to throw off their shoulders. Mr. Griffen showed that the united wealth of this country was 0,500,000,000,000 per annum, and the increase upon this every year was 135 millions, going into the pockets of the idlers and the loafers—(the Chairman Hear, hear)—and being one hundred million more than all the working-men possessed in savings ..banks, co-operative stores, friendly societies and trades unions. It was said that Home Rule would be detri- mental to the working-men of this country,but he denied that. It would be a fine stroke of business for this country. 30,000 Irishmen passed through Warrington in 1890 to seek work in Lancashire and Cheshire, and the competition of these men with English workmen would be put an end to by Home Rule. He urged working-men to vote for Dr. Houston. (Applause.) Mr. BENJAMIN moved the following resolution : " That the opinion of this meeting is in favour of the labour vote being cast solidly in favour of Dr. Houston, believing that the interests of the working classes will be best promoted by strengthening the Liberal party, and those assisting them to bring about remedial legislation on behalf of the working classes." He remarked that there were a lot of Tories present, and if they had the moral courage of their convictions let them come on the platform and refute the statements made. (Applause.) As to mining royal- ties he said the total amount paid in them in 1888 by the country was over six million pounds. (" Shame.") What would this mean if given as an increase in wages ? It would mean that the working-men could do without Birmingham Joe's pension scheme. (Hear, hear.) I Speaking of the better housing of the poor, be said they needed no better illustration of the necessity of this than some of the hovels behind a principal street in War- rington. It was high time they were pulled down. He would not hesitate to sag that the majority of the land- lords who owned these pigsties were Tories. (The Chair- man: I know that.) Let some of the Tory hangers on there come and reply to that. (The Chairman: They can't.) Mr. Benjamin alluded to sweating as experienced by him from Tory masters, and said fortunately he now worked for a man whom every workman honoured. He wished to God there were more masters like him. He had called his workmen together arta told them to vote as they liked; it would not interfere with them in their employment no matter how they voted. There was no intimidation there. (Applause)' . .

Mr. Wm. littowuni seconded the resolution. One of the very first steps he said, after the adoption of the payment of members would be the formation of a labour party. There were the parties of Conservatism and Liberalism, and why should there not be a party of Labourism ? Some one asked why the Warringtoa working-men did not bring forward a candidate. (Mr. Malkin explained that this was impossible on ac- count of the expense.) Mr. Knowles reviewed the claims of the Tory party to be considered legislators for the working-man,and was subjected to considerable interrup- tion by Mr. Diggle. The CHAIRMAN said there were 500 homes in War- rington declared by the Medical Officer iinfit for human habitation, and 85 per cent.of these, he could prove, be- longed to Tory landlords. (Laughter.) He asked why people were allowed to live in the homes thus con- demned? (" Shame.") What they wanted was disin- terested men in the Council, who would fight the battle for them, and "break the neck" of these Tory land- lords who kept such hovels. (Applause.) Mr. JOHN Paws subsequently spoke, and WAR much interrupted by Mr. Diggle, against whom he directed considerable sarcasm. (Mr. Diggle, on being desired by the Chairman to desist, wanted to come on the plat- form, but permission was refused.) Mr. Price attacked and ridiculed the Pension Bill for giving a man ss. a a week at 65, after paying a certain sum and £l. a year for 40 years. He denounced plurality of votes, men- tioning the case of a parson who had 50 votes, and ask- ing whether that man was 50 times better than himself, and said the way the principle operated in the election of Boards of Guardians was a scandalous shame. (Ap- plause.) The motion was put and carried, with one or two dis- sentients.

Mr. FAIRFLX then addressed the meeting. In arguing in favour of Home Rule he met the assertion that Irish- men were lazy and shiftless by citing his experience of their industry and success in Canada where they had no such hard conditions to contend with as in Ireland. (Mr. Diggle also considerably interrupted this speaker.) A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the meeting, MONDAY NIGHT'S MEETING.

Another mass meeting was held at Bridge Foot on Monday night, at which about 2,000 persons were pre. sent. Mr. W. Pierpoint Lrst addressed the meeting, and Aubsequently Dr. Houston amidst tremendous cheering. wag amen up in his carriage, and standing on the box seat addre7ied the erowdt Mr. T. Birchall taking a seat beside him. In gppyse of his remarks Dr. Houston :!421 said he had heard that I,l*.'dit from Mr. Wm. Pierpoint i;:: that some one had been saying at Working-men could be bought by the SOO for a pint of .‘"ItC apiece. This was a gross slander upon the working-merf, and they l would show on Tuesday that it was and w0u,...4 bui it back in the teeth of those who dared. to utter .ite Mr. T. Birchall, who rose amidst much cheering, then delivered an address, and amidst great applause remarked that if anybody thought his voice was to be silenced because he was under a number of Tory Directors, he mistook his man. While he had life

and breath he would stand by the working-men. —Mr. John Walker, who had accended to the top of the carriage, and was received with nauch cheering, then spoke. Mr. Pierpoint, he said, had done nothing for Warrington even when he had had the opportunity, and urged that a man who by sheer hard work and specia capacity and making the best use of it had run step by step to his present position was the better man for the choice of the constituency.—Dr. Houston was afterwards driven off amidst enthusiastic cheering, Messrs. Birchall and Pi&-point accompanying him.-114r. John Healey moved a resolution declaring Dr. Houston a fit and pro- per candidate, Mr. John Price seconded, and Mr. Malkin supported it, and it was carried, with but four dissentients.

MEETING AT BANE QUAY. A meeting in furtherance of the candidature of Dr. Houston was held in the Workingmen's Mission Room, Bank Quay, on Monday evening. Mr. A. H. Crosfield, who was the principal speaker, said it was proposed to extend to Ireland the same powers of government, only in a modified form, which their colonies already pos- sessed. The foundation of the empire was due to the fact that the number of nations which formed that vast empire were satisfied with the conditions of their Government. If they tried to consolidate the empito in the same way that they had been treating Ireland the empire would not have held together this long ;it would have gone to pieces. They had a great many conflicting interests at Westminster, and Irish questions had either been shelved, or they were mismanaged. When Mr. Gladstone attempted to deal with them they knew the violent opposition been- countered from the Tory party. He had to cut his Bills down and spoil them, or they would not have gone I through the House of Lords. (Bear, hear.) They had met their opponents' objections to the Home Rule Scheme, they had met them in argument so completely that they had not got a leg to stand upon. (Applause.) Mr. Benjamin and Mr. Willets also spoke. Before the poll opened on Tuesday a brief meeting of Liberal workers was also held in the open air near Catherine-st., and afterward i most of those present pro- ceeded to record their rotes and afterwards to yr, rk for Dr#Houston.

'the Board, with having divulged what lie called " the private business of the Committees" pre- vious to its coming before the Board meeting. Mr. Ratcliffe point-blank denied that he was an offender in this respect,. but spoke of the charge aa a serious one, and demanded that it should be investigated. It ought to. have been sufficient for Ur. Ratcliffe to assert his innocence ; and the chairman would have done well to follow custom by accepting the denial and withdrawing the statement. But what of the charge itself? Is it necessarily a wrong thing to make known business 'Which has been transacted in Committee? The question raises an issue of some importance, Inui one, as it seems to us, upon which there is much misconception. Broadly speaking, it may with truth be said that the Committee business of public b,i)dies is public business, apart altogether from the question of its having been bought before the Board, or Town Council, as the ease may be. There may, of course, be cases in Which, in the public interest, it is desirable to pro- ceed with secrecy—but these are exceptions and do not affect the general rule. In St. Helens and 'setne other towns, reporters are permitted to attend Committee meetings; and the ratepayers 'are the gainers thereby, for if something is being "gene of which they do not approve, they may,by a timelY expression of opinion, prevent an unwise 'step being taken. We are quite aware that it is customary when a decision has been taken, for members "I a Committee to stand by it as a whole; but it does not follow that the public Should be kept in the dark as to that decision. Icor does it follow that a dissenting member is ' 11'4 entitled, if he should think fit, to carry his *Pposition to the final issue when the matter in j question is laid before the general body for con- firraation. Indeed, it is his duty to take that 'tours°, if he thinks a wrong step is being taken ; and he is justified, in the meantime, in making the matter public so that he may have the support of the public. Suppose, for instance, that a Board hes resolved, with the sanction of the public, to spend £5,000 on a Public Flail; but that, at a later stage, in Committee it is proposed to, accept Plans involving an expenditure of £B,OOO, will any rational person say that an opponent of such a uenr departure is not justified in immediately mak- ing the matter public, and in opposing it by every legitimate means in his power? Or t ike another CIN ; The B>mitary Committee 44 the Warrington ClukpOkaion, have, by a small autiority at a small meeting, decided to purchase ircrai a Nottingham firm a boiler for their Long- ford Works, at a cost of £069. A section of the Committee have protested against this because, irk the first place, it is contrary to a resolution 'Passed by the Town Council to enter into any sontract exceeding £2O unless the matter be sub- Mitted to public tender; and because, in the second place, it is contrary to public policy to deprive townsmen of an opportunity of obtaining, in open competition, the contracts of the town. We hold that, under those circumstances, the Minority are in duty bound not only to make the matter public, but to oppose the confirmation of the minutes when they come before the Town F°uneil. No Committee is infallible ; its business ts subject to revision ; and when, as in this in- Stance, it is founded upon injustice, and grossly irregular, there should be no hesitation about refusing to confirm the transaction. It will thus be seen that the only suund doctrine, in our jodg- 'tient, is that public business should be transacted linder the eye of the public, in order that there May be some assurance that it is done in the inte-
rests of the public. [ Since the above was placed in type, we are Pleased to find that the principle for which we

oentend has been recognised. There was a meeting last evening of tho Warrington Town Council, and the members, after some discussion, refused to * confirm the minutes relating to the purchase of the boiler for Longford Works.]

Helens THE result of the Parliamentary St. Election. Election in St. Helens was un- doubtedly a grievous disappoint- Tent to the Liberal party. As between Mr.SEroN- ife44a and Mr. W. B. KENNEDY,. Q.C., there can ne question as to which was the most likely to erve the interests of the masses. But it is clear that a large portion of the electors do not as yet Understand their own interests, and are unsettled ?4,.. the Home Rule question. The Liberal Union- though not numerically strong, have at least rlived themselves sufficiently strong in the in- „ilence they possess to determine elections in such rwteeslis St.Helens. Who can for a moment doubt, t if the Gambles and the Pilkingtons had been r: in the old times, on the Liberal side, the iberal candidate would have been returned by , substantial majority, instead of being defeated °Y the small number of 59 P They are of course, 113 nauch entitled to their own views as any other tri lembers of the community; and there is nothing oj it, as the Liberals believe themselves to be in t ue right, but to continue the struggle for justice nntil, with Home Rule granted, Ireland will cease tcs block the way. Liberal Unionists may then be ecsuited upon, for the most part, to rank them- te2.ves again on tho side of the Liberal party, and u. Helens will be seen in its true colours as a cl'iheral borough. It is certainly hard to suffer eleat, and for a second time to come within 60 v ntes of winning; but progress is unquestionably 411°Ivn in comparing the election of 1886 with the 131'eseut election. It is not unlikely,as things are that there will be another General Election before long. Let the Liberals of St. Helens take heart and continuo the struggle. It may be l'egarded as certain that they will achieve a victory when they next go to the poll. . -

div.head: ELECTION NOTES.
div.p: ELECTION NOTES.

Wednesday's " Observer " says :—" R. Pierpoint, Esq., M.P., is at present staying at No. 685, St. Austin's, Warrington. Dr. Houston, the eminent Q.C. from Dublin, who has been in Warrington for a short time,will return to his native land at once, as it is found that the air of Warrington does not agree with him.—Court Circular."

But why not give the latest from the " Court Circular ?" It is as follows :—" R. Pierpoint, Esq , M.P., is still staying at " St. "Austin's ; hut it is understood that this is tho only connection he has with the " Saint." It is proposed that when he sots out on his journey to Westminster, he should wear" primrose" stockings, " blue "breeches, and " orange " vest, with coat and cap of the "War- rington Volunteer" style. To complete the har- mony of the arrangement, it is suggested that be proceed in a Wilderspool dray; and "take his seat "on a barrel of" treble X."
Now that— The hurly-burly's done, And the battle's lost and won, . .

_ so far as Warrington is concerned, a word may be said about voters' pledges. It comes in the result to this, that they are less and less to be relied on— on the Tory as well as on the Liberal side. If the Liberals had polled within fifteen per cent, of their promises, Dr. Houston would have been re- turned by a fair majority. But the polling showed a falling away of about 20 per cent.; and from figures which have reached us, since the election, from a reliable source, we are in a position to say that the Tory poll, large as it was, was in a similar way close on 20 per cent, less than the pledges they had obtained. It will thus be understood how it happened that both parties in Warrington were hopeful of victory, and how each party was, to a certain extent, deceived.

There is a strong feeling on the Liberal side that canvassing ought to be abolished; but the difficulty is to frame a bill which would accom- plish that object without interfering with ordin- ary freedom of intercourse. Besides, it sometimes happens that an elector desires to canvass the views of one or other of the candidates, and per- sonal visiting best serves this end, On the other hand, where pressure is applied, canvassing be- comes a breach of the spirit if not of the letter of the Ballot Act,

It is due to Dr. Houston to say that he made as much headway by his house to house visits as by hiz platform speeches. His ready address, frank manner, and "sweet reasonableness" won him praise even from opponents—many of whom were brought to admit that he was rig it and they were wrong, thus becoming converts .to Homo Rule. And then as was said of Raleigh, he can " toil ter- ribly." His speeches were often made after being "on his feet" all day; but there was never any sign of weariness, either bodily or mental. Now that he is better known in this country, lie is cer- tain to find his way before long to the House of Commong.

iarn Crosfield in Warrington rejected Mr. VVi.:3 1885 ; but another constituency hag reCOgiiisocl his sterling worth. He was returned for Lincoln, on Monday, by a majority of 224, his return being all the more acceptable from being a Liberal gain. This success was heartily welcomed by the Liberals of Warrington. Not unmindful of his old friends, Mr. Crosfield paid a visit to the town on Tuesday afternoon, and mot of course with an enthusiastic reception at the various committee rooms of the party. -- What about secret voting under the Ballot Act? There was great complaint at Warring- ton, on Tuesday, that votersrwhilst marking voting papers, were too much exposed to the view of the officials, and of others in attendance. The voter could only screen himself by taking special precaution. This ought not to be. It is to be hoped that better provision will be made in future; and that those who have charge of the forthcoming polling arrangements will take care that the voter shall have a chance of being " altogether out of 81glit " whorl ho is marking hia ballot paper.

The election for the Newton Division takes place on Monday next. The Liberals have an excellent candidate in IVlr. W. Neil!; and if they work hard in every district they will return him to the House of Commons. Unlike Mr. Legh,he is in thorough sympathy with working-class legislation; and as the Division includes a largo coal district, he ean count on a majority amongst those who, as Shelley has it, " waste a sunless life in tho unwhole- some mine." Mr. Legh is amongst those who ought to be taxed as ground landlords. His interests are not the interests of the electors, and they will do well to seize the present opportunity of making a change in the representation.

The Tories have no memory for history, or th ey would not be Tories. Although hankering after Protection, they have been trying to raise a pre- judice against Home Rule by saying that the late Mr. Parnell wanted to "protect "Irish manu- facturers. As we pointed out the other week, he took this ground after conferring with the late Lord Carnarvon who was in Lord Salisbury's Cabinet as Lord Lieutenant of Ireland. It was one of the Tory moves of the day; but formed no part of Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule Bill as approved by the Nationalists. Oblivious of these facts the "Observer "quotes Mr. Parnell as follows:

" I have claimed for Ireland a Parliament that shall have power to protect Irish manufacturers if it be the will of the Parliament and of the Irish people that they should be protected. . . . I claim this for Ireland, that if the Irish Parliament of the future considers that there are certain industries in Ireland which could be benefited by Protection, which could be nursed by Protection, and which could be placed in such a position as to enable them to compete with similar industries in other countries by a course of Protection extending over a few years, the Parliament ought to have power to carry out that policy." Very good; hut the date of this speech, which was made at Wicklow, is October sth, 1885, when Lord Salisbury was in office, and when the Tories and the Parnellites were in alliance ! We repeat —it was a Tory move, and it failed ; and nothing has been heard of this Protection except on the part of the Tories.

In the absence of argumtnt on matters politi- I cal, our Tory contemporary pounces on a printer's blunder on the card of admission to the Bank Quay Station on the occasion of Mr. Gladstone's visit. In the hurry, as people who were anxious to go to the station were waiting,a few cards were sent out before the proof was read in the usual way, the error being immediately afterwards discovered and rectified. It is obviously wrong to use both " Mr. " and" Esq." but it is the sort of blunder that will happen when the P.D. is on the rush.

But what of the " Observer ? " Is it quite free from blunders? Will somebody say how it hap- pened that on a notable occasion our contempor- ary in a staring head-line of the paper, as well as in the body of the report, announced the" inhibi- tion" of a certain clergyman of the town, whoa as a matter of fact he had been " instituted." The difference in meaning in the two words is about as wide as the poles asunder. But the blunder wasn't a printer's blunder ; it arose out of the ignorance of somebody who used big words which he didn't understand. The proverb is somewhat musty about the people who live in , glass houses ; but it will serve. IMO

Tint 110 MR IRON TRADE. There is still but little alteration in the condition of the English iron market. Trade in all branches is quiet. The Cleveland Ironrnasters' Association returns for June show that 76 furnaces are now in blast in that district. against 3 in May, and that the production of pig-iron has risen from 6,124 1 to 57,765 tons. A welcome diminution of stocks to , the extent of 39.491 tons is recorded. No. 3 Cleve- land pig is now down to 40s. pet ton. In manu- factured iron and steel there is little doing ; but late rates are fairly well maintained. In tinplates there is less enquiry. , . Shipbuilders on the whole are ,nl3, moderately employed, and in the majority of engineering establishments slackness prevails. The coal trade generally is less active.—lron

BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, RUNCORN. After being closed for some months through a disas- trous fire which occurred in geptember last, this place of worship will be opened on Tuesday next. The sacred edifice has been much improved and a powerful organ of high quality of tone has been secured. A full des- cription will be given in next Saturday's Examiner. RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. The monthly meetin,, was held on Thursday evening. Mr. J. Pritchard presided and there were present Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Dr. McDougall, Mr. S. Taylor, aud Mr. G. Moss, clerk. The School Management Cornmitt2e reported that the percentage of attendance for the past month was 84.6 corresponding period last year 81. The total average attendance was 3,029, last year 2,863; increase 186. Eleanor Davies was appointed a pupil teacher at Greenway-road school at a salary according to the scale of the Board.

SALVATION ARMY " BOMBARDMENT " AT RUNCORN. On Tuesday the officers of the Liverpool district of the Salvation Army " bombarded " Runcorn. There were present Major and Mrs. Miles, staff officers ; as well as ,40 field officers. The morning was spent in house to house visitation, over 800 dwellings being entered, and Iprayer offered to more than 200 families. In the after- noon and evening there were processions led by the band consisting of the officers of the division, 'after which well attended meetings were held in the barracks, High-st. The services were read by Major Miles, and several of tile officers gave earnest and interesting addresses.
When in want of a ebaste and elegant wedding or birthday resent go to PRITCHARD* 51, High-Bt.—Advt.

MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN, RUNCORN. The Sunday school anniversary was celebrated on Sunday at the Seamen's Institute, Station-road, when sermons were preached by Mr. T. S. Bolton, missionary to lodging-houses and workshops, Liverpool. Special anthems and hymns were sung. In the afternoon the service of song entitled, "The Little Children "was given by the choir and scholars. Mr. Bolton prcsided. A free tea was provided by Mr. Walter Collier, of Church-st., for the seamen whose vessels were lying at Weston Point and Weaver Pool, and these people gladly availed them- selves of the boon. It has been decided to continue this tea every Sunday afternoon while Runcorn Docks are closed. Two open air services were held in Devonshire Square. On Monday evening the service of song was repeated, under the presidency of Mr. R. Rawlinson. Addresses were delivered by Mr. Mundin, Ship Canal missionary, and Mr. Bolton. The collections realised a good sum.
JOSEPH PR/TCHAILD'S sale shop is 51,High-st., his workshop 4, Bridge-st.—Adet .

ST. MICHAEL'S 13AZAA.R, RUNCORN. This bazaar was brought to a most successful termi- nation on Saturday night, and the expectations of the most sanguine were realised. It had originally been intended that the bazaar should be held in marquees in a field behind Stanley-villas, but in consequence of rain the first day's proceedings took place in the Public Hall. There being a promise of fine weather, a removal was made.to the marquees on Thursday night, and the ladies are to be congratulated upon the expedition with which they put things in order, and the charming manner in which -they displayed their wares. Sports, organised by the Rev. G. W. Kingston, were amongst the attractions. Each evening the grounds were beautifully illuminated by Mr. W. E. Lea, by means of fancy lamps. The amount realised during the three days was £458, made up as follows :—Thursday £240, Friday £lOB, and Satur- day £llO. As the Vicar only asked for £3OO, there will probably be a handsome margin left after paying ex- penses. A word of praise is due to the Rey. G. H.Seeley, who rendered invaluable service as lion. sec. to the bazaar. Both PRITCHARD'S Shops Rill under personal supervlsion.aud customers may rely upon receivingevery attention.—Ada.

SHIP CANAL NAVVIES AND THE NEW RAILWAY. •A large number of navvies have left Warrington during the course of the past few days for Chester- field, the scene of the new cross country railway, in the hope of obtaining regular employment.
