div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 9, 1899
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 9, 1899
LIBERAL MEETING AT RUNCORN.

SPEECH BY MR, T. P. O'CONNOR, M.P. On Thuasday evening, a public meeting in sup- port of Mr. Brunner, was held in Runcorn public hall. The proceedings were timed to commence at 9 o'clock, but considerably before that time the building was crowded, and the utmost enthusiasm prevailed. Mr. P. Speakman, C.C., presided, and he was supported by the candidate, and Mr. T. P. O'Connor, M.P., and Mr. A. Mond and the local leaders. Mr. O'Connor and Mr. Brunner each rec- eived an 'ovation on entering the hall, the cheering lasting several minutes.

The—Chairman, in opening the proceedings, said he felt proud to see so large and enthusiastic an audience. He urged them not anly to attend these meetings but to work hard to secure Mr. Brunner's triumphant return. (Cheers.) Mr. E. W. Humphreys said the Ulster question was playing a prominent part in this battle, and he read a letter ftom a Nonconformist minister in Bel- fast. which showed that there was a large number of ministers in favour of Home Rule. Mr. A. Mond moved a resolution of confidence in Mr. Gladstone, and pledging the meeting to secure the return of Mr. Brunner as a true aud loyal sup- porter of the Grand Old Man. (Cheers.) Mr. Whitley had stated, said Mr. Mond, that tlie late Government had kept all the pledges which it had ever made. (Laughter.) At the -last election the Tories went in on the cry of " No Coercion," and they had since- passed a perpetual Coercion Act. (Cheers.) They promised Ireland a Local Govern- ment Bill, same as the English,and they had a kind of death-bed repentence. and had brought in a measure which was as different from the English as chalk was to cheese. But that miserable bill was only born to be slaughtered and buried in a back yard. (Laughter and cheers.) Mr. W. M. Sowerby seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously amid cheers. Mr. Brunner in replying said he had been asked to explain a point in his answers to the temperance party in that neighbourhood, with regard to

div.head: COMPENSATION TO PUBLICANS
div.p: COMPENSATION TO PUBLICANS

He would not pledge himself against every scheme of compensation. (Hear, hear.) And for this reason that if a wise and moderate scheme of com- pensation was brought forward by a responsible Government, such a scheme as would help the tem- perance cause and not hinder it, he would vote for it. (Cheers.) It it were proposed to give the owner of the house from which the license was taken away, the cost of altering the house into a dwelling or a shop he would vote for such a mea- sure, for the reason that a common-sense English- man loved fair-play and because it would be the cheapest bargain the people of this country had ever matte. (Cheers.) Referring to the old-age pension question he said he was as satisfied as he was that the sun would Tise to-morrow that the working people if they would support the Liberal party would get far away ahead of a miserable ss. a week at the end of ariother 40 years. (Cheers.) Ile thanked them froat the bottom of his heart for their expression of o..mfidence, and expressed the confident hope that they would return him to his work ia the House of I Commons. (Cheers.)

I Mr. T. P, ()Connor, who was received with pro- longed cheer, said that the Tory party had had several losses during the past few days, and they Ihad had some gains. The,: gains were considerably under their losses up to die Izesent time, and as time went on he thought their lOW WOuld• in- crease, and their gains considerably subsitle. (Cheers.) After a reference to the broken pledgeg of the Conservative Government, Air. O'Connor spoke on Home Rule. To those who knew him he need not give the assurance that absolute religious toleration had been the conviction which nothing in the world would lead him to abandon or even to trifle with—(hear, hear)—and he would go further and say that absolute religious toloration had been the conviction of nearly every Irish Catholic either in or outside Ireland. (Applause.) That assertion was backed up by generations and centuries of Irish history. Had there not been in Irish history the double phenomenon of a Catholic majority ready to follow, and Protestant leaders ready to lend ? In the next Irish Parliamentary party there would be ten or twelve Protestants out of 85 or 86. He was sorry the proportion was not larger. The Irish Catholics would be glad.if they could get 20 or 30 Protestant members. Could they point to another religious creed with such an overwhelming majority which had given so large a representation to the minority of tt different creed ? Ireland, instead of havingto Loam, hail much to teach to other naticna in religious toleration. (ApplaUse.) The speaker next proceeded to show how intolerent Belfast was compared with Dublin and other Catholic centres in making public appointmeuts, citing the facts which have previously appeared in our columns, lie said let Mr. Gladstone put into his Home Rule Bill any provisio whatsoever to protect religious liberty in Ireland, and he would not say one word against it, and neither would any Irish Catholic. (Applause.) Mr. Gladstone meant to retain the supremacy of the ' Imperial Parliament, and to give local self-govern- went to Ireland. He did not say that the reserve power of the Imperial Parliament would be exer- cised on light grounds. So long as the Irish Parlia- ment stuok within its charter, the Imperial Parlia- ment would not interfere; but if they went outside their charter or were insane or wicked enough to ' commence a religious persecution, then the reserve power of the Imperial Parliament would be exercised and the Irish Parliament sent back within the limit of its charter. (Cheers.) It was said that Ireland would seek separation from England. He denied it (applause) and no reasoning man could he of that opinion. Ireland could not get separation if she wanted it. Not a soldier, sailor, barrack, or boat would be under the control of the Irish Parliament. There was every safeguard in Mr. Gladstone's Bill. But trade was the great governor in the affairs of nations, and without the trade of England, Ireland would he thrown into a state oi starvation. It was foolish to say that they wanted to dismember the British empire. He appealed to them to extend to Ireland the policy that had been so successful in the colo- nies, and he was coufident that the result would be the same in Ireland as elsewhere, and would range Ireland among the loving daughters that looked to the Empire for protection and for liberty. (Cheers.) Their policy was reconciliation, peace, and religious liberty. (Loud cheers.) A. vote of thanks to the Chaif man nod Mr, O'Connor concluded the proceedings.

LIBERAL MEE LING. AT CLIFTON. On Thursday evening a Liberal meeting was held in the Primitive Methodist School, Rock Savage, under the presidency of Mr. W. M. Sowerby. A speech was delivered by Mr. Brunner, (and a vote of conftdenc., carried.

MR. BRUNNER AT ST. LUKES. A meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. Brunner was held in St. Lukes Schoolroom, Run- corn, on Thursday night. Mr. J. R. Frith presided, and on the platform were the Rev. J. Simpson, Messrs. A. Mond, T. Clegg, D. Bisbrown, and E. W. Humphreys. The Rev. Tno. Simpson moved a resolution of confidence in Mr. Brunner and pledging the meet- ing to use its best efforts to secure his return. Re supported Mr. Brunner, he said, because he was a Radical and true as steel, and because the Liberal party bad a programme, while the Tories had but a hollow mockery of a programme. (Applause.) Mr. A. Mond seconded the motion. Alluding to the claim of the Tories as the friends of the work- ing men, he said Mr. Whiteley,parrot-like, repeated stray scraps from the Newcastle programme. Ile was masquerading in Liberal clothes. The Tory party were no further now than they were when Lord Beaconsfield described them as" catching the Whigs bathing and stealing their clothes." (Laughter.) Speeches w3re also delivered by Mr. T. Clegg and Mr. D. Bisbrown, and the motion was carried.

-- MR. BRUNNER AT WESTON. Last night Mr. Brunner addressed a meeting at Wes- ton- Point and another at Weston Village. Both were largely attended and his speeches were well received. Speeches were also made by Mr. A. Mond. Mr. A. K. Norman presided at Weston Point aud Mr. T. Handley at Runcorn.

MR. WHITELEY AT RUNCORN. On Wednesday evening Mr. Whiteley addressed two meetings at Runcorn, one at Mill Brow Board School under the presidency of Mr. S. Pope, and another at Shaw-at., under the presidency of Mr. £. Itnison.

MR. WHITELEY AT WESTON. Mr. Whiteley spent a full day at Weston on Tuesday. At noon he addressed about 200 quarrymen at Quarry Bank. Severalof these present asked the candidate a number of questions which he answered satisfactorily to the questioners. In the evening he addressed a good meeting at Weston Point school, under the pre- sidency of Mr. L. Rozenberg and the usual vote of confidence and support was passed. There was a meeting also held in the Church School at Weston, and the building was crowded. Mr. John Weston of Run- corn presided.

div.head: WIDNES DIVISION.
div.p: WIDNES DIVISION.
MR. DEACON'S CANDIDATURE.

A mass meeting of Liberals was held in the Drill Hall, Widnes, on Thursday evening, in support of Mr. Henry Wade Deacon's candidature for the iVid- nes Division. The hall was filled to its utmost capacity, and when Mr. E. K. Muspratt, C. 0., took the chair there were 3,000 persons in the building, and many hundreds more were unable to gain admission. Among those on the platform were the candidate, Mr. T. P. O'Connor, M.P., Mr. T. S. Timmis' J.P., Dr. Thomas (Garston), most of the local Catholic clergy, and a large number of in- ' fluential residents.—Mr.W.B.Shores (Liberal agent) read a letter from Mr. J. H. Gossage, J.P., dated from Lucerne, in which he said:—" I most heartily support Mr. Deacon, and entirely agree with the political opinions expressed by him. I shall cer- tainly be home to vote for Mr. Deacon, and give him any help in my power. That he will be re- turned I feel certain."

The Chairman, referring to Mr. Gilliat's speech in that hall the previous night, said he had no opinions of his own. (Hear, hear.) The promises of the Tories were vague ; the promises of the Liberals were specific and clear. (Cheers.) Mr. H. W. Deacon, who was received with loud and prolonged cheers, rose to propose a vote of confidence in Mr. Gladstone and the readers of the Liberal party. He said that if the Liberals were serious they roust vote at the coming election. Every Liberal in Widnes must vote next Tharsday. As he had said before, lie believed he had gained in the out districts of the division, but ho did not hesitate to say that he relied on them, the men of Widnes, to send him to Westminster (cries of" You'll go," and; cheers.) He knew that there were many Liberals who could not see their way to vote with them on account of the Home Rule Bill. He regretted it, extremely regretted it, but he would not use hard words, but he earnestly hoped that before very long they would be able to see their way to join them once more. (Cheers.) As regarded his (Mr. Deacon's) views, he could only say that if they did him the honour to send him to Parliament he would with heart and with spirit support their great leader in granting justice to Ireland. (Loud cheers.) Mr. T. Sutton Tim mis seconded the motion.

Mr. T. P. O'Connor, who was greeted with cheers then addressed the meeting in terms similar to the speech delivered at Runcorn and reported elsewhere. The motion was carried enthusiastically, and the pro- ceedings concluded with the usual votes of thanks. THE NOMINATIONS.

On Thursday between the hours of eleven and one o'clock, Mr. W. W. Rutherford, of the firm of Messrs. Miller, reel, Hughes and Co., solicitors, Cook-street, Liverpool, sat in the Board Room of the Widnes Town Hall, on behalf of the Sheriff of Lancashire, to receive the nominations of candidates. Promptly at II o'clock, Mr. J. S. Gilliatt. the Conservative candidate, entered accompanied by Major Cross, Mr. R. Lewis and his election agent (Mr. W. T. Husband). Shortly afterwards : Mr. H. Wade Deacon, accompanied by Mr. H. B. Snores, his agent, arrived and the two candidates, who had not previously met, were introduced to each other by Major Cross, and they stood for some minutes conversing together. Five papers were handed in on behalf of Mr. Deacon and nine on behalf of Mr. Gilliate and no objections were taken. Both candidates agreed that the votes should be counted on the night of the election which is on Thursday next, and the Tett..lrning officer said, lw would arrange accordingly. RUNCORN BOARD 0-fi' COAIMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Thursday. Mr. F. Wiswall presided and mere were present Messrs. P. Speakman, J. Pritchard, 11. J. once, W. IL Wass, H. Coward, IL Abel, D. div.head: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

The Medical Meer reported that the number of deaths registered during the past month amounted to 31. Of these two were inquest cases, and of the remaining 29, 4 were due to inflammation of the lungs. 5 to phthisis, 4 to mesenteric disease, 3 to diarrlia.a, 2 blood disease, 2 to heart disease, and one each to arteric fever, croup, premature until, disease of liver, natural decay. inflam- mation of the living membrane of the brain, disease of the arteric, dentition and bronchitis. The 31 deaths showed an average death rate of 18.6 and exclusive of the inquest cases of 17.4 of the estimated population.— The surveyor said there were 35 deaths during Juno last year.

div.head: 1110EPA'AYS AND BUILDINGS COMMITTEE.
div.p: 1110EPA'AYS AND BUILDINGS COMMITTEE.

This committee recommended that the footways on the Victoria-road Viaduct be made with granolithic pavement; that Messrs. Stuarts' tender. for laying an additional length of 1,000 yards of granolithic pavement be accepted, and that the contract be for 2,000 yards in- stead of 1,000 yards ; that a steam road roller be hired from the Altrincham Local Board at the rate of 275. per day for rolling Victoria-road; that six seats be pur- chased (the sites in Victoria-road, Norman-road, and Heath-road to be fixed by a sub-committee) ; that the offer of Mr. Walter Collier to give a strip of land in Greenway-road, at the corner of York-st., as shown on plan on condiicn that the Board flags the space in front of his premises be accepted ; that counsel's opinion be taken as to the liability of the Marquis of Cholmondeley to make stood the surface of Runcorn Hill, broken up by removal of minerals ; that the plan of Messrs. Greenall. Whitley, and Co., for the erection of hotel and two shops in High-st. and Waterloo-road be approved subject to yards being provided in the event of the shops being used as dwellings.—Mr. Bisbrown moved, and Mr. Speakman seconded the adoption of the minutes.— Carried.

div.head: SUNDAY CLOSING. ,_
div.p: SUNDAY CLOSING. ,_

The Parliamentary Committee stated with regard to the letter (with petition- enclosed) from the Association for stopping the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors on Sunday requesting the Board to adopt the petition in support of the "Sale of Intoxicating Liquors on Sunday "Bill referred to this Committee at a meeting of the Board held on the 7th April last. the Committee begs to report that it considers this matter extraneous to the duties of the Board and would 'point out that the Board has no power to deal with any subjects other than those specified in the Acts which it is elected to administer. Mr. Pritchard moved.—Mr. Cries seconded. The minutes were adopted. Mr. 13isbrown voting against.

TRCHINCAL INSTRUCTION. _ _

The Techincal Instruction Committee, recommended that grants be made to the Runcorn School Board, from time to time for Technical instruction of sums not to exceed £220, in the aggregate. The Chairman moved the adoption of these minutes, and said the amount mentioned was exactly what the County Council granted to the Board, and the Committee considered that the expenditure must be confined within that sum. Mr. Speakman seconded, and pointed out that the County Councill had made a grant of £440 towards the building of the Institute; and it was necessary that amount should be increased by subsciptions from gootkmen, in the locality, and tie took that opportunity of pressing upon the public generally that had techincal instruction at heart that the children should have benefits as soon as possible. (applause.) The minutes were passed. FoVNTAINS.

On the minutes of the -OZ-e-rwal . Purposes Committee Mr. Speakman stated that the condition of the foumains in the town was disgraceful, and he suggested that the Committee have them put in order so that they could be used.—The Surveyor said they would be as bad as ever in a iortnight,and Mr,Bisbrown thought persons caught tampering with them should be prosecuted. After- wards it was resolved that the fountains be put in order and the Committee consider the provision of a water supply for dogs and horses.

FINANCE. The Finance Committee reported that the receipts for the month amounted to £552 15s. lid, and accounts' amounting to £7BB 83. 9d. were passed for payment. There was £2,0d3 17s. 63. of the general district rate to be collected.

div.head: EXTENSIVE ROBBERY OF JEWELLERY
div.p: EXTENSIVE ROBBERY OF JEWELLERY
AT WIDNES.

On Thursday, at the Widnes- Petty Sessions, before Messrs. J. Brock and F. A. Stapleton Brether- toe, three youths from Liverpool named William Barker (nineteen), Thomas Collina (sixteen), and John Parr (seventeen) were charged with burglan- °wily breaking into the pawnshop of Horatio Syred, Waterloo-road, Widnes, sometime between midnight on Saturday, the 25th ult. and on Monday morning the 27th ult., and stealing therefrom jewellery valued at £34 10s. George Tear, manager of the shop, deposed to securely fastening the premises early on Sunday morning, the 28th ult. When h went to the shop at nine o'clock on Monday morning he found that some glass had been removed frorrahe roof of a shed at the back of the shop, and entrance effected to the shop in that manner. Several watches, wedding and keeper rings were missing from the shop, as well as several other articles, the total value of which he estimated at £34 103. Police-consta- ble Evans deposed arresting prisoners in Liverpool on Wednesday. They all admitted the offence. The police inquiries had not been completed, and on the application of Superintendent Keighley prisoners were remanded until Monday next.
MARRIAGE OF MISS MAY REYNOLDS AT LATCHFORD.

On Thursday there was a scene-of-unusual anima- tion witnessed at Latchford in consequence of tile marriage of Miss May Reynolds, fourth daughter of the late Captain Reynolds, of Raddon Court, to Mr. Arthur Norris Wyatt, of Knutsford,and Earieswood Gorey, Wexford, Ireland, second son of the late Mr. Arthut Wyatt of that district. There was a very large congregation. The ceremony was performed in Christ Church, by the Rev. J. W. Wynne Jones, vicar of Carnarvon, and the Rev. B. B. Prescok,t, vicar of Christ Church. The bride was given away by her uncle Mr. Jas. Reynolds, of Fox Hall, Frods- ham. Captain James Williams, of Brecon, Wales, was the best man, and the bridesmaids were Miss Wyatt, sister of the bridegroom, Miss Reynolds, Miss Isabel Reynolds, Miss Sylvia Reynolds, Miss Joan Reynolds, and Miss Dorothy Reynolds, sisters of the bride. The bride's attire consisted of a plain white satin dress with a. long train' and a tulle veil descending to the feet. She carried • a beautiful bouquet of tuber and white roses. The bridesmaids were each arrayed in dresses of dark green silk, covered with white muslin, and dark green straw hats trimmed with green and white, and green shoes. They each wore a pretty diamond shamrock brooch, the gift of the bridegroom. The service was fully choral, the organist playing the usual wedding march before -the couple left the church. The bells rang out the customary peals after the ceremony. A flag floated from the top of the business establishment which adjoins Redden Court, and in the neighbourhood of the mansion a number of tradesmen and cottagers exhibited flags, a line of bunting extending from the corner of Wash-lane to the opposite building in Knutsford- road, on a centre piece of the canvas appearing the words" Health and happiness." There was a very numerous company at the subsequent wedding breakfast, which was partaken of at the mansion. The happy couple took their departure in thg om.l 'At) afternoon for Killarney. Palm's BANKING COMPANY.—On and after Monday, the sub-branch of the above company, situated in Main- st., Frodsha,m, will be open daily for the convenience of customers. The new premises have been neatly fitted up, and furnished with every convenience. METHODIST FREE CHETIVII.—On Sunday. the annual Sunday school anniversary sermons were preached in the above church, morning, afternoon and evening,. by the Rey. R. Trotter, circuit minister. Special hymns and anthems were sung by the choir, elder sc. holars, and friends, accompanied by instrumental music Mir. P. Earlam was at the organ. The attendance was extremely good at the evening service. Die collections realizedi £l5 12s. 11., being an increase of £.l. n the previous year's collections. WESLEYAN METHODIST Cnapst.—The anniversary ser- vices in connection with the Kingsley Wesleyan School were held in the above chapel no Sunday afternoon and evening, the preacher being . Mr. H. Wainwright, of Ormskirk. As usual, the thou' and scholars rendered excellent selec.tions of sacred hymns. The offertories for the two services.amounted to £ll ss. 414. FALL or THE WIND MILL.—On Saturday morning, the Kingsley wind mill, without any warning whatever, fell to the ground. lortunately, there was nn one in its vicinity. The owner of the Mill House residence, with the property attached, Mr. S. Beckett Chadwick, late of Crofton Lodge, Runcorn, had passea beneath the structure only some ten or fifteen minutes. previous. As there have been great improvements of late carried out here, and. some of the premises attached to the mill taken down, it is thought that the foundations had become loosened, hence the collapse of the fabric.
Two men have been killed and a number seriously injured owing to the burning of a bridge across the Ebro at Tortoss. -- - .
_ An elderly man named Frederick Goodhand, living in Ileneage-stieet, Birmingham, murdered his wife in a fit of jealousy on Wednesday and immediately committed suiciae.

THINGS HEARD AND SEEM IN ELECTIONEERING.

The canvass on both sides in the Nr,rthwich divi- sion has been very keen and strict. Mr. Brunner's son, Mr. Roscoe Brunner, has been electioneering in Runcorn, and has canyassed a number of streets in his father's interests with much saccess. On Thurs- day Mr. and Mrs. Brunner, and Mr. I'. Speakman spent some time in canvassing, and they were every- where well received.

There appears to be a third candidate in the field, or else the inhabitants of Canal-street are labouring under a delusion. A canvasser went into that district a short time ago, soliciting suffrages on behalf of Mr. Brunner, but a number of the tenants declined to pledge their votes to him, on the ground that they were 'voting for Jonathan Horse. field." I fancy that Mr. Horsefield, whose influence in that neighbourhood is very great, will if he can transfer hi ri adherence to Mr. Whiteley, in whose in- terests he is working.

-Here is a story which puts in the shade Mr Whiteley's oft repeated story of the pint, the quart, and the hogshead. It is told by Mr. Snape, of Widnes, the Liberal candidate for Heywood, that a Manchester football team went to play a match with a Liverpool club, and the latter, in honour of the event, arranged to entertain their visitors to a luncheon before the match. The " feed " came off, but so well did the Liverpool men cater for their guests that the latter did not show any disposition to leave the viands. Things began to look serious, and at last the host said "Come, it's tvrenty minutes to three and the game begins at three o'clock," bat was considerably astonished to. receive the reply "Oh, the playing team's coming by the 2.45 train; we're only the luncheon team." Mr. Snape applies the moral—that his hearers should be in the fight- ing, and not the lunching team, very effectively.

Here is another: A.minister was called in to ad- minister consolation to a dying man. The clergy- man told the man's wife that her husband was in a critical state, and that being unconscious at the time he could not speak to him. But, he said to the woman, he hoped that she would not miss any opportt.nity she might have of speaking to her hus- band of his condition, and of preparing him for his change. Whereupon the woman answered, "Yes, sir ; you may depend upon we, sir. There's never a night, sir, but I nudges him in the side, and says, 'John, you little know the torments that are being prepared for ye." The Government. Mr. Snape adds, would soon know something of the torments being prepared for men who had misused their power and had imposed laws upon the Irish people in violation of their pledges.

The action of the United Alkali Company in posting the following notice in all their works ought to be followed by ail employers of labour, ia order that no undue pressure may be brought to bear upon any elector :—" General Election, 1892. The directors wish that every facility should be given to the men in the employ of the company to record their votes, and, in order to prevent any cause of complaint of undue !:nr.ueriaa bdfng as in favour of any candidate, meetings on or canvass- ing in any 0,1 the works are strictly prohibited."

There has been shown in the window of Runcorn Liberal Club, this week, the cartoon issued by the Tories of Salisbury, in which an impersonation of the devil taking Mr. Gladstone to bell is repre- sented. The caricature is called "The G.O.M.'s Last Journey," and the words upon it are— Oh, the devil's got hold of the wire, And is dragging G.O.M. to the fire, For Home Rule he'll burn, And give G.O.M. his last turn, Oh, the devil's got hold of the wire. The =tom has caused considerable indignation.

In the present contest, in both Widnes and Run- corn, references are constantly being made to the Nonconformists in Ireland, and every attempt is made to raise up sectarian bigotry against the Catholics. It will interest Methodists to know that there are 34 Methodist candidates before the consti— tuenciesc and not one is a supporter of the policy of Lord Salisbury.

"it is your solemn duty as you honour God and love your fellow-men, to vote—to vote at any cost and trouble, and to vote on the side of righteous- ness Speaking generally and broadly, the conflict will be one of moral progress against ob- stinate moral declension—of purity against im- purity—of sobriety against drink and drunken- ness—of justicl agtinst class interests—of the many against the few." So says Dr. Stephenson.

Mr. T. P. O'Connor, M.P., has thrown himself in- to this election battle with all his old ardour and energy. He delivered two magnificent speeches to crowded and enthusiastic meetings at Widnes and Runcorn on Thursday night. He had previously that day spoken at Flint and in Wales, and at lace, near Wigan.

An influential meeting of Temperance reformers at Runcorn, after consideration of the attitude which the two candidates take in the Temperance question, have passed a resolution recommending all temperance and social reformers of the town and neighbourhood to vote for Mr. Brunner at the coming election,and to seek in other ways to secure his return. In Widnes division, Mr. Wade Deacon has the support of the temperance party.

Mr. Brunner has this week issued to the electors a pamphlet, which contains his fourth election address, his Parliamentary record, Mr. Gladstone's appeal to the nation, and the Cheshire Liberal pro- gramme. The record clearly sets forth how Mr. Brunner has voted on all the great questions of the day, and the clauses he has been the means of in- serting in Bills. There were also passed through his instrumentality the following Acts of Parlia- ment :-1888, Clerks of the Peace to Stipendiary Magistrates' Act ; 1890: An Act to prevent the spread of infectious diseases among human beings (smallpox fevers &c"); 1891 : Au Act to make easy the transfer of literary and scientific Institu- tions to local authorities; 1892 Brine Pumping (Compensation for subsidence) Act. Mr. Brunner has a record of which any member might well be proud, and there is no doubt that the electors will return him to Westminister to continue his useful labours. Accompanying the pamphlet is an admir- able portrait of Mr. Brunner which is well worth preserving.

div.head: DEATH OF OF A NONAGENARIAN.
div.p: DEATH OF OF A NONAGENARIAN.

We have to record the death,on Wednesday morn- ing, of a venerable and much respected inhabitant of Moore,the oldest in the district,Mr. John Banner, who died thPre on Wednesday morning. The de- ceased was born on the 20th of September, 1801, so that he was in his 91st year. He was formerly a coal dealer at Moore, his father having been the landlord of the Red Lion Inn at that place. The subject of our obituary bad lived about 511 years in the cottage in which he died, and with his wite who passed away about two years since, he en- joyed 63 years of happy matrimonial life. He had had excellent health until a few months since, and possessed a wonderful memory almost to the last.. Ile was a smoker and not an abstainer,, an early riser, a moderate eater, and careful and abstemious. in all his habits. In former days when educatioa was not so largely diffused as at present,Mr.Banner having an advantage over most of his neighbours. in that respect used to be applied to by people. from all parts of the district to read, and occasion- ally, to write letters for them. It was his delight. to recount some of the stirring ecents.of the early part of the- century for which he retained a clear recollection. Among his experiences there was one which he was always ready to relate for the edi- fication a his acquaintance° of more modern date, to whom it would seem altocot incomprehensible in. , the light of the changed conditions of tie times. ,He would describe how. there was an alarm that the great Napoleon was going to land at Fiddler's Ferry, and how he formed one cS about 200 young . men volunteers of Moore, Hatton, Dutton, and adjacent villages who armed themselves with pick-. axes, scythes, staves, and other implements,to meet._ the invader. The death of Mr. Banner, so univer- sally esteemed as he was, at such a patriarchal out age, has caused a feeling of mourning throughout the neighbourhood; and his funeral will no doubt be largely attended.

A young farmer named Henry Barratt, of Gonglatex, Cheshire, welt out shooting alone on Tuesday, and was found dead from the effects of a gunshot wound. At Valence on Tuesday, the novice, Mathias Radek, was guillotined for the murder of Father Ildehouse, secretary of the Trappist Monastery of aignebeils. A bicycle race from Paris to Nantes. and back, a idistance of 622 miles, has been won by M. Allard in 61 , hours 28 minutes. M. M. Meyer was second arriving A, hour and 52 minutes later.

div.head: BEFORE TUE MA.GISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE TUE MA.GISTRATES.

ANOTHER LOOOING-1101JSE DEN. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, Bridget Kimblin, 5, Morris's Yard, off Silver Square,was charged by Mr. Norman, inspector of nuisances, with keeping a lodging-house without being registered.--A constable deposed to finding in the kitchen, four men asleep on the floor, a man lying awake on the table, and a man in a chair. In the front room were found two beds, two women and a boy occupying one, and a woman the other. In the back room was a bed sup- posed to be occupied by the defendant's daughter-in- law and her husband. The place and the bed. clothes were very filthy, and there was a very offensive smell. —Mr. Norman said the defendant had been three times convicted of similar offences. It would occupy all an In- spector's time to keep to keep the people straight in the locality in which this house was.—The defendant was fined 10s. and costs.

DESTRUCTION OF TELEGRAPH INSULATORS. At the Warrington County Sessions on Wednesday, Alfred Sankey, a boy, was charged with wilfully break- ing, on Sunday afternoon, certain insulators by throw- ing stones at a telegraph pole in Warrington-road, Winwick. He pleaded guilty. Mr. John Doherty, superintending engineer, for the post office telegraphs department, North Western district:, said the destruction of these insulators was a growing evil. Upwards of 200 had to be repaired during the present year, having been broken by boys, out of sheer wilfulness. You could not measure the mischief done by the value of the insulators broken. That was not of so much consequence as the inconvenience caused by stopping communication. If an insulator was broken the wire fell down and became entangled with other wires, and each of these became inoperative.—Major Pickmere, one of the magistrates: Have you ever given information to the police about it? —Mr. Doherty said he had frequently, and the Home Secretary had issued circulars on the subject to all the Chief Constables in the kingdom. He (Mr. Doherty) did not like to fly at game like the defendant; probably he acted more heedlessly than wilfully, and he womd be satisfied if the Bench would indemnify the Company for the cost they had been put to, and admonish the lad.— The boy's father pleaded for him, and both ot them shed tears.—The magistrates gave the lad a severe caution and fined him Qs. Qd_

CHARGE OF CRIMINAL ASSAULT UPON A WOMAN. At the Warrington County Sessions on Wednesday, James Singleton, was charged with committing an indecent assault, also with committing a common assault about half past eleven p.m., on the 25th ult. on Margaret Andeston, his sister-in-law, a single woman, of Legh-st. Golbourne. Mr. Stuart,of Wigan, defended. She stated that between Newton, and Golborne, that defendant in the presence of his wife committed the offence upon which the wife pulled one of her boots off and " thrashed "him with it. The complainant denied having told Mr. Flibbert, of the Blue Bell Inn, Newton, a pcor law Guardian, that the defendant had only put his hand upon her shoulder. She made several conflicting statements in her evidence. She said she believed he had misbehaved himself to her out of spite, because she would not give hint his dinner on one occasion.—Mr. Hibbert deposed that on the 27th ult. she told him that Singleton had only put his hand on her shoulders,and she did not know what she was do- ing to summon him, also that he and she had had a dis- pute about some money.—Evidence was given that the complainant had had too much drink at nine o'clock on the night of the 25th, though she denied this. The pri- soner, it appeared, was sober.—P.C. Jones said Ander- ton complained to him of a criminal assault by the pri- soner, and he apprehended him under a warrant, and he said, "He is not a gentleman for issuing a warrant for ' her, and believing her. It is not right. I shall get five years."—The Bench considered the prisoner had been guilty of a common assault, and fined him 20s. and costs, in default a month's imprisonment. ELECTION CELEBRATIONS. Mary McCoan and Annie McCoan, her daughter, were charged at the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Wednesday, with being drunk and disorderly. on Friars' Green, also with assaulting James Henry Samson, a boy, and with using objectionable language—all on Tuesday night. Annie McCoan was also charged with obstructing the police by attempting to rescue her mother from their custody. It appeared that Samson was passing with some companions along Friar's Green, where a party of Irish women including the defendants took offence at some blue in his coat, and a melee en- sued in which bricks and stones were used as weapons. Mary McCoan rushed at him, and pulling out a knife, inflicting a slight wound on his face. She was arrested by the police, and the daughter interfered and at- tempted to rescue her. They used most filthy language. After hearing the evidence from which it appeared that the defendant Mary might not have meant to wound Samson, the Bench took this view of the matter and dis- missed her, but fined Annie ss. and costs.—Annie Ryan and Bodelia Knockton were then charged with being drunk and disorderly in Dolman's-lane, on Tuesday night, also with assaulting P.C.'s Turner and Delahaye. —lt appeared that the women were fighting and on the police interfering threw a piece of brick and a stone at the constables. The stone struck Turner on the fore- head, though he said it did not hurt him much.—Knock- ton said she and Ryan were singing about Pierpoint. He ought to coma and defend them. It was all through him that they were brought up. (Laughter.)—The Chief Constable : You have soon turned Pierpoint. I have heard something about you. You had blue on.— ,Knockton : It was green. I have green on my dress now.—Theprisoners were fined ss. and costs each.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE couRT.

SATIIIIDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess and Mr L. Voisey POCKET PICKING.—John Thompson, John Roberts Sarah McDonald, Thomas Brogden, and Thomas Thoma were charged with being suspicious characters, and frequenting Bank Quay railway station on Walking Day for an unlawful purpose.—Evidence was given by several railway officials to the effact that the prisoners loitered about the station from 11. 15 a.m. to 4. 17, when they were arrested. At 1.15 p.m. one of the prisoners was seen to put his hand in Mrs. Pritchard's pocket; the female prisoner and another prisoner attempting to screen the pickpocket's movements. The lady was afterwards questioned by a railway official as to whether she had missed anything, and she informed him that a purse and railway ticket had been abstracted. During the day many complaints were received as te people hav- ing had the contents of their pockets taken.—Several witnesses gave evidence to the effect that they saw th prisoners loitering about.—Detectives from Liverpoo and Manchester proved that Thompson, Roberts, and McDonald were convicted thieves, and that Thomas had been seen in the company of thieves at Manchester.— The prisoners were committed for twt:, months.—John Riley was committed for one month for attempting to pick the pocket of Mrs. Jones, a constable's wife, a Market Gate on the same day. THEFr.—John Collins was charged with stealint, the sum of 3s. Bd. from a labourer, named McGrah, whilst the latter was asleep in Brouchemitt's lodging house. It appeared that the prisoner entered the room of McGrak and abstracted the money from the waistcoat pocket of the complainant, whilst the latter was asleep. He was afterwards charged by Detective-sergeant Monaghan with the thett, and he admitted stealing the money And offered torefund it.—One month's imprisonment,

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Greenall) and I Aldermen Francomb and Harrison. DRUNIC—James Leigh, hawker, was charged with be- ing drunk at Market Gate, on Sunday afternoon, also under a warrant with being £22 in arrears with pay- ments for the maintenance of his wife. The order was made In 1889, and the warrant had been out since March. He was sent to jail for three months. ARMY DESERTION.—John Gibbons was charged with being a deserter on the 2nd inst.. from the Ist battalion of the South Lancashire Regiment stationed at Orford Barracks. He had got over the barracks wall and had changed clothes with a man, who was under the influence of drink.—lnspector Spinks said the prisoner could be charged with stealing the plain clothes he had on.—Alderman Francomb : Exchange is no robbery.— The Chief Constable said the uniform was brought to the Police Station, and the plain clothes were demanded, but no charge was preferred against the prisoner as to the clothes.—The prisoner said the man had his military cap yet.—Gibbons was handed over to the military authorities. DRUNK AND I DISORDERLY.—Lawrence Mannion drunk and disorderly in Buttermarkst-st., on Saturday, 55. Charles Harrop, 3, Egerton-st., was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Florsemarket-st.' on Saturday night, also with assaulting P.C. Roper. The constable said the prisoner had come on the Stockton Heath 'bus and would not pay his fare, and they had thrown him off the 'bus, and cut the back of his head. He was drunk in Horsemarket-st., and would not go away, upon which witness took him into custody. The pri- soner then kicked him several times. Witness and P.C. 16 got him to the station and he behaved most violently all the way to the station.—The prisoner said the police- man cut his head.—The Stockton Heath 'bus driver de- posed to the prisoner assaulting him and threatening to murder him. He tumbled off the step of the 'bus and cut his head.—Thomas Rowe said he saw the driver try- ing to push the prisoner backwards off the steps,and ad- vised him to come away quietly. His head was bleeding. He told the constable what he had seen, and the con- I stable pushed him. Witness tried to get him home, but could not,and went back and was taken into custody by the constable.-10s. and costs.—Ellen Carter, drunk and disorderly on Friar's Green, on Saturday night, dis- missed.—Martin Curley and Patrick Kilroy were charged • with being drunk and disorderly on Fnar's Green on Saturday night, also with breaking a cast iron utensil at the Police Station. They were lying down in the street drunk, shouting and singing.—Curley said the utensil • was accidentally broken.-103. and costs each.—Adam Ellis drunk and disorderly in Wilderspool-road, on Sunday morning.-205. and costs.—Martin Daley, in Winwick-St., on the 25th ult., ss.—Dominic McGowan, in Rylands-st., on the Monday morning previous, ss. and costs. UNSEEMLY BEHAVIOUR.—EIiza Smith for this behaviour in Winwick-road, on Sunday morning,was sentencad to three months' hard labour. CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—Samuel Dagnall, hawker, 32, Oliver-street, and Joseph Titchett, labourer, 22, Brick- street, were charged with cruelly treating a horse in Wilderspool-road, on Saturday night by whipping it unmercifully.—A witness named Dolan stated that the defendants were whipping the animal brutally. It was overloaded and could hardly stand, and stopped about every 20 yards for breath. Witness informed P.C. 6.— The constable corroborated. The horse was so weak it could scarcely stand. He had to take the whip away from the defendants, and brought them and the horse and cart to the police station. The horse had to be taken away from the cart opposite the police station or it would have fallen.—lnspector Spinks said the animal could hardly breathe and almost dropped.—lnspector Dowty, gave evidence as ta the condition of the horse. The horse had been hired from a Mr. Hamb- lett.—The men were each sent to prison for a month with hard labour.—Alderman Harrison complimented Dolan on appearing against the defendants and said if he could be allowed something as a reward, even a medal, he would deserve it.—Dolan said there were many things carried on in that town that would be reported if those who observed them had time, and which called for punishment. DRUNE.—James Mahon, of Haydock, drunk near the gas works on Sunday morning, was fined ss. ASSAULT ON A WouAn.—Wm. Smith was charged with violently assaulting Ellen Thompson, of Buckley- st., on Saturday night. He came into her husband's hoase and would not go out, and began tupping him, and struck her with a chair.—Wm. Thompson, the com- plainant's husband,said the defendant came to her house and asked for a certain girl. He said she was not in,and the defendant then assaulted him,and he had to strike him back to de:end himse/i. The defendant gave witness a black eye by tupping him with his head. He struck wit- ness's wife with a chair, and picked up a chair also a washing pan to strike her,but he prevented him.--Another witness named Warburton corroborated,and said the de- fendant threw a pot at him. Two constables deposed to his violence.—The defendant said Warburton gave him a black eye with the poker. The defendant was sentenced to three months' hard labour. He threatened with an oath to break Warburton's head when he came out,and was called back and sentenced to an additional month for contempt of court. FIGHTING.—Maria Gibbons, factory hand, 7, Old-road, and Margaret Price, fustian cutter. Silver-st., for fight- ing in Bridge-street, on the 24th ult., were dismissed.— James Swindells, labourer, 241, Winwick-road, Andrew Ford, engine fitter, 11, Kerfoot-st., and George Broad- hurst, greengrocer, 235, Winwick-road, for fighting in that road on the 25th ult., were mulcted in costs, 7s. each.
TOESDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett:_
DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Edward Wilkinson, 5, Haydock-st., drunk and disorderly in that street on Monday night, was fined ss. including COSLS. WEDNESDAY.—Before_ Councillor James Fairclough and
Alderman Harrison.

DRUNK AND D I ;0121 E—RTY:LIIO.II-0-1: Connolly charged with being drunk and disorderly in Church-street, on Tuesday night, also with using objectionable language on Saturday, was dismissed, the Bench excusing her con- duct on Tuesday as it was election day.—Mary Tomkins, drunk and disorderly in Hall-street on Tuesday night, was discharged on the same ground.—Cornelius Delany, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Irlam-street, on Wednesday morning was dismissed. TIIURSDAL—Before Alderman Sutton and Captain

Ridgway. DESERTION OF FAMILY.—John White was charged by Mr. B. Shearer, on behalf of the Guardians, with ab- sconding from the town and leaving his children charge- able to the Union. He kad been away in Yorkshire and subsequently at Salford,where he was apprehended. The cost for the maintenance of the children had been £l5. He was sentenced to a month's imprisonment. DRUM/T.—James Thorpe was charged with being drunk in Irlam-st. He came to the police station and wanted to go to Liverpool, thinking the building was the rail- way station. He became very disorderly, and was put out, but came back in a quarter of an hour and created another disturbance. He was put out again, and ordered to go away but clung to a lamp post, using abominable language and refusing to stir. He was then locked up. He was discharged on promising to leave the town. FRlDAY.—Before Aldermen Harrison (chairman) and . .

Wright. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Cartledge, sweep, for being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-st., on the Ist ult., was fined ss.—Martin Kelly was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Stoney Yard that morning. He was throwing bricks through his father's windows and on the way to the station he was very violent and tore his clothes. He was also charged with assaulting James Thomas, of the Royal Arms, Bank-st.—Thomas said the prisoner broke two windows in his house, because he could not have beer in his house without money when drunk. He also struck him across the counter.—The Chief Constable said the police of the olden time were the men to settle such characters. They used to carry a good stick for them and save the town and county a good deal of expense. A mouth's imprisonment. NON-MAINTENANCE.—Joseph Green, carter, Leigh, Frederick Goodwin, labourer, 19 Winwick-street, Edwa d Grounds, 22, Pinner's Brow, A. Houltram, bottle blower, St. Helens, John Sherwood, Widnes, Thomas Lythgoe, Warrington, H. Taylor, Liverpool, and W. Taylor, Pitt-st., were charged by Mr. S. Shearer, on behalf of the Guardians, with non-maintenance of relatives left chargeable to the Union, and orders were made against them. UNSEEMLY BEHAVIOUR.—Maria Barrett, of 3, Naylor- st., for this conduct, in Battersby-lane that morning, was sent to prison, for seven days.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS.

WEDNESDAY--Before Mr. Comber (chairman), and Major Picktnere. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Job Brimelow, at Poulton, on the 19th ult., 53. and costs ; James Eckersley, at Poulton, on the same date, 53. including costs.— Edward Sharpies, at Croft, on the 26th ult., ss. and costs ; David Lythgoe, at Croft, on the same date, ss. including costs ; Wm. Hill, employed by the Cheshire Lines Committee was charged with being drunk and refusing to quit the Dog and Patridge at Poulton, on the 27th ult., with assaulting P. C. Fleming in the execution of his duty, and with damaging the officer's uniform to the extent of 10s. P. C. Fleming said the landlady asked him several times to go and he refused npon which witness was called in to him, but he still refused, and seized him by the throat. He struggled with him and he tore his trousers and cape. With the assistance of Sergeant Barnes he got him to the lock up. He was fined ss. and costs, and the damage. CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—James Smith of Atherton, and Henry Cook, of Chowbent, driver, were charged with cruelty to a horse at Southworth-with-Croft, on the 12th ult.—Mr. Dowty said the animal was nearly 20 years of age and in wretched condition and was being used for a conveyance with seventeen passengers, having been driven eight miles.—P.C.'s 761 and 1318 corroborated.— Smith said there were only ten passengers, and the horse was in good condition.—Smith was fined 20s. and costs, and Cook was dismissed. ASLEEP ON HIS LURRY.—Ed ward Owen, for being asleep on his lurry on the night of the 21. t ult., at Penketh, was fined ss. including costs. Flowrino WomEN.—Annie Weston, Maria Simpson and Nancy ROSCO 9 were charged with fighting at Sankey Bridges on the 27th of June. They were bound over in £5 each to keep the peace for 6 months.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. C. Reynolds and Mr. James

Handley. THE MASONIC HOTEL—Peter Corns, of Widnes, was granted authority to sell at the Masonic Hotel, Runcorn, under the license formerly held by the late Hugh- Tracey. MISCELLANEOUS.—Sarah Bowen, Sarah Price, Samuel Cox, and John Steel, were fined for drunkeness.—Jonas Hunt, Mason-St., summoned Mary Baker for an assault, dismissed.—Mary Ann Parker was sentenced to seven I days' imprisonment for sleeping out.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY. JULY 9. 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. JULY 9. 1892.
ST. LUKE'S NEW CHURCH.
LAYING OF THE FOUNDATION STONE.

On Monday afternoon the foundation for St. Luke's church was laid on a site in Liverpool-road, a short distance beyond the present Bank Quay Mission room carried on in connection with Holy Trinity Church. The clergy, and choristers, the latter in surplices, and the members of the building Committee, assembled at the Mission Room and marched thence, accompanied by the Right Rev. Dr. Ryle, Bishop of Liverpool and the Mayor of War- rington, who wore the civic chain. Among those present in addition to them were the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton and Mrs. Carleton, the Rev. W. E. Glenn, curate in charge of the mission, the Rev. Canon Dodd, rector of Stretton, and Mrs. Dodd, the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, rector of Winwick, the Rev. Canon Greenall, the Rev. F. W. Willis, rector of Warrington, and Mrs. Willis, the Rev. F. C. Timing, curate of the Parish Church, the Rev. T. M. R. Young Hughes, curate of St. Paul's, the Rev. F. Slater, vicar of St. James's, the Rev. E. S. Jackson, vicar of Sankey, the Rev. J. J. Langham, vicar of Padgate and Mrs. Langham, the Rev. J. J. Carson, curate of Winwick, the Rev. E. D. Garven and Miss Garven, the Mayoress, Lady Greenall, Alderman Wright. Alderman and Mrs. Harrison, Councillor James Fairclough, Mr. Buckton, Mr. John White, Mr. McGregor Mrs. Davies, Mr. G. F. White, Mr. H. J. Westbrook, and Mr_ Dunbobbin. On reaching the foundation stone, where a numerous company had collected to witness the ceremony the usual service was conducted by the Bishop who was assisted by the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton and the , Rev. Canon Penrhyn, the hymns being accompanied on I the harmonium by Mr. R. Evans. The stone was to have been laid by the Hon. Elizabeth Wilson Patten, but I in her absence, Lady Greenall, at the request of Mr. 'Carleton, erformed the ceremony, declaring that in the faith of Jesus Christ she placed the foundation stone in the name of God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Ghost. A silver trowel was handed to her with which to perform the work, which bore the following inscription :—" Presented by the Building Committee to the Hon. Elizabeth Wilson Patten, on the occasion of her laying the foundation stone of St. Luke's Church, Bank Quay, Warrington, July 4th, 1892. The BISHOP, after laying the stone, delivered an address. He remarked that he need hardly say that that occasion was a most interesting one. They were assembled there to see the foundation laid of a new church in the large, growing, and very important town of Warrington, a town by no means, the least im- portant in his diocese, and one for which he had no doubt there was a greater future yet to come than had been dreamt of in times past. (Hear, hear.) He should be unworthy of the name of bishop and the office that he held if he did not feel a deep interest in every additional church which was built within the diocese to which God had called him. When he entered upon it 12 years ago he found a population of 12,000 people, and for that huge population there had then been provided only 170 parish and district churches. Any- one who felt for the souls of others must have felt what a great spiritual famine there must needs be, and how far short the Church of England came of her position as the established church, the church of the poor, the church that professed to provide for the souls of the people living in this country. This consideration caused him many anxious thoughts, and he did all he could to stir up others to come forward and by their means enable more churches to be built, and he desired to thank and bless God that so much had been done in the short space of 12 years. At least 1 35 new churches had been added to the churches of the diocese. The church about to be built would make one , more, and he hoped that before very long it would be furnished and completed. He trusted it would prove a blessing to all the inhabitants af that part of Warring- ton and to that great town itself. The system of the Church of England which provided a minister for every district, and looked to him to remember that he was bound to be pastor, visitor, and friend to every man, woman and child living in that district was an admir- able system, and one that could never be surpassed, and where it was properly backed it could not fail to be a great blessing. It was to the volun- tary principle of which so much was heard to the voluntary exertions and offerings of the Church of England that such results were due, and they 11 furnished an admirable proof that that principle was valued in the Church of England as much as in any church or denomination in the land. The Bishop then expressed his deep regret at the loss the rural deanery 1 of Winwick had sustained in the removal by death of their rev. friend, Canon Whitley, whom he described as a fine specimen of a grand old English clergyman, who had stood by the Church in evil and in good report, and carried out its work in the way the Church intended it to be carried out, and had left behind him no enemies. 1 His lordship reminded those present that £l,OOO was yet required for the completion of the school, and , appealed to the liberality of Church people to supply the deficency. When they had, he observed, such liberal friends as Sir Gilbert Greenall, and others there, who were giving an example and a pattern of 1 what could be done, he did trust that there were yet others in Warrington who would say that they would not be left behind, but that they would have a hand in this business as well as Sir Gilbert Greenall. The bishop then explained that the Hon. Elizabeth Wilson Patten was prevented from being present by the weak state of health of the venerable Lord Winmarleigh, but remarked that he had not the slightest doubt that she and her father took an interest in what was passing there, and that she would have been happy to come if she had been able to do so.—The remainder of the service was then read, and the benediction having been pronounced by the Bishop the proceedings concluded.

div.head: BEIN' BOTHER'T !
div.p: BEIN' BOTHER'T !
Aw'm in a deawnreet fix this wick, To oather prose or rhyme : This darn'd elecshun's tarn'a my yed,

An' knock'd me eaut o' time I - Aw feel ez if aw'd like to bowt, A hundert miles away; Fer aw'm inclined to think aw'st get mischief if aw stay. To hear um'rangle i'yon snug, Each sheautin fer his mon ; Yo'd think sum window panes hed crack'd, ,

Er th' hauf o'th' roof lied gone! Eaur Cocker tells us plump an' plain, He's gooin't vote fer Legh ; An' swears by aw that's good he'll put Th' Gladstonians" up a tree !" An' Mat, a Tory, sta'nch an' true, Gets ravin' o'er Home Rule ; An' sez a chap ez votes fer that, Wants purrin' to the Dule ! Baur good owd Butler then breyks in, Wi' argyments genteel ; An' vows he duzn't care a d—m! He'z gooin't vote fer Neill. He wants to see the Grand Owd Mon " Once moor at th' yed o'th State ; To save this country fro disgrace, Befoor it gets too late. Straight into aw the Tories theer, He gies it um red hot ! That pizent mutton saddle seems To bother tam a lot ! Then th' Boss o'th' Buildin' Club ull try To say a word or two, But aw's o'er then ! the fat's i'th' fire! An' ther's a pillyloo Owd Booth's Salvation Army Band Nare aiquil'd this fer nize ! Yo'd shudder if yo heerd um bless Each other's limbs an' eyes ! No wonder, then, aw'm botheit mitch, An' want to slip away Peril aw don't, aw railly fear

My wits ull go astray! "0 would I were" a Sammy Brid, Wl' backert's-flyin' wings; Then I wud flee an' be at rest, Wheer th wild canary sings: Or reet away to Bungaroo, Wheer th' os.trick lays her eggs; Theer aw cud surely be at peace— Yores truly,
TUII 0' PEGS. Nyowton, God bless o', July Bth, 1892.

div.head: DEATH OF THE REV. CANON WHITLEY.
div.p: DEATH OF THE REV. CANON WHITLEY.

The death of the Rev. J. Whitley, Rector of Newton-in-Makerfield, which occurred on Sunday morning at three o'clock, came as a surprise to a large number of people, many of whom were not even aware that he was unwell. The deceased gentleman, who it appears was 79 years of age, was about 10 days be tore his death officiating at two funerals, one being that of a very old friend. It was whilst awaiting the arrival of one of the funerals that he took a chill, from which he rallied, but afterwards he had a relapse. Dr. Taylor who is acting for Dr. White, of Warrington, was called in, but pneumonia supervening, he obtained the assist- ance ot Dr. Starkey Smith. their services how- ever, were unavailing, and the deceased became un- conscious in the early part of Saturday morning last, and passed quietly away, as stated, without having recovered consciousness. The Rev. Canon Whitley was born in Liverpool, on the 25th July, 1813, but his family originally came from the village of Whitley in Cheshire. As a boy he attended a public school in Faulkner Square, Liverpool, and con- ducted by the father of the late Mr. Clarke Aspinall. After due preparation at this school, he matriculated at Queen's College, Cambridge, and after a course of studies, graduated B.A. in 1837, proceeding to his M.A. in 1840. On leaving College, he proceeded to Durham, for his divinity, and in 1837 was ordained by the Archbishop of York as curate of Scarborough, where he continued until 1839. In thatyear he received the appointment of incum- bent of Openshaw,Manchester. His inclination, however, was for a country parish, as being more in accordance with his ideas, which were those of a model country gentleman. He laboured in the rapidly growing parish of Openshaw from 1339 to 1846, when he received the appointment at Wargrave. He could not, however,take up the duties immediately after being appointed, and these were undertaken by his brother, the Rev. Canon Whitley, D.D., Vicar of Bedlington, who came into resi- dence soon after the retirement of the Rev. Mr. Palairet. At that time, although a church had existed at Newton for something like 100 years, it did not carry with it a parish, being only a donative church. Wargrave Church was built some 50 years later, and was styled the Parish Church of Newton-in-Makerfield, and the in- cumbent bore the title of Rector of Newton. Some time after Mr. Whitley's appointment, the people of Newton clamoured for a parish to be assigned to their chuich, and public meetings were held to further the object. After much argument, Mr. Whitley, to use his own words, "cut the painter," and gave the Newton people their desire,and to this day their parish is known as St. Peter's, whilst Emmanuel Church, Wargrave, re- tains its title of the Parish Church of Newton-in-Maker- field. When the deceased gentleman came to Wargrave he found the church very much out of repair, and things in regard to the service most incomplete. There was no organ, and his wife had to supply the needed music !rem a harmonium, and she also acted as leader or tutor of the choir. She also was of great assistance in the work of the parish. Since his appointment, the church has undergone much alteration; the harmonium was discarded and a small organ occupied its place; but this also has given place to the present effec- tive instrument. The church has been re-seated, re-roofed, additions to gallery, and many other important structural alterations and additions have been carried out. His life at Wargrave has been singularly peaceful and uneventful, as he was essentially a peacemaker and arbitrator. and an adviser in the confidence of a great number of people, He was largely trusted, and frequently acted as executor and ' trustee, and guardian of children, and many are greatly indebted to hie wise management of their property. He was one of the founders of the• Earlestown Building Society, and he remained a trustee up to the time of his death. He has often spoken of the services ha used to conduct for an old friend of his at the church of " St. Peters ad Vincular," in the Tower of London, but he was a man, who was most reticent in regard to his early life. He was instrumental in securing the erection of Golborne and Earlestown churches, and spoke of them as his god-children. Ile was made a honorary canon of the diocese of Liverpool in 1882, and rural dean of Win- wick in 1883. He leaves one son Mr. Charles Whiteley.

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

The funeral took place on Tuesday at Stretton. A service was held in the Wargrave Church at 12 o'clock, conducted by the Rev. J. Wadeson, curate, when there were present Rev. Canon Whitley (D.D) brother, Mr. Charles Whitley, son, Mr. C. W. Owen (cousin), Mr. Hart. (principal mourner), linvs. Canon Rycroft, Canon Penrhyn, F. Willis, H. S. Byrth, W. Richardson, J. Smith, F. W. Johnston, T. R. Matthews, E. W. W. Kaye, J, Davies, and Jas. Allatt, Messrs. T. W. Legh, J. E. Pardey, T. J. Gillespie, C. B. F. Borron, R. Stone, A. Peake, and J. Starkey, Colonel McCorquodale, Drs. Watkins, flandyside,Valentine and H. Thompson,and the past and present sidesman of the church. During the ser- vice the choir sang the deceased's favourite hymn" Lead kindly light." The coffin which was of plain polished oak with brass mountings, bore a plate with the inscription "John Whitley, born July 25th, 1813, died July 3rd, 1892." There was only one wreath upon the coffin, and this was sent by some members of the family. Many other wreaths and crosses were sent, which had been placed upon the grave. After the service the coffin was I borne out of the church by the sidesmen to the hearse, and the funeral cortege left about 12.30, and proceeded by road to Stretton, the interment taking place at the parish church, and many of those mentioned above were present at the grave side. The choir was also present, and sang the hymn "Thy way not mine 0 Lord." The remainder of the service was conducted by the Rev. H. S. Byrth, vicar of Bardesley. and formerly curate of Wargrave.

div.head: CHARGE OF WOUNDING.
div.p: THE CHARGE OF WOUNDING.

At the Magistrates' Court, Warrington, on Thurs- day, before Alderman Sutton and Captain Ridgway, Thomas Savage, of 33, Back School Brow, was brought up on remand, charged with wilfully and maliciously inflicting grievous bodly harm on James Owen, his brothet-in-law, of 4, Orchard-street, on the 20th ult. Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, Town Clerk, appeared for the prosecution, and said the prisoner had at first been charged with inflicting the wound with intent to do bodily harm, but he withdrew the charge of intent. The case arose out of jealousy on the part of the prosecutor and the prisoner as to the latter's wife. Sarah Owen, the prosecutor's mother, said she went to her daughter's the prisoner's wife's house in con sequence of something she heard on the 20th oft. Thepri Boner was abusing his wife, and had &caller a black eye and bruised her face. Witness said if she was as strong as she was two years ago she would give him a good hiding. He began throwing crockery about, and some words passed between the three of them, he smashing all he could lay hands on. Her son, James Owen, came up,and the prisoner saw him in the yard,and threatened he would kill him if he came in. Owen went in, and the prisoner immediately set upon him. There was a struggle, and they bath fell. They got up, and Savage threw several pieces of broken crockery at Owen, one of which hit him on the temple,and it bled, and another hit him on the cheek bone. Savage said. " How does that fit ?" Her son went into the yard,and Savage went upstairs, and jeered at him through the window. The prosecutor threw several pieces of brick at him, and one of them broke a pane. Both men were drunk. The prosecutor was taken to the Infirmary. William Clark, of 7, Essex-street, a youth, gave generally corroborative evidence. He said the prisoner at the upstairs window pointed a stick at the prosecutor as he stood in the yard as if the stick were a gun and said he would shoot him, and the prosecutor then threw the pieces of brick. Owen's mother asked him to go away but he said no ; I ,will give him illusing my sister,—and went in and then the struggle commenced. Arthur Lomax, 17 Crossley street, and another youth, said Owen went in and struck Savage first hitting him in the face with his fist then they struggled and fell.— Dr. Bowden, senior house surgeon, at the infirmary, deposed to finding that the prosecutor's skull was fractured, and trying t.s remove pieces of plate from the head, and broke off two pieces. He made another attempt to extract the material but did not succeed. There was another slight wound on the left ear. The prosecutor, was not out of danger. The prosecutor, who was very weak and ill, had to be seated while he "gave evidence. He said he was married, but lived with his mother, and not with his wife. The prisoner's wife was his sister. He gave an account of the circumstances mainly agreeing with the prisoner's evidence, except that he denied striking the prisoner, or telling Mr. Owen, that he would give him it for ill-using his sister. He was not drunk and did not know whether the prisoner was or not. The cause of the quarrel, was that Savage, wanted to say he caught him with his (witness's,) sister the prisoner's wife, but that was a lie.—P.C.Newey, hav- ing given evidence, as to the apprehension of the prisoner, he was comsnitted for trial at the Liverpool Quarter sessions, bail,,in two sureties of £lO. each, being con- sented to.
THE SMOKE BALL CASE.

Mr. Justice Hawkins, on Monday, gave Judgment in the case of Carhill v. the Carbolic Smoke Ball Company, in which plaintiff claimed the £lOO reward offered by defendants to anyone who contracted the influenza after using one of their smoke balls according to directions. His Lordship gave judgment for the plaintiff, thinking she had earned the reward.
