div.head: MR.LATHAM'S CANDIDATURE. 1
div.p: MR.LATHAM'S CANDIDATURE. 1

MEETING IN STOCKTON HEATH SCHOOLS.— SPEECH BY DR. HOUSTON. A largely attended meeting was held in St. Thomas's Schools, Stockton Heath, on Thursday night. Mr. J. Crosfleld presided, and was supported on the platform by Dr. Houston, Q.C., Captain Rodgers, Mr. L. Broderick ( Wilmslow), Mr. S. T. Woodhouse, Mr. . Pierpoint (Warrington), Mr. W. Davison, Mr. Langland, and Mr. Butler. The CHAIRMAN congratulated the electors on having permission to meet in that room, and upon the fact that the election in that division had been conducted with such an absence of rowdyism, and distort ance of the meetings. He congratulated the electors also on having the privilege of voting by ballot, because he remembered when the voters in Cheshire could not call their souls their own, and were driven to the poll like so many sheep, and were afraid that if they gave their vote for a Liberal they would lose their emoluments and be turned out of their farms. Voters had now the pro- tection of the ballot, and they had to thank the Liberal party for it. The Tory party resisted it as long and as hard as they possibly could, and they might well, because it took away from them one of the greatest powers they possessed, of getting what he called an unfair House of Commons. The voters were afraid of voting according to their consciences in some parts of the country to-day. The Tory party were trying to frighten the voters in the agricultural districts by telling them that their votes would not be secret. That was perfectly untrue. They had got a candidate who was well worthy of their support in Mr. Latham. (Applause.) He was very sorry that gentleman was not able to be present, he having two meetings in other parts of the division. He remembered Mr. Latham's father well. He represented Crewe for some years, and he was acknow- ledged by both parties to be one of the greatest authori- ties on any question affecting the land in this country. He was glad to say that they had a candidate who was a worthy son of a worthy father. (Applause.) The Chairman proceeded to combat the charge of being separatists made against Liberals supporting Horne Rule, asserting that the Home Rulers were the true Unionists—(applause)--who wished to unite Ire- land and England by the bonds of sympathy. It was the sympathy being shown by the English people giving them hope for the future, which made them more contented and peaceful than they had been in this century befmre. It was not Mr. Balfour's Coer- cion Bill that had done so. Coercion never pacified a nation yet, and never would. (Hear, hear, and " No.") The Chairman, dealing with the argument that under Homo Rule the Protestants would be oppressed by the Catholics, cited facts by way of contrasting the ab- sence of persecution by Dublin Catholics of Protestants there with the unfair dealing of Belfast Protestants with Catholics. He quoted John Bright as saying that Ulster Protestants had purchased Protestant ascendancy at the price of the ruin and degradation of their country. If the Home Rule Bill was carried,he continued, we should see such peace and contentment and prosperity in that unhappy country Ireland, that it had never seen in the life of any man living. (Applause.) All the measures promoting the happiness,contentment, and prosperity of England had come from the Liberal party, and had been opposed by the Tories. If they had ever done any good it was through fear of the people,not through sympathy. The meaning of 'Toryism was selfishness. (Hear, hear.) And he would strongly advise those in that division,es- pecially farmers and farm labourers,if they would be re- presented by a gentleman who would show sympathy towards them and attend to their interests, to vote for Mr. Latham and not Mr. Egerton. (Loud applause.) Mr. W. PIERPOINT next spoke. He commended Mr. Latham to the electors as a candidate in whose address =moderate politician could see anything to take excep- tion. After reading the passage in Mr. Latham's address advocating agricultural legislation to give the farmer compensation for improvements and the like, the speaker strongly supported his policy in this respect, and cited his own experience in having to manure expensively an exhausted piece of land lie had taken under Mr. Smith Barry, pointing out how impossible it would be for ordinary farmers to do this because if their inability at present to get compensation for thus increasing the value of the land. He advocated the formation of district parish councils, and remarked that he would like them to take great interest in preventing the closing of pub- lic footpaths,encroachments en main roads, and absorp- tion of common land, mentioning how Penketh Common had been enclosed, for the benefit, not of the township, but of a few freeholders, and remarking that there were public footpaths in this district looked on as private property and barred with gates. Mr. Pierpoint also supported Mr. Latham's principle of giving the manage- ment of all schools where there was contribution of pub- lic money to the ratepayers, and cited a case to the contrary of a school " not five miles from there," over which, though it was in receipt of a public grant, the clergyman set himself up against the managers, and claimed absolute control. The clergyman and manag- ers were both Tories, and this was the first instance they had heard of where a Tory parson had set himself against Tory managers of a school. (Laughter.) He concluded by proposing :—" This meeting considers Mr. A. M. Latham a fit and proper person to represent Hnutsford division in Parliament, and pledges itself to use its best endeavours to place him at the head of the poll on Monday next." (Applause.) Captain RODGERS seconded. Referring t the allot- ments question he gave an interesting account of a con- versation lie had had in Lincolnshire with a Conservative who, ha said, stood at the head of his profession, of Lincolnshire Ram breeding. This farmer had given to him testimony of his experience or allotment holders which showed that they were better farm labourers, and that since they held the allotments they had not had to go into the Workhouse during the winter as formerly; also that men were induced by the inducement of holding them to leave the towns and come to the country. The Liberal measures carried by the Conservatives, said the speaker, had" simply been passed to dish the Whigs," but in passing them they had done well for the Liberals, having broken through old principles and left it for the Liberals to drive home the wedge. (Applause,) Con- servatives loved power too much to become true Liberals. The true Liberal divested himself of power to lay it on to the people. The Conservatives thus would cl aim for one person two or three votes ; the Liberals did not go in for this sort of thing, but were going to throw it off. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN said he like the rest of those present, deeply sympathised, with Dr. Houston in that he was not that day member for Warrington. (" It was their loss.") He knew what Warrington was as well as most people. (Laughter and ap- plause.) He had fought in Warrington politically 40 years, and he knew what Tory tricks and dodges were—(laughter)—and what the influence of the beer barrel was in Warrington. That constituency did not fight straight and square. (Cries of " Hear, hear.") It was not in Warrington a question entirely of Liberalism and Conservatism, but the Liberal party there had to fight against the beer barrel. (Loud applause.) He was sure they all admired the pluck and endurance Dr. Houston had shown in fighting the election there. Every credit was due to him, and the Liberal inhabit- ants of Warrington were proud to have had a candidate who had fought such a noble battle. (Much cheering.) Dr. HOUSTON, who rose amidst tremendous cheering, said tkat was positively his first appearance in the char- acter of a defeated candidate—(laughter)— and he supposed he ought to be greatly depressed, but he was not at all as depressed as he should be. (A laugh.) He could assure them it had not turned a hair or taken a feather. (another laugh.) Pos,ibly they might think it was because he had so little of the one and none at all of the other. (Applause and laughter.) He was told that day that he had been very ill, but he could assure them he never felt better in his life, and he expected to live to fight many a good fight. (Loud applause.) He was very much obliged to them for the very kind reception they had given him. He was probably a little out of place in an agricultural consti- tuency, because he was a town-bred man, and he knew very little about farming. Of course he could tell a. sheep from a goat—(laughter)—but he was entirely unlearned in the knowledge of manures, and the rotation of crops was an unfathomable mystery to him. (A laugh.) Captain Rogers had said that he understood where the agricultural shoe pinched. He (Dr. Houston) ' could see it was somewhere about the corn. (Loud laughter.) Now, to come to business, he wanted to know how they were going to vote, that was the question. The election was coming on very soon, and they would have to make up their minds. They all knew the advice that " Punch" gave to those about to marry—don't. His advice to those who were about to vote Tory was—don't. (Ap- plause.) He would give them some striking arguments why they should not vote Tory. They might perhaps sus- Peet by that time that he was an Irishman.(Laughter and applause.) Now, they knew their old friend the Scotch- inan—(laughter)—who said that honesty was the best policy, and that they might believe him for he had tried " baith." (Much laughter.) The Irish had tried both. Some years age when this Home Rule Bill question came to the surface the Tories began to be wonderfully friendly with the Nationalists of Ireland. The Tories sent a real live Lord-lieutenant to interview Mr. Parnell. In a general way they winked their right eye, and said" If you vote for us you will see what we will do for you." And—it was the only foolish thing the Nationalists of Ireland ever did—they believed the wink meant Home Rule, and accordingly voted Tory to a man. Well, they did not get Home Rule, but they got Coercion, which was a very different thing because he lived in Ire- land, and knew what sort of a thine it was though they did not clap their paw on film. (Laughter.) But now, mark his words, he was speaking that night to a meeting more or less composed of workingmen, and if the workingmen of this country voted Tory they would get something that would have the same relation to the things they wanted to get as coercion bore to Home Rule. (Cries of" Hear, hear.") And if they voted Tory and they got that thing he would say "Serve you right." (Loud applause.) Now they wanted very badly some of the things mentioned that night and many other that might be mentioned, but they would never get these things—mind he told them now—till the Irish people had got the thing that they

wanted, Home Rule. (Great applause.) Home Rule stood like a wall of brass between them and their rights. It was not the fault of Ireland—(cries of " No ")—it was their misfortune that it wasso. (Hear, hear.) But the fact was so, and he wanted the workingmen who heard him that night,they were longing and thirsting for those rights that had been withheld from them so long,to understand that unless and until Ireland was given what she justly demanded they would not get one jot or one tittle of their just demands, they would be withheld from them till that great justice had been done. (Loud cheersng.) Dr. Houston then proceeded to deal with what he described as the" great Ulster bogey," with which he said the Tories were trying to frighten the electors, that of the persecution of Ulster Protestants by the Irish Catholics, and after advancing the facts with which he had already made the constituency of Warrington well acquainted, illustratiag his remarks by pointing to a map to show the geographical significence of Ulster as compared with the rest of Ireland. He expressed his readiness to be per- secuted in the same way as the Protestants of Ireland , are persecuted and to wear the crown uf martyrdom on such terms all his days ; and the more he was martyrised the better he would like it. (Applause.) As a high official had told him, the Catholics of Ireland would as soon think of cutting their right hands off as enquiring what was the religion of a man who stood for a corporate office. Why then, assome that the people of Ireland, under a local Par- liament, which would be held in the light of day, under the eyes of civilisation, under the eyes of Europe, America, and the colonies, would reverse the practice which had been invariable In the country? It was a shame, a cruel shame, for these people to be getting up, with Lord Salisbury at their head, and maligning and calumniating the people upon whom they had been trampling. (Applause.) He had said that the Irish people were determined to have Home Rule. History bore him out in that. Neither tricks nor toils had turned them by one hair's-breadth from the path they had pur- sued. They had sacrificed their property,and what was much more valuable, their liberty, ay, and many of them their lives in the great cause of Irish.nationa- .

lity. (" True.") And did his hearers think that Mr. Balfour's Coercion Bill and Mr. Balfour's Star Chamber was going to turn them aside from that historical path. ("Never.") They had trodden it for seven long centuries, and they would tread it for seven centuries more if necessary. (Hear, hear.) It was handed down from father to son, children were brought up in that faith ; they sucked it in with their mother's milk, and he an Irishman standing upon an English platform that night, told them it was useless to try to turn the Irish people away from the attainment of their object. Everything that had been done in Eng- land, 80 or 90 Coercion Acts, the gallows, pitch caps,and all the other machinery of tyranny had not succeeded in the past, did not succeed in the present, and would never succeed in the future. (Enthusiastic applause.) And now it was the business of the English electors to see that this Home Rule question was settled. The present state of things was an injury to the empire—(hear,bear) —and a danger to the empire. It was the weak point in the armour of Great Britain, it was the great stain upon its history. She who had been holding up the flag el liberty all over the world, that had been extending her assistance to struggling nationalities all over Europe, she would not extend her sympathy and her assistance to the struggling nationality that was within a stones throw of her own shores. (" Shame.") How could she hold up her head, how could she taunt Russia with her autocracy as long as Dublin Castle lived ? It was idle for them to imagine that any- thing but the one solution of this question ever would be accepted in Ireland. Let them make up their minds to that. The corollary from that was that they work- ing-men were kept out of their heritage because Irishmen were kept out of theirs. Dr. Houston then passed in review some of the reforms demanded in Eagland, and dealing with the allotments question said Mr. Chamber- lain had been a Judas, but was now running Ananias close by stating that there were 130,000 allotments under the Tory Allotments Bill, whereas the Government them- selves admitted the other day that there were only 2,700 comprising only 1,100 acres. (Great applause and laughter.) He concluded by saying, that unless a Liberal Government were placed in power, whether it was an Allotments Bill or any other Bill they wanted to have carried in the interests of the labouring classes they had not the smallest chance of getting any real or substantial measure of redress. (Applause.) All he had got to say was—vote for a Liberal. (Renewed applause.) The resolution was put and carried unanimously. On the motion of Mr. RUTTER, seconded by Mr. PIER- POINT, a vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman, and the meeting concluded.

div.head: WARRINGTON" TRIP DAY."
div.p: WARRINGTON" TRIP DAY."

As in former years the Saturday after Walk- ing Day was takan advantage of for the promotion of a number of Works' trips from Warrington. All of these, favoured on the whole with fine weather, appeared to have passed off suczessfully. A large number of the employes of Whitecros Wire Com- pany, with their wives and children, were eon- veyed by two trains from Bank Quay Station to Blackpool, the first leaving at 6.45 am., the second at 7 a.m. Blackpool was reached in good time. giving all a full day's enjoyment, as the weather was fine up to 5.30 p.m., when rain fell heavily. An enjoyable day was, however, spent. The trip , arrangements were successfully made by the secre- tary, Mr. Samuel Dunbobbin, and a committee. aMessrs. Crosfield and Sons' workmen, to the number of over 500, proceeded by train, leaving about half-past eight,to Southport. Mr. W. H. Robinson had the man- agement of the trip. At the celebrated watering place they passedi a delightful day, many disportimr them- selves n the electric launch on the lake, and tie' winter and botanic gardens, Kew gardens were visite , admis- sion being kindly granted for the men at half price. The exhibition of pictures at the Alexandra Hall was also a centre of attraction. The excursionists reached home about half-past 10 o'clock. The excursion in connection with Messrs. Rrlands B 7„ works numbering nearly 800 reached Blackpool Oil Monday morning at 8.30. The weather was fine throughout the day, and a pleasant time was spent. The return journey was commenced about 8.15, and War- rington was safely reached at ten p.m. The arrange- ments for the excursion were in the hands of Mr. T. Wadsworth as secretary,and a small committee of work- men. This proved to be the most successful excursion ever held in connection with the works. The workmen employed at Messrs. P. Walker and Sons, King-st. and Dallarn Breweries had their annual excursion on Saturday. Scarborough was the place selected this year. Over 600 workmen, with their friends, left Bank Quay Station at 5 a-m., and after a pleasant run reached Scarborough in time for a late breakfast. The return journey was accomplislied in very good time, the party arriving at Warrington after midnight. The manager, Mr. Fulton-Smith, was res- ponsible for the arrangements, and he was ably assisted by Mr. Potter and Mr. John Baird,who accompanied the trip. The firm, as usual, defrayed the entire expenses of the excursion, as well as granting the day's wages aud allowance money to each employe. The employees of Messrs. Richmond and Co., Gas Stove Makers, Academy-street, Warrington, also had a trip to Blackpool, on Saturday. A special train convey- ing the trippers started from Bank Quay Station at about 6.30, Blackpool being reached shortly after nine. At half-past one the heads of the firm, together with a number of friends, partook of an excellent dinner at the Albion Hotel. After it had been done full justice to, Mr. Richmond, the managing director, said that he hoped that the excursion might become an annual event. The conditions of employer and employed could best be served by meetings of that kind. They were brought to feel that they had common duties and common pleasures, and that they had many things in common, and they wanted to find those things out— wanted to lessen, as far as they could, the points of difference, and to increase those feelings of amity which turned toil into a pleasure. (Applause.) During the short time they had been connected they toad had their reverses and successes ; but he was glad to say that the successes had predominated over the reverses. (Applause.)—Mr. Williams said he had much pleasure in seconding the remarks of Mr. Richmond. Ile trusted that would not be the last occasion on which they would meet in Blackpool. (Applause.; ;They thanked the directors very heartily far the grand treat they had afforded them. k Applause.) Mr. Ward, Mr. Hardy, and Mr. Davies also addressed the gathering, and, after a cordial vote of thanks had been passed to Mr. Rich- mond, the party dispersed. The trippers started home at about nine o'clock, Warrington being reached shortly after eleven. Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co.'s men had a trip to Blackpool, Mr. Wm. Gleave having charge of the arrangements. The men left Warrington at 8.10, and on reaching their destination dispersed them- selves in various directions, and visited the Aquarium, the botanic and Winter Gardens, the baths, the pier, Bm. There were about 900 trippers, and they enjoyed themselves immensely, having a delightful day. The following figures will give some idea of the num- ber of people who left Warrington by rail over the holi- days: At Bank Quay Station on Saturday, special trains were despatched, the following being the num- bers :—Whitecross Wireworks (two trains),l,4oo, Black- pool; Walker's Brewery, 950, Marborough ; Monks' Hall and Co., 900, BlackpoOl. ; Richmond and Co., 500, Black- pool ; and Messrs. Crosfield, 600, Southport, in addi- tion to this 300 persons were booked to Blackpo.ol, 100 , to Liverpool, 40 to Colwyn Bay and Llandudno lOO to Chester ; 150 to Frodsham ; 103 to Wigan, where a demonstration of miners was held , 100 to Daresbury ; and 60 to Lymm. On Monday the employes of Messrs. ylands, Church-st., had a trip to Blackpool, 800 making the journey. The school book- ings on Walking Day were Bold-st. 500 to Daresbury ; Silver-St., 700 to Helsby ; Wycliffe, 700 to Dunham Hill, and Holy Trinity, 900 to Frodsham. At the Central Station the traffic was correspondingly., large, the Sankey Wire Mills excursion on Saturday to Southport muster- ing 800 ; Messrs. Edelsten's 70, and Messrs. Fletcher and Co., 150. The bookings to Southport, Liverpool, and Manchester were very heavy, 1,500 trippers going to the first named place, independent of the workmen's excursions.

div.head: XIIE WIFE FORA MINISTER
div.p: XIIE WIFE FORA MINISTER

lify idea of a minister's wife, as it rests in the cradle of fancy in this old head and heart, is as follows :—She ought to be about 5 feet 4 inches in height—that is, her head would about come up to Your shoulder, if you are as tall and awkward as I think you are. She ought to have blue eyes, and kind of fluffy, light-coloured hair that always gets loose around her ears and gathers into little ringlets, and, when the wind blows, it has to be rushed out of her eyes. She ought to have red elaeeks when she runs down to the gate to say g°°d-laye when you get into your carriage, and, if You compliment her on her appearance, she ought to laugh, not giggle, and show a set of white teeth She doesn't keep inla tumbler nights. She ought to be addicted to white muslin dresses about this time of year, with a great belt around such a small waist that it looks like putting a chain 00 a humming bi.d. She ought to appear as sweet f_tiad fresh to you as the white blossoms which drop "vgn from the locust trees on your hat brim, and us.natural and unaffected. She ought to be acconi- Plashed, too, but, as you are only '25 and she 18, ,If Bhe phys the piano and loves music, and it tichances to be "Sweet Violets" or "Climbing up le golden Stair," it is all right, for she is a lossom yet, and you must wait for the fruit. Of course she will not be st. Lid or reserved, and • school girl; ill say the preacher is a fool to follow but at the same time they would give considerable of their railroad stock for those red cheeks and white teeth, but you my son, can tet.them for nothing if you understand your • uBL'ess• Then again you must expect a failure 14 her church 'work. div.head: ?Letter to the Charm
div.p: ?Letter to the Charm
WARRINGTON ELECTION.
Sir,—During the recent election, I stated publicly that I had been informed that " there were 500 voters in Warrington whoee votes could be bought for 500 ',pints of beer."

To this statement some of my Tory friends are taking exception: and it is for their information and to pre- vent misapprehension by the general public that I now make known that such statement was made by me upon the joint auraorlti:3 of a Tory Town Councillor and a leading member of the Tory party of Warrington. If a slanderous imputation has been made upon the political honesty of a portion of the electors of Warring- ton, the Tory party are to blame for it and must be held responsible.—l am yours faithfully, W. PIERPOINT, Marlfield, Grappenhall, Warrington, July 8, 1892.

Sir,—May I ask you to allow me through the medium of your columns to emphatically deny a rumour that is ,being assiduously circulated by the Conservatives that 'Mr. Latham contemplates retiring from his candidature the Knutsford division.

This rumonr appears in a local Tory piper, and is only one of a similar class of " alleged rumours " that a,re being started by a series of local Tory papers. Last week it was a Liberal candidate in another diyison of Cheshire who was about to retire, a statement that was entirely devoid of truth.

if these are samples of the accuracy of the news (?) 'disseminated by this series of Tory Journals people will *soon think that statements appearing in a Tory print are 'utterly unreliable and misleading. That is just What we want.—Yours truly,
R. IL RAYNER, Election Agent for Mr. Latham. a, GGoper-st., Manchester, June 27th, 1892.
THE ALLOTMENTS ACT, 1887.

Sir,—By means of information obtained from the Government by Mr. F. A. Charming, who has repre- sented East Northamptonshire from 1885 to 1892, the uselessness of this Act has been demonstrated in a way which supplies the strongest confirmation of our re- peated amtention, and must te zpecially mortifying to the Tory Government and its supporters, who are never tired of alleging that by its means vast 'numbers of working-men have been supplied with land. Unfortunately the information was not given until so near the time of the General Election that it greatly adds to the difficulty of making thisdamav,ing revelation as widely known as it deserves to be. We trust, how- ever, that your readers will take note of the facts which are now supplied on tha unimpeachable authority of the
Government, and which demonstrates beyond cavil, by the most determined partizan the absolute failure for practical purposes of this much-vaunted but useless measure.

Mr. Joseph Chamberlain has recently stated that 130,000 allotments have been.obtained by means of the Allotments Act, 1887. Contrast this statement with the information supplied by the Government, showing that only 2,700 allotments have been so o6tained. The following is the information supplied by the Government :—" The total area obtained by Rural Sanitary Authorities for letting in allotments by lease or purchase is 1,100 acres, let in 2,700 allotments." Yours faithfully,

THE GENERAL ELECTION.

1 Sir,—At last the eleetions are taking place, and we stand face to face with the greatest political battle known to this country. Owing to many abstentions out of respect for our present Unionist friends, we suffered defeat in 1886. Since then there have been many changes : we have been better educated to the real state of affairs, and from the lips of those who studied them, and we find the policy of Unionists nothing else but selfishness. Having condemned themselves to this state of things, I ask myself the question, have Ino interest as a workingman in our dear old country's we!- are, and why should I stoop to the dictation of those privileged few whose ambition is and always was te over-ride their poorer citizens? Lord Salisbury certainly warns you that in the event of Ireland getting Home Rule Ulster will rebel. Upon what grounds he bases his authority I know not. I can only find one, that is, with regard to Belfast ; they have a majority of three to one, that is, the Unionists over Home Rulers. This is but the solitary instance in the whole of Ireland. Who can say with any fairness and honesty that the voice of Belfast shall have the sway when the whole of the rrst of Ireland, including Ulster itself, is against the Unimist policy? If Ulster is so loyal that Home Rule must be prevented for her good pleasure and vet so disloyal thal Home Rule must not be granted for fear she rise in arms, at least a touch of humour is added as an amusing set off to the seriousness of 00 problem at issue. . . . . . . . _

1 The best safeguard against revolution is reform, and the strongest preventive against the doctrine of confisca- tion is wise concession. I ask the royalty owners of the United Kingdom in the interests of the mining and iron and steel trade industries, and of the nation, and of themselves, to be wise, and above all, remembering the progressive and democratic age in which we live, to be wise in time ; there is danger in delay. I commend all working-men to acquaint themselves with the figures, and must say in conclusion, that the question of royal- ties must be faced if this country is to hold its own with other nations who are our competitors in trade ; and if our legislators are animated by national patriotism and honesty, they will soon see the necessity for urgent and drastic action in the matter.—Yours, &c.,
A WORKING-MAN.

div.head: GOOD SUGGESTION.
div.p: A GOOD SUGGESTION.

Sir,—l think as one of the humble supporters of Dr. Houston in the late contest, we ought to show him, in some tangible form, how much we have appreciated, the brave and noble stand he has made, in trying to wrest from the hands of the beer trade the representation of Warrington. It is not for me to go into all the points as to why the seat has not been won. Suffice it to say that I shall be willing to subscribe to any object that will b 3 most fitting to mark the great respect and sympathy we have with him in the noble effort he has made. Believe me to be sincerely yours, P.S.—I enclose my card.
C. B.

Sir,—New that the Warrington election is over and we have fought and lost, may I suggest that we as a body of Liberals, which are mostly composed of the working- men of this town, join ourselves together and subscribe something towards a testimonial to our worthy candi- date for the gallant fight that he has made, in trying to wrest the seat from the stronghold of Toryism. I know there are many working-men that would gladly take up the matter and would esteem it as an honour to give their support towards this object. Let us give him something so that he will be able to show to his fellow- countrymen the esteem, honour, and affection which we have towards him as an Irish gentleman, for his honesty of purpose,and the straightforwardness that he has shown while he has been conducting this campaign. Surely we have not much cause to be discouraged at the result of the poll when we come to consider the tremendous influence that we had to contend against. Of course, there was " Wilderspool " to fight, which is always an important factor in the Warrington elections, then we had the publicans of the town working hard for ' the party that is pledged to support them in their trade; they knew that it was a case of "now or never" with them, then we had all the men of influence from the outskirts of the town arrayed in opposition to us, and, last but not least, we had a section of the party who are working daily for the uplifting of the people from the moral degradation of sin which is caused in nine cases out of ten through drunkenness. They are trying to lift them up to the high social scale of soberness and morality. These men admit that drink is the greatest curse we have to contend with as a Church, and yet, when the time comes for them to exercise their rights as citizens, for tie cause of temperance, they go and sacrifice their principles in order to vote for a party that has pledged itself to uphold the liquor trade of this town. Is it ever likely that War- rington will cease to be known as one of the most drunken towns in the country, when we send men to Parliament to represent us that have been got there by the aid of the beer barrel, which was quite evident on the day of election? All honour to our worthy candi- date for the plucky fight that he and his wife have made against such tremendous odds. When they go back to Ireland they will carry with them the good wishes and heartfelt sympathy of every true and honest Liberal, for the cause which Dr. Houston has so nobly upheld while here on behalf of his fellow country- men. We owe to him a debt of gratitude which we feel we can never repay. We acknowledge that we have been defeated, but we have this consolation, that we have been fighting for a just and honourable cause, and knowing that in the end justice will prevail. • A WORKING-MAN.
NEWTON DIVISION_ELECTION.7.MR. LEGLI
AS A GROUND LANDLORD.

Sir,—The question of the hour here is, svlio is to be returned for the Newton Division? The opinions, abili- ties, position, and general fitness of both candidates have, during the last few weeks, been prominently brought under our notice. Mr. Legh, as a ground land- lord, has not,however, been so fully brought to the front as I would like. With your permission, sir, I will give a few particulars, and will contrast the terms on which Lord Gerard leases his land with those of Mr. Legh. The terms on which land is leased are known only to a small minority of the electors, although everyone is deeply in- terested indirectly. The land is a monoply which can- not be increased like a manufactured commodity, hence it behoves the fortunate possessors not to use their feudal rights in an austere manner. Lord Gerard leases his land for 929 years at a penny per square yard all over his estate. The first year's rent is free; he does not charge for the streets, and no technical obstacles are thrown in the way, and I must not forget to state that due courtesy is shown to all inquirers. One penny per square yard is equal to say £4O per Cheshire acre per annum, and as the average price for farming land is- about £4 per Cheshire acre per annum, the leasing for the 999 years is therefore good business, 1,000 per cent. increase. Notwithstanding this apparent high price, Lord Gerard is considered the most liberal ground landlord in this district, and he is meeting the require- ments of ,the people. Mr. Legh's charges, on the other hand, very according to position. They are lid., 2d. and 21.0., per square yard, which represent say, £6O, £BO, and £lOO respec- tively per annum per Cheshire acre, being 1,500, 2,000, and 2,500 per cent. increase. Mr. Legh charges for the streets; he does not give the first year's rent free, and there are °Den also technical difficulties in the way. You will, I think, see Mr. Legh ass. ground landlord goes in for his full pound of flesh. When recording our votes we should remember this and act accordingly. It seems to me he extracts everything he possibly can out of the district, and he vii tually gives nothing in return. Then look at the conditions on which he leases land. In look- ing over one of his leases to-day, I find that, after des- cribing the boundazies and measurements,and giving the number of square yards the lease goes on to state : " Together with all appurtenances belonging to the land hereby demised, except all mines of coal and cannel and other mines and minerals whatsoever lying under the same land, with liberty at all times for tne Trustees or Trustee for the time being under the said lease with their or his assigns, or their or his under tenants, workingmen, agents and others by means of tunnels, drifts and other works extending from out of and into any muses in adjoining or other lands, but not seas to authorise the boring or digging from and through the surface of the land hereby demised to dig, sink, search for, get and carry away the said mines and minerals and dispose thereof at pleasure without making any satisfaction to the lessee or his executors, administrators and assigns and his or their tenants for any damage to the surface thereby occasioned."

Mr. Legs charges for the land about 20 times the amount he gets for it for farming land, and yet, if the buildings erected on it be damaged, or sink or fall down through the mining operations, you will see the clause I have quoted exempts him from any claim for compensa- tion, and I believe three-fourths of the people who lease land do not know such a clause—which seems to mob be a most iniquitous one,—is in the lease. Then, again, Mr. Legh is an absentee landlord, one of the greatest clams a district can have. Those who are old ecough

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 9, 1892
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 9, 1892

to remember the town in the good old days of the Wm. Mercer, who, with a few others were at the head of every good object, and contrast them with the present regime, cannot but exclaim, " Oh, for the old times to return." It was not then take a 1 and give nothing. The Lake and Castle Hill were not shut up in those days ; and if any of the inhabitants took a walk by Dean Dam, and happened to meet Mr. Mercer. they were sure of a kindly salute. He never turned them back or threa- tened to do so, neither did he say—" Do not come this way again." With regard to the Lake and Castle Hill, I am sure there is not an inhabitant in this district but feels and feels very keenly, being shut out from a privilege which the people have enjoyed and appreciated as far back as the oldest resident can remember. The attrac- tions of the Lake and Castle Hill brought a large num- ber of visitors to the town, and the hotel keepers and small tradesmen were thereby benefited. Some visitors may have been a little rough, but an extra policeman at busy times could put this right. Looking at the matter all round, I have come to the conclusion Mr. Legh has not done what he could and should have done for Newton, and that we cannot be any worse than we are by his retirement ; and for a mining constituency like this a different man altogether is re- quired.—l am, yours truly, July 6th, 1892.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE'S CAMPAIGN.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE'S CAMPAIGN.

Mr. Gladstone, continuing his election campaign, ad- dressed a great meeting of Liberals in the Theatre Royal, Glasgow, on Saturday afternoon. He pointed out that it was the main and principal current of Liberal 'minion which ought to win, and he urged the electors to vote in concurrence with this main stream. Describ- in: the situation in Ireland, he said the alarm against Home Rule was only felt in the part in which the Pro- testants formed a large majority. It was to the ascen- dency party that Irish difficulties had been due. But now they could not ignore the fact that they had the vast majority of the Irish people set upon a great national purpose, and, as he believed, actuated by a real frater- nal spirit towards their fellow-countrymen. On the other hand, they had a limited portion of the Irish peo- ple arrayed against them. They must look the division and the danger in the face, and he was confident that the more liberty they gave to the masses of the Irish people the h s risk there would be of the surrender of that liberty into the hands of ecclesiastical powers. There had, however, been a change in the Irish mind. It was more rooted than ever in its hostility to the gov- ernment inspired, modelled, and directed from Dublin Castle; but it had more confidence in the British people. The proposal which the Liberal party made in 1886, and which they trusted and believed they were now about to carry to a triumphant issue, had been to Ireland and to the political relations of the two countries a bright star amid the storm. A resolution declaring the devotion of the Liberals of Glasgow to Mr. Gladstone was enthusias- tically adopted.

div.head: MONDAYS MEETINGS.
div.p: MONDAYS MEETINGS.

Mr. Gladstone addressed meetings on Monday at Stow and Gorebridge. At the former place he said the best work of the Parliament now expired had been so im- perfect, so partial, so full of shortcomings and draw- -1 _cks that to repair that work would form a very serious part of the business of the next and perhaps eten of the following Parliament. A motion expressing 3r "'deuce in the right hon. gentleman was met by an amendment disapproving of his action with regard to the Church of Scotland and the Home Rule question. Only the or four persons supported the amend- ment. _

--Speaking at Corebridge, the right hon. gentleman said he did not think there was any room for the charge that labour questions did not receive sufficient attention from Liberal politicians. The question of registration was as much a labouring man's question as was the question of an Eight Hours Bill, and to bring the fran- chlse into an efficient qtate was one of the „,oreat objects o" the Liberal party. Again, in striving to place upon the rates the necessary expenses of elections, and to in- crease the number of labour representatives in Parlia- ment, they were fighting the battle of the working-men. It was not right that constituents should have to bear the burden of maintaining these labour representatives, who should be placed by public law in a condition of inde- pendence. He distinctly affirmed that questions of vital importance to the labouring man occupied the predom- inant place in the proclaimed creed of the Liberal party as it was now framed. Be warned workingmen against "independent labour candidates." Never in all the ' vicissitudes of politics had an independent labour candi- date got into Parliament, and he believed that the few hundreds of votes such a candidate obtained were simply deducted from the Liberal poll and put the Tory candi- date in. Passing on to the eight hours question, he thought the working classes generally had not made up their minds on the subject, and tbat they required guid- ance in coming to a conclusion. As to the miners, all admitted that eight hours below ground out of the twenty-four were enough for any human being, and he regarded the adverse vote in the Hduse of Commons as simply the expression of honest doubt whether the con- ditions had yet been fully realized under which their object could be definitely and effectually attained. It was his earnest desire that that object might ere long be brought within manageable compass, and that few ses- sions might pass without their realizing their great purpose. .

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

Mr. Gladstone addressed a meeting at Dalkeith on Tuesday evening. He began with a congratulatory reference to the results of the elections so far as they had gone. Nine seats gained upon a total of contests which was still under sixty promised, he said, what he should call a satisfactory result. To the quesuion whether he would give to Scotland a measure of Home Rule as large as that which he proposed that Parliament should give to Ireland, he answered that if Scotland deliberately thought it her duty and her right to demand that mea- sure, he had not the least doubt that it would be given. With reference to the agitation for the disestablishment of the Church of Scotland, the right hon. gentleman said that the Scotch representation havingshown the opinion of the country to demand disestablishment he bad ranked himself behind Dr. Cameron on this question. He quoted the Duke of Devonshire as aseenting to the doctrine that disestablishment was a local question for Scotland to decide for herself. He himself had been charged with having taken an improper course on this matter, and appeals and been made to the electors of Midlothian to withdraw their confidence from him on this ground. But it was the very ground upon which he claimed their confidence—the broad principle that if Scotch opinion was to prevail upon Scotch localluestions it must pre- vail upon all Scotch questions.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.

Mr. Gladstone on Wednesday addressed the fifth meeting of the electors cf Mid-Lothian at Corrstorphine. The right hon. gentleman, who was suffering from a slight cold, said that he did not see, so far as the elec- tions had gone up to the polls of Tuesday, in what way their results were to be made ccnsistent with the contin- uance of the present Administration. In reply to Mr. Balfour's contention that the claims of the Liberal party rested upon prospectuses and not upon dividends, he enumerated no fewer than twelve Liberal measures, which had been frustrated by Tory tactics. itiferring to the losses of the Liberal party at the elections, he said that they had adopted a new and ingenious system by which they returned to Parliament the very men who did not represent their views, by splitting what was a majority into two minorities, and thus letting in the very man who contradicted in every act the opinions of the majority. At the conclusion of Mr. Gladstone's speech a few dissentients put some questions to him, which were answered, and they then moved an amendment to the vote of confidence, which, however was lost, and the vote passed by an overwhelming majority.

div.head: CROFT.
div.p: CROFT.

STRAWBERRY FAlR.—This fair was held on Sunday, when there was a large attendance of visitors. Straw- berries were, however, scarce, though there was a moderate supply of cherries. The day was fine until about four o'clock, when a heavy thunderstorm burst over the village, and lasted about an hour.

RESIGNATION OF TIM RECTOR.—We understand that the Rector, the Rev. 'l'. P. Kirkwan, M.A., F.R.S., has now practically resigned the living of the parish of ' Croft, which he has held for upwards of 53 years, and he and his family will leave the parish next week for their new residence, at Bowdon, Cheshire. The rev. gentleman will, however, conduct the services in the church until his successor has been appointed. The "Liverpool Diocesan Calendar" says :—" The Rev. Thomas Penyngtop Kirkman, of Croft Rectory, near Warrington, was educated at Trinity College, Dublin ; graduated B.A. in 1834,and M.A. 1848, and also F. R. B. He was ordained deacon in 1835, and priest in 1836, by the then Bishop of Chester. He was formerly curate of Bury. from 1835 to 1837,and curate of Lymm from 1837 to 1839, after which time he became the incumbent of Christ Church, Croft, in succession to the Rev. Mr. Banning.the first incumbent of the parish. On his leav- ing the parish and resigning, the living, the Rev. Mr. Kirkman was afterwards made rector of the parish in 1845, on the division of it from the parish of Winwick. The patron of the living is the Earl of Der. The Rev. gentleman 15 the author of numerous works, including " Philosophy without Assumptions," Longman's, 1877; " The Theory of the Polyhedra," "The Theory of Groups," Sm.

At Wilts Assizes, on Tuesday, Lewis HamiltQn. alias Gurd, the murderer of Henry Richards and rolice- Sergeant Holden, was sentenced. to death. In the Divorce Division, on Tuesday, Mrs. Hawtrey, wife of tne well-known actor, sought a decree for resti- tution of conjugal rights. A decree was granted order- ing Mr. Hawtrey to take back his wife in fourteen days.

At Marlborough-st. Police Court, London, on Tuesday, a German named George Wensel was committed for trial on a charge of murdering Detective-Sergeant Joyce who was endeavouring to effect his arrest—and attempt- ng to murder Frank Rubmana and Henry Belzer.

div.head: POLICE FORCE.
div.p: THE POLICE FORCE.

The minutes of the Watch Committee contained the report of one of Her Majesty's inspectors of Constabulary which stated that the management, numbers and disci- pline of the force had been efficiently maintained. In accordance with a recommendation contained in the report, the committee have resolved to appoint one additional constable making the total number of the lorces3. . .
On the motion of the Mayor, seconded by Alderman Harrison,the minutes were confirmed.

div.head: NEW BUILDINGS.
div.p: NEW BUILDINGS.

The Street Improvement, &c. Committee recom- mended that the plans of the following buildings, &c., be approved :—Additions to printing works, Sankey-st., for Mr. James Wood ; additions to the Central Hotel, for Messrs. Peter Walker and Sons; additions to tube works at Atherton's Quay, for Messrs. Monks, Hall,and Co., Limited ; addition to house and shop in Lovely- lane and Percy-st., for Mr. Wm. On the motion of Councillor BLACKER:MST, seconded by Councillor B. T. Fatactoiram the minutes were con- firmed.
A QUESTION.

Councillor DIXON had given notice that he would ask the Chairman of the Street Improvement Committee "if any error had been made in allowing the property to be erected by Mr. William Jeffery, in Padgate-lane, and if one had been made, would he give full particulars, and who is responsible for it ?" but he was not in time, and the question was not put.

THE BOILER QUESTION.—A SCENE: EXTRAOR- DINARY LANGUAGE BY ALDERMAN BURGESS. The minutes of the Sanitary Committee contained several resolutions with regard to Longford depot. They were as follows :—(1) That the tender of Messrs. Bryan, Donkin, and Co., Limited, to supply Perret's bars for Longford at £l6O be accepted. (2) That Mrs. Beamont the owner of the land at Longford, lee requested to re- fer the question of the sale of the field adjoining the depot, ;and containing about an acre of land, to Mr. Wm. Owen, to fix the price to be paid by Corpora- tion. (3) On the recommendation of the Longford Sub- committee, the tenders of Messrs. Manlsve, Alliott, and Co., Limited, for a steel boiler, with all necessary des- tructor ironwork, for the sum of £669 be accepted. The work to be completed within eight weeks from date of contract. (4) That the Borough Surveyor be instructed to prepare drawings and specification, and obtain ten- ders for the construction of the destructor, with all necessary alterations to buildin,gs. The Committee also recommended that the tender of Mr. T. Stanley Carter sunply provender for thQ next six montia be ac- cepted. Aldefroan fiurtovA, fricnied the confirmation of the minutes with the exception of one giving an increase from 353._ to 375. 6d. a week to Inspector Church.
- Councillor Flooo, asked if they were in order in discussing this proposal which was not on the agenda. The Mayor, said it was in order as the minute was on the written minutes.

.• Alderman BURGESS, said he objected to this proposal as it was passed when there were only three members at the committee, one of whom objected, and because Inspector Church had not asked for an increase. Councillor LIEEITERD, seconded the adoption el the minutes.

Councillor FLOOD, moved that the minutes be con- firmed with the exception of that providing for the purchase of a boiler,from Messrs Manlove, Alliott, & Com- pany, Limited, for the sum of £669. He pointed out that there was a standing, order of the Coancil providing that all tenders of over £2O should be advertised for, but that in this case the order had not been complied with. The proper and legitimate course in this case would have been to ask local and other manufacturers to tender for this boiler, and, therefore, he thought the minutes should go back to the Sanitary Committee. (Hear, haar.) Councillor HILL seconded the amendment, as he thought £7OO should not be sent out of town if the articlecould be got in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BEAMAN, in supporting the amendment, said there was nothing special abeut the boiler that they need go out of town for it. It was nothing more than a plain, multi-tubular cylindrical boiler, and he thought local firms would make the boiler quite as well as the firm mentioned,while h. was of opinion that the quoted price was excessive. (Ilear,hear. He thought the thing had been done in an irregular way from beginning to end, as they were violating a standing order pf the Council in accept- ing a tender of over £2O without advertising. That matter, he could tell them, had crated quite a furore in the town. Most of the business of tha Sanitary Com- mittee did seem to ooze out, and softie members seemed to divulge alinost every pettifogging thing transacted by the Committee. (Hear, hear.) Mr. BOWNELL also supported the amendment. He thought as good a boiler could be made in town. Councillors DIX9N, Minn, and BOLTON also supported the amendment.

Councillor HEPHERD said the minute objected to was almost in the exact words of one passed by the Longford sub-Committee which was moved by Councillor Beaman and seconded by Councillor Bonnelf. How those two gentlemen could oppose it now he failed to see. Councillor 11Es.ToN supported the amendment. Alderman HARRISON : Has the ooiler been supplied ? Alderman BURGESS : Oh, no.

Councillor H. ROBERTS said that having thought the subject over in every aspect he could not do other than support the amendment. He had asked in Committee whether it was necessary to go to Manlove. Alliott, and Company,fni a specification and he was told that it was, but he had his own opinion about that. He thought their own officials ought now to be in a position to get out a specification and drawings which would put them in a positton to invite the whole world to tender. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BURGESS said a resolution ivid been passed by the Committee asking the Borough Surveyor to write to Manlove. Alliott, and Company though that resolution did net appear on the minutes. (Hear, hear.) They sent a specification, and on the proposal of Coun- cillor Iterltarrs a member of the firm came down and explained certain things. Mr. Roberts afterwards pro- posed that the matter of the boiler should be referred to to the Longford sub-Cmimittee, and the sub-Com- mittee decided, on the proposal of Councillor BEAMAN, seconded by Councillor BONNELL, to recom- mend that the tender of Messrs. Manlove, Alliott, PejCo. be accepted. The recommendation was :signed by Councillor Beaman, as Chairman of the sub-Committee, Councillor Bonnell, and himself (Alderman Burgess). -So far as he himself was concerned, he had very little to do with the matter. He contended that the standing order with regard to the tenders of over £2O had often been violated. Just the previous week they had given a large order for provender. Councillor H. ROBERTS: As convener of the commit- tee, I told Inspector Norman that it was to be adver- tised. Councillor FIEPHERD : It was adverted. Alderman BURGESS said that in that case he would withdraw what he had said. Councillor FLOOD objected to the lengthened remarks of Alderman Burgess. Alderman BURGESS said that the Council did not know the length el time wasted by Councillor Flood on the committee in trying to get salaries raised. Couhcillor FLOOD protested against personalties. Councillor H. ROBERTS said that although the applica- tion to Messrs. Manlove, Alliott and Coy, was made in Alderman Burgess's absence it was inspired by him. It was all very well for him to come there and say he had had nothing to do with it; he had been the active motive power in the whole thing. (Hear hear.) If they had not heard his voice they had seen his hand. (Hear, hear.) The faet of the matter was that the members of the Sanitary Committee were just verging upon an open revolt against the dictatorship of Alderman Burgess, and the sooner the Council understood it the better_ (Hear, lianr. . _ . . _ . . . .

Alderman BunnEss said that with regard to the last observation of Councillor Roberts that universal revolu- tion against the dictation of the Chairman of the Sani- tary ornmittec could easily be set at rest. It did not need to travel into Bewsey-street to fetch an authority to do it. He was there ready to be dismissed. Let Councillor Roberts move it, and there was an end, but do not let him sneak in here in that sort qf a way ; they could not have it. Councillor H. ROBERTS (rising to his feet) : What does Alderman Burgess mean by sneaking ? The Ittyou was about to put the amendment to the Council when— _ ... _ . .
Councillor H. ROBERTS, interposing, said " I rise to a point of order; if you rule me out of order I am finished." The MAYOR What is it ?
- Councillor H. ROBERTS: Alderman Burgess has re- ferred to me as acting the part of a sneak. The Mayog : Was it t‘ sneak "that he said ?
Alderman BURGESS (loudly) I say sneak. Councillor H. ROBERTS : I ask for the withdrawal of that ebjectiouable word. (ilear, hear.)

div.head: HAYDOCK.
div.p: HAYDOCK.

ANOTHER FLTAL COLLIERY ACCIDENT.—At noon OR Thursday, a collier named William Donald,aged nineteen years, residing at Boston, Haydock, was working at the new Boston Fit, which belongs to Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., Limited, when one of the props gave way, and the earth dislodged completely buried him, with the result that he was instantly killed. COLLIERY FATALITY.—Wm. Hughes, aged 36, of Hay dock, was., on Tuesday morning, walking through a tunnel is. the Pewfall Pit, belonging to Messrs. Richard Evans and Co, when a reap attached to to some boxes broke, and deceased being struck on the head was in- stantly killed. The unfortunate man had worked his notice out, and was leaving the service of the firm with his tools when he was killed.

div.head: LOWTON.
div.p: LOWTON.

Tun FORTHCOMING STRI7GGILE. Mr. Caleb Wright again " captains " the Liberal cause, whilst Mr. W. C. Jones is to fight for the Conservative cause. Both par- ties have set to work in real earnest, and besides pla- carding the hoardings with different kinds of literature suitable to each of the parties and appealing to the elec- tors to -"Vote for Wright" or "'Tote for Jones," they have icade a house to house canvass. The Liberals are very well organised, and are looking forward to again re-electing Mr.Wright,by a larger majority than in 1836. The election will take place on Thursday next. THE HOLIDAYS.—an Wednesday evening-of last week all the mills in the Leigh Division, in which Lowton and Pennington are included, ceased work, and only recom- menced on Tuesday morning. As on previous occasions of a similar character, excursions to several places of resort were run and were largely patronised. The vil- lage presented a rather deserted appearance, from the Thursday until Monday evening, but on Tuesday, when work 4V as recommenced, it presented its usual appear- ance.
In the Royal Western Club Regatta yesterday the Iverna beat the Meteor, by four minutes. Polling will take place in only twenty-six constituen- cies to-day (Saturday.)

Mr. Stadbolt who accomnanied the late Captain Dale in his fatal balloon ascent at the Crystal Palace, and who was seriously injured died at the Norwood Cottage Hospital. CRICKET. Surrey beat Scotland by innings, and 46 runs; Harrow second innings 116 ; Notts out for 289 ; Sussex 79 for five wickets.

SINOMAR INCIDENT AT A FARE.—An extraordinary incident was witnessed on Monday, in a farm-yard of Mr. William Dale, Rush Green, Lyinm. A large crow flew into the yard and commenced to eat. Suddenly., the bird was attacked by a cock, and a ,fierce fight ensued. The battle ended in the death of the crow, after a prolonged and severe struggle. 'Ns LOCAL BOA RD.—The monthly meeting of this Authority was held in the Board-room, Lymm. on Tues- day evening. There were present—Messrs. J. Gregson (chairman), H. Harrison, F. Swallow, B. Whitelegge, W. Brazendale, I. Perri ns, S. Appleton, J. Holt, A. Mclntyre, and the officials.—The Surveyor reported that the open drain on Rush Greeo, which has been a source of annoy- ance for some considerable time, had been covered in.— A letter was receited from the Local Government Board enclosing a letter from Mr. Underwood, in reference to a nuisance which he brought before the Board at the last meeting. It was decided to inform Mr. Underwood that the matter had been reported on by Dr. Fox, and that necessary steps would be taken. The following is a copy of a letter received from Dr. Fox on the sub- ject ;—" The matter to which reference has been made to the Local Government Board has been under the observation of the Board's officials for some time, and, in my opinion, the action which the Board has taken from time to time has been adequate to the requirements of the case.—This was all the busmess of public impor- tance. • DEATH OF A RUI4CORN FOOTBALLER.

Mr. Thomas 11. Davies,of Frederick-st., the popu- lar three-quarter back of Runcorn Football Club, died on Thursday morning at 8 o'clock. About a fortnight ago Mr. Davies contracted a cold on the cricket field, and he subsequently suffered from intlamation of the brain and typhoid fever. Mr. Davies who had been connected with the Football Club for eight years, was a most brilliant player, and last year was the .highest scorer with 31 tries. lie had represer.ted his county in several import- ant engagements. lie was personally well liked by all with whom he came in contact. He was 25 years of age. The funeral takes place at Runcorn cemetery, to-morrow, (Sunday.)

div.p: UNOPPOSED RETURNS.

Burton-on-Trent, Staffordsliire.—S. Evershed (L). North East Cork.—W. O'Brien (N). Mr. O'Brien has already been elected for Cork City. North Cork.—Flynn (N). Down, West.—Lord Arthur Hill (C). Nottinghamshire, Newark.—Vicount Newark (C). • THURSDAY'S POLLING.

Contests took place on Thursday in about 30 county constituencies, and in 36 boroughs, including coveral in the metropolis, and the important constituencies, of Hull, Leeds, Sheffield, and Dublin. The returns on Thursday night commenced with the defeat of Mr. Ritchie, President of the Local Government Board, who was supposed to hold a safe seat in St. George's in the East, but was displaced by Mr. Berm, with the substan- tial majority of 393. In Limehouse, another of the Tower Hamlets, victory also attended the Liberal cause, the former member, Mr. H. S. Samuel, who in 1888 had a majority of 892, being displaced by Mr. S. Wallace, with a majority of 110. In the same densely-populated district of London a third Liberal gain, was scored in Bow, and on the Sur- rey side of the Thames a seat was gained in Camberwell, where there is also a large working-class populatiOn. A seat was also gained in North Kensington, where Sir R. Lethbridge was returned in both 1885 and 1836 by large majorities, that for 1886 being 951. In Sheffield all the old members were re-elected, but in Hull a Liberal gain was recorded in the Eastern District.
In Leeds a desperate attempt was made to defeat Mr. H. Gladstone, who, however, retained his seat, though by a majority of only 353, agtainst 2.256 in 1886. . . .
The net Liberal gains are now 20, which is equal to forty on a division, and as the government majority at the dissolution was 68, it is now reduced to 28.
RESULTS DECLARED YESTERDAY.

Results in over thirty district borough and county constituences were declared yesterday (Friday), and the outcome will be found below. The fortunes of war ran during the day with remarkable evenness. All the same some of the results declared are of a surprising character. Tim first polls to hand showed parties "as you were " in the Wirral Division of Cheshire, and in the Denbigh Boroughs, Colonel Cotton-Jodrell and Mr. Kenyon both holding their own, the latter with a greatly reduced majority. The first break in the monotony of the returns was the loss of the Conservative -seat in West Cambridgeshire, where Sir Charles Hall, the Recorder of London, sustained defeat, a minority of 976 in 1886 being converted into a Liberal majority of 387. This was followed by a more unexpected Liberal victory in the Cricklade Division of Wiltshire, where as popular a man as Mr. Storey-Maskelyne. who had a most hand- some majority in 1886, was ousted from possession by nearly 1,000 of a majority. Liberal hopes ran high, but as the afternoon advanced there was a change in the flow of the tide, and the announcements were made of Unionist victories both in Wales and in Ireland. Sir P. Pryce Jones defeats Mr. Hanbury-Tracy in the Montgom- ery district by a majority of 118. The returns from Dublin city evoked widespread surprise, giving the representation of the Irish metropolis over entirely to the Parncllites (3) and the Unionists (1). Mr. T. D. Sullivan figures among the rejected Nationalists, and Dr. Meade. the Lord Mayor, a Parnellite., is beaten by Mr. Kenny, Q.C., a Unionist. News of this overturn of the Nation- alist party in Dublin city was followed later by the announcement of the rejection of Sir T. Esdmonde in Dublin county (South), his place being taken by the Hon. H. Plunket, Conservative. This gave a gain of three Unionists seasts on the day. North Somerset, which declared for the Liberals by a majority of 19, left the gains and losses of the day equal. The balance thus far maintained was upset between 3 and 4 o'clock' by the defeat of Mr. Justin M'Carthy in Derry City, this being another gain for the Unionists, against which must he set off a Liberal victory at Pembroke, the days' return leaving a gain of four seats to the Liberals and four to the Unionists.

Otertion abbrts. IV THE ELECTORS OF THE BOROUGH OF WARRINGT 0 N. anNTLEMEN,—I beg to tender my best thanks to those electors who supported me by their votes on Tuesday last. I also especially thank the large and enthusiastic body of friends, both Conservatives and Liberal Unionists,who worked so hard and devotedly in the great cause of the maintenence of the Union. I am happy in be lieving that my fellow-townsmen, whilst seeming my return to Parliament as successor to their old representative Sir Gilbert Greene', Mart.. ,have not forgotten his long and honorable services to the Borough. Allow me again to thank you for the great honour which you have conferred upon me, and, in doing so, to add that I though I am beholden for it—primarily to those who voted for me, lam proud to consider myself now as the epresentative of the whole of the Borough of Warrington. I am, Gentlemen, Your obedient servant, ROBERT PIIIRPOINT. St. Austin's, Warrington, July 7th 1892.

The Directors of the Manchester Trust Limited, recognis- ing the need of other facilities than those already afforded for the investment of money by way of deposit, have decided to give special attention to this class of usiness. and have taken suitable premises at No. 73, King-st., Manchester, for the purpose. They have accordingly arranged the system of secdrity set forth as follows. One of the principal features of the system they have devised is the establishment by trust deed of Specific Trust Funds, whereby, independently of the credit and resources of the Manchester Trust Well, with its subscribed capital of £500,000 and reserves, securities at least equal to the amount of the deposits must always be held absolutely charged as security to the depositors. The security thus obtained is of an absolute character, and constitutes for the depositor an insured and guaranteed in- vestment. both as to capital and income, free from all market fluctuations and vicissitudes. The depositors in each fund will be secured— (Firstly).—By a first charge upon the securities lodged in Use fund. (Secondly). —By the guarantee of the Manchester Trust Limited. The Manchester Trust Limited will receive on deposit large or small sums (not under £10). For sums of £5O or over the Trust will issue certificates in the registered name of the depositor. These will be transfer- able by Special transfer form and can he sold and transferred at any time, like consols, bonds, or shares. Deposits may be for fixed terms, at fixed rates of interest, or the Trust will issue certificates, with coupons for the interest attached payable half-yearly, which may be arranged for special dates. These notes will be re-payable any half- year on seven days' notice. Large sums of over £l,OOO nosy if desired, be treated as a special trust fund, to which specific securities May be allocated. For sums under £5O (or over that amount if desired for the convenience of the depositors) pass books will be issued, re- payment being made either at fixed dates or on seven days' notice. rrO THE ELECTORS AND NON-ELECTORS OF THE ALTRINCHAM DIVISION OF THE COUNTY OF CHESTER. G ENTLEM EN,- The Dissolution of the present Parliament termin- ates the further period of trust which you have for many ye Ira reposed in me. Always proud of your confidence, I have endeavoured con- tinually to do my duty. Very much I have enjoyed my work. Many friendships have grown up between us. greatly I have valued your counsel and adviae, with the continual expressions of your kindliness and goodwill. On the occasion. now several years-ago, of my passing my seventieth birthday, I felt it my duty to inform you that I , thought a representative younger than myself should be selected by you. In that choice you have now my earnest and hearty good wishes, Though I shall no longer have the honour of representing this important constituency, yet I shall ever feel my interests bound up with yours, and shall do all in my power to serve you. With an abiding sense of gratitude for the high honours 3 on have conferred upon me in previous Parliaments. Believe me, gentlemen, Yours truly. WILLIAM CUNLIFFE BROOKS. Barlow Hall, 28th June, 1892.

PARLIAMENTARY ELECTION, 1892. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE NORTHWICH DIVISION OF CHESHIRE, GENTLEMEN. It is nigh upon twenty years since I settled among you, and during those years I have served you in every public office to which you could elect me. There is no community in all England than can show a nobler record of work done during those years for the well- being of all the dwellers within its borders. Northwich, Runcorn, Wlnsford, and Middlewich, in taxing themselves uncle,. the Public Libraries Acts, have given to their people free access to the thoughts of the noblest minds of all time; In adoptiLg the Technical Instruction Act they have gi-en to , the young an opportunity, eagerly embraced by large and Increasing numbers, of training for hand and eye and mind, , fitting them for fuller, brighter, happier lives. Verity this is a community a man may be proud to represent. With all this work I have sympathised, and to the fullest extent of my powers have joined, with all my heart. As I have worked and voted hitherto, I pledge myself to work and vote hereafter, if again you do me the honour to return me to Westminster. As President of the Cheshire Liberal Federal Council I fully endorse the platform it has adopted, every point in which has my heartiest approval. Five years ago I asked for your suffrages as a aupp rter of Mr. Gladstone, and after a contest, during which the argu- ments for and against Home Rule were presented to you with a clearness and fniness rarely, if ever, equalled, you elected me by a majority as emphatic as it was decisive. To-day the same issue is before you, and my attitude towards it is unchanged. Once more I come before you as a devoted adherent of the statesman who, in the sixtith year of his public service—a service as unprecedented in its term as in the noble quality of its achievernents—is now and for the last time appealing to his fellow-countrymen for their approval and support. At such a time I may well be pardoned if. omitting any state- ment of my own. I refer you to his address to the Electors of Midlothian, and say that it is the dearest wish of my heart to be permitted to aid in the work of carrying to a successful Issue the reforms therein set forth, so fraught with happi- ness to millions of our fellow-men. Finally, I would ask every man in the Northwich Division to remember on the Polling Day that a vote given for me is a last vote for arr. Gladstone—a last opportunity of rewarding for a life's service the man who has laboured so long, so stead- fastly,and so successfully for the people's good. I remain, Gentlemen Your faithful servant, JOHN TOMLINSON BRUNNER. Winnington Old Hall, Northwich, 30th June, 1892.

TO THE ELECTORS OF THE WIDNES DIVISION OF SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE. I GENTLENEN,—At the unanimous request of the District Liberal Councils. I have consented to stand as the Liberal Candidate for the Widnes Division at the General Election ; the time has now come te ask for your votes and interest. As I have always lived in Widnes, I am well-known to most of you, and since my selection by the District Councils I have had many opportunities of explaining to you my views on the political questions of the day. If elected as your representative in Parliament, I shall give a hearty support to Mr. Gladstone's Irish Policy, for I be- lieve that in granting Home Rule to Ireland we shall perform an act of justice which will bring peace and happiness to that country. I feel confident that Home Rule can be granted to ths Irish nation not only without the slightest danger of " separation" or " disruption of the Empire," but to the great advantage of the United Kingdom. I am in favour of the Dis estab3stiment and Disendow- ment of the Church in Wales, because they are desired by the Welsh people, and because I believe it to be an intolerable injustice t°3 maintain the Church of the minority as an Established Church against the will of the large majority. It is my earnest intention to assist so far as I can in ameliorating the conditions of labour, and In removing legis- lative obstacles which hinder the working classes in their eifforts to improve their lot. With.these objects in view lam in favour of an extension of the Factory Acts, of the insertion in all contracts issued by the Government or public bodies of provisions against " sweating." of the amendment of the Employers' Liability Act, and of a reform of the Poor Laws. The hours of labour when they are excessive should be shortened. I shall, if elected, support the Miners' Eight Hours Bill, and I will give most careful consideration to legis- lative proposals of a similar nature. The welfare of the community requires a reform of the Licensing Laws. lam in hearty agreement with the prin- ciple of the Direct Veto, and ash in favour of Sunday Closing and the transference of the lieensing powers to a popularly elected representative body. The interest which I have always taken in Educational matters is well known to you. I look for an extension of our system of National Education, so that the children of the poor, no less than those of the rich, may receive the highest possible training wherever they show the necessary capacity for it. The system of Technical Instruction, in my opinion, also requires to be greatly improved and developed. I approve of a thorough reform of the Land Laws, to obtain amongst other things, the repeal of the laws of primogeniture ° and entail, the freedom of sale and transfer, and the en• franchisement of leaseholders. The condition of the rural population demands immediate attention, and I am in favour of the creation of District and Parish Councils endowed with compulsory powers of acquir- ing land for allotment', and public Durosei ftP, fair price; and entrusted wit thr!vninageine.i f,•f. litl atiaird. If o.t.letect, I shall support proposals for the reform of the Registration Laws and the adoption of the principle of "One Man One Vote " ; the Payment of Members of Parliament and the official expenses of Returning Officers. lam also in favour of shorter Parliaments and the " mending or ending" of the House of Lords. Changes in the Incidence of Taxation are imperatively needed to secure the taxation of ground values and mining royalties, the equalization of the death duties, the division of ' rates between owner and occupier, and a "free breakfast table." If you do me the honour of returning me as your represen- tative to the House of Commons I shall endeavour to the best of my ability, to promote the welfare of our country, and to further and proleC;, the interests of tho electors of the Widnes Divis'on.—l am, Gentlemen, your Obeilent Ser- vant, -Appleton House, H. WADE DEACON. Widnes. lune. 1892.

CROSBY AND WALKER'S GREAT SUMMER SALE. CATALOGUES FREE BY POST. Messrs. F. WILKINSON AND CO.'S Curtain Factory, the Anglo-Scotian Mills, Peeston, near Nottingham, of which we gave several illustrations and an extended notice in our last Autumn Number, was distroyed by fire at an early hour on Saturday, the 30th ult. The estimated damage amounts to £lOO 000, which is partly covered by insurance. The fire is said to have been caused by the flame of a candle, which a workman was holding, lighting the cotton on a frame as he was adjusting the threads. Owing to the inflammable nature of the stock, the flames spread with great rapidity, and not- withstanding the efforts of the brigades, the whole of the five- storeyed wing was soon alight, and was rapidly reduced to ruins. An enormous stock of lace curtains, curtain machinery, and an entire lithographic plant were contained 1 in the building. Some adjacent property caught fire, and was with difficulty saved. Several hundred hands will be for time thrown out of employment. Exactly six years prev- iously to the day Messrs. Wilkinson's Beeston factory was the scene of a similar conflagration. It was then that the Borrowish Mill was stcured, and this, with the old Chilwell Mill, are both running to their fullest extent. Mess's. Wilkinson, although greatly inconvenienced by the fire, will be in a position to WI their customers' orders.
